chunks.title: FAQ: Is YakkamonWorld the official Yakkamon website?
chunks.text:
Q: Is YakkamonWorld the official Yakkamon website?
A: No. The official pre-registration site is yakkamon.com, and the official documentation is at docs.yakkamon.com. This site is a fan-run portal that explains things in plainer language and isn't affiliated with the Yakkamon team or SunflowerLand.

chunks.title: FAQ: What is Yakkamon?
chunks.text:
Q: What is Yakkamon?
A: A creature collector crossed with idle farming. You hunt and catch wild monsters out in the world, then put them to work farming, gathering and producing around the clock — so your farm keeps running while you're away. You can craft gear and take other trainers on in the arena.

chunks.title: FAQ: Who makes Yakkamon?
chunks.text:
Q: Who makes Yakkamon?
A: Thought Farm, the team behind Sunflower Land: over 1 million players, more than 100 open-source contributors, and over five years of building live and in the open.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is Yakkamon free to pre-register?
chunks.text:
Q: Is Yakkamon free to pre-register?
A: Yes. Season 0 pre-registration is free and needs nothing but an email address. You don't need a wallet, and you don't need to be an existing Sunflower Land player.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I need to be an existing Sunflower Land player?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I need to be an existing Sunflower Land player?
A: No. Yakkamon is a completely new game and anyone can pre-register with just an email address. Sunflower Land players are welcome — your Bumpkin Level decides when your access code unlocks — but nothing about Sunflower Land is a requirement.

chunks.title: FAQ: Which network does Yakkamon run on?
chunks.text:
Q: Which network does Yakkamon run on?
A: Ronin, a blockchain built for games with much lower fees than networks like Ethereum. It's also where the free mint happens, on the Ronin Launchpad from 14 September.

chunks.title: FAQ: What is the official Yakkamon website?
chunks.text:
Q: What is the official Yakkamon website?
A: yakkamon.com is the only official Yakkamon website. The official X account is @yakkamon_game and the official documentation is at docs.yakkamon.com.

Yakkamon will never ask you for a seed phrase or a private key. Pre-registration only ever asks for an email address. Anyone asking for anything more — in a DM, a giveaway or a lookalike site — is trying to steal from you. This site (yakkamonworld.com) is an unofficial fan portal and will never ask you for anything at all.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is there a video version of any of this?
chunks.text:
Q: Is there a video version of any of this?
A: Yes. We run a YouTube channel at youtube.com/@YakkamonWorld with short 2–3 minute explainers covering pre-registration, access codes, the free mint and each gameplay system. Every episode is indexed on our videos page, each one linked to the written version — the same ground as this site, for anyone who'd rather watch than read. The channel is also linked from the Community page.

Two to start with: What Is Yakkamon? The 2-Minute Explainer ↗ covers the game, the team behind it and why pre-registration matters. How To Pre-Register ↗ walks through signing up, and the verification step you need done before the 10 September whitelist snapshot. For the mint itself, the 9/1 dev stream recap ↗ covers the waves, the snapshot and the calendar in four minutes.

chunks.title: FAQ: Where can I ask a question that isn't answered here?
chunks.text:
Q: Where can I ask a question that isn't answered here?
A: We run an unofficial Telegram channel and chat group. The channel posts pre-registration updates as tiers unlock; the chat group is where you can ask anything, and our access bot will tell you your access date if you send it your Bumpkin Level. Join at t.me/YakkamonWorld, or see the Community page for all the links.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I need to know about crypto, or own a wallet, to take part?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I need to know about crypto, or own a wallet, to take part?
A: Not to pre-register — that only needs an email address. A wallet only becomes relevant if you want to take part in the Free Mint from 14 September, since that's an on-chain claim. If you plan to do that, you'll want a Ronin-compatible wallet set up beforehand. The Genesis Monster airdrop at launch doesn't require any action or wallet setup on your part — it's based purely on your final leaderboard rank.

chunks.title: FAQ: What's the difference between my rank, my tier, and my wave?
chunks.text:
Q: What's the difference between my rank, my tier, and my wave?
A: Three words that get used close together, so they're easy to blur:

Trainer number (your rank) — your exact position on the leaderboard, like #4,521. It's permanent, and it's what every other reward is calculated from.

Tier — a points milestone you've passed on the reward track (for example, 1,000 points unlocks Tier I). Passing a tier unlocks its reward on its own.

Wave — the batch you're let into the game with when early access opens. Higher ranks are in earlier waves.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does my rank actually get me?
chunks.text:
Q: What does my rank actually get me?
A: Your trainer number decides two things at once: which Genesis egg (the egg your founding monster hatches from) you're given, and which wave you play in. Here's the full ladder:

RANK 1–3

🌩 Storm + ⬜ Echo

WAVE 1

RANK 4–10

🌩 Storm + 👻 Ghost

WAVE 1

RANK 11–50

🌩 Storm — the newest and hardest to earn

WAVE 1

RANK 51–250

⬜ Echo

WAVE 1

RANK 251–500

👻 Ghost

WAVE 1

RANK 501–2,000

🌸 Bloom

WAVE 1–2

RANK 2,001–5,000

Rare Egg

WAVE 2

RANK 5,001–20,000

Early access — no airdrop at this rank

WAVE 3

RANK 20,001–100,000

Early access — no airdrop at this rank

WAVE 4

RANK 100,001+

❌ No early access — you wait for full launch

—

🌩⬜👻🌸 Genesis Legendaries — top 2,000
✨ Rare Egg — ranks 2,001–5,000
Waves 1–4 — who gets in first

Twice as many Legendaries. Legendary monsters used to stop at rank 1,000. They now run all the way to rank 2,000. Storm is new and sits above the old top tier — only the top 50 are airdropped one, and the top 10 receive Storm plus a second Genesis Legendary.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does my rank actually get me?
chunks.text:
Every band held or improved — and two names changed. Echo is the monster that used to be Legendary Egg A; the 251–500 monster (Egg B, then Bloom) is now Ghost; the 501–2,000 monster (Egg C, then Tide) is now Bloom. Storm was added above the ladder rather than pushing anyone down it. Utilities are published: Storm speeds up Yakkamon in a large area, Echo doubles output nearby, Ghost keeps neighbours at full stamina, Bloom regenerates HP in combat. The table →

There is a hard cutoff at rank 100,000. Pre-registering does not qualify you for early access on its own — you have to finish inside the top 100,000 on points. Everyone below that waits for full launch.

Of those who do get in, the top 5,000 also receive a Genesis Monster NFT, and within that the top 2,000 get a Genesis Legendary.

chunks.title: FAQ: When do I find out my rank?
chunks.text:
Q: When do I find out my rank?
A: Trainer numbers and tiers are revealed shortly before early access opens in November or December 2026. Until then the leaderboard is still moving, so a rank you hold today isn't locked in — and neither is anyone else's.

One exception: the free mint takes its own snapshot of the leaderboard on 10 September. That rank decides your mint waves and nothing else — the airdrop and your early-access wave are still settled at the final lock.

chunks.title: FAQ: Does signing up early guarantee me a good rank?
chunks.text:
Q: Does signing up early guarantee me a good rank?
A: No, and this is the single most common misunderstanding. Signing up early sets your Monster Egg tier (which starting egg you get) and nothing else. It doesn't reserve a leaderboard position and it doesn't guarantee early access. Every rank is won on points.

chunks.title: FAQ: How do I actually earn points?
chunks.text:
Q: How do I actually earn points?
A:
Daily nurture — tap your egg 3 times, once a day. Pays 6 points rising to 10 a day at a 30-day streak, with a 36-hour grace period — though that only covers a whole missed day if you nurture after 12:00 UTC.

Quests — link your Discord and Twitter/X accounts, post weekly, and take part in the community.

Referrals — points for every friend who signs up through you.

The free mint — minting on the Ronin Launchpad from 14 September earns 250 points (see section 4).

$FLOWER deposits — open now (since 9 Aug, 8:00 PM ET / 10 Aug UTC). Points are boosted two ways: a weekly multiplier paying 3× through the opening week and falling 0.2× each week until it rests at 1× (week 3 held at 2.8× after the week-2 pause), plus a size bonus rated per deposit that doubles at every step — +10% at 50 $FLOWER up to +80% at 50,000. The full schedule →

Daily actions compound: streaks and referrals stack over time, so an early start is genuinely harder for someone else to overtake later.

The exact numbers: referrals pay 75 each — your first five instantly, and after that only once your friend has linked a wallet and deposited 100 $FLOWER — the free mint pays 250, and one-time quests (Discord, X, wallet) pay 10 each. Ninety days of perfect nurture is roughly 856 points. Full leaderboard guideline →

chunks.title: FAQ: Is there more than one leaderboard?
chunks.text:
Q: Is there more than one leaderboard?
A: Yes, and they pay out completely differently:

Final ranking — your all-time points total. It never resets and pays out once, at early access in November or December 2026. This is what decides your trainer number, your Genesis Monster and your wave.

Weekly ranking — based only on the points you earn that week, and it resets every week. It pays a resource box, food box, raffle ticket and loot box, every week until early access.

Most people only play the first one. The weekly board is a fresh contest each week against everyone else's weekly total — not their all-time one — which makes it far more winnable. How to play both at once →

chunks.title: FAQ: What time of day should I nurture?
chunks.text:
Q: What time of day should I nurture?
A: After 12:00 UTC, and then keep to roughly that time. The game day rolls over at midnight UTC, and separately you get 36 hours from your last nurture before the streak resets. Those two clocks only line up in your favor in the second half of the UTC day: nurture at 08:00 and your window expires partway through tomorrow, so a missed day still breaks the run; nurture at 20:00 and it stretches past tomorrow entirely.

Noon UTC is 8:00 AM in New York, 1:00 PM in London, 8:00 PM in Manila and 9:00 PM in Tokyo — so in the Americas you're usually fine already, while further east a morning nurture leaves you no slack at all. The full reasoning →

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I reach a Legendary rank without depositing $FLOWER?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I reach a Legendary rank without depositing $FLOWER?
A: The top 50 — the Storm band — is realistically a paid bracket, since a large deposit made in the opening week is worth tens of thousands of points and no amount of free play matches that. Below it things are genuinely contestable, and the Legendary line now sits at rank 2,000 rather than 1,000. Referrals pay 75 points each and are uncapped — your first five instantly, and after that only once your friend has linked a wallet and deposited 100 $FLOWER of their own. Roughly 66 valid referrals are worth as much as a 5,000 $FLOWER deposit — but past your fifth, each one now depends on a friend spending money. A free player with real reach can compete for the 101–1,000 Legendary bands; without it, aim at the top 5,000 where the Rare Egg A band starts. The free-to-play guide →

chunks.title: FAQ: What if I'm not Bumpkin Level 100+, or don't play Sunflower Land at all?
chunks.text:
Q: What if I'm not Bumpkin Level 100+, or don't play Sunflower Land at all?
A: You're not shut out. Your Bumpkin Level only affects when your access code unlocks during pre-registration — it has nothing to do with your leaderboard rank. Lower tiers opened automatically day by day, and anyone can now use a referral code from another trainer. See the access code walkthrough.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is the Genesis Monster tradable, or is it locked to my account?
chunks.text:
Q: Is the Genesis Monster tradable, or is it locked to my account?
A: Fully tradable. Genesis Monsters arrive with in-game XP already on them, they're revealed live when early access launches, and the airdropped copies will never be minted again. The wider Genesis collection is bigger than the airdrop, though: the Yakkapedia puts total supply at 75 Storm, 275 Echo, 400 Ghost and 2,000 Bloom, with the copies not airdropped going into the free mint, a trainer raffle and future events.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does signing up early actually get me?
chunks.text:
Q: What does signing up early actually get me?
A: One thing: your Monster Egg tier. Eggs are handed out in registration order, and once a tier fills up it's gone.

Sign-up position | Monster Egg |

1 – 10,000 | 💎 Platinum |

10,001 – 25,000 | 🥇 Gold |

25,001 – 50,000 | 🥈 Silver |

50,001 – 100,000 | 🥉 Bronze |

100,001 – 500,000 | Basic |

A Platinum egg is mainly a cosmetic and early-collectible difference — the team has confirmed the sign-up tiers function that way rather than as a power difference. Every monster works as a worker for you regardless of which egg it came from. It is not a head start on the leaderboard and carries no claim on early access.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does "the leaderboard locks" mean?
chunks.text:
Q: What does "the leaderboard locks" mean?
A: It’s the moment your rank stops moving and the airdrop is settled. The team’s wording is that you have to earn your rank and hold it until the leaderboard locks — and that once it does, the airdrop is closed for good.

Two things follow from that, and they matter more than most people realise:

Reaching a rank isn’t enough — you have to still be there at the end. Sitting in the top 2,000 today guarantees nothing if others pass you before the lock.

It only happens once. There is no second airdrop, no later window, and no way to buy in afterwards.

The lock now has a position, if not a date. The official Important Dates page puts it one week before early access launch, with rewards sent out three days later. Launch itself is November or December, so the exact day is still to be announced — and the team has said the leaderboard will be hidden as launch approaches so it can’t be gamed on the final day. Practically: don’t plan to coast and sprint at the end, because you won’t be able to see the finish line.

chunks.title: FAQ: I signed up late — am I locked out of the airdrop?
chunks.text:
Q: I signed up late — am I locked out of the airdrop?
A: No. The team is explicit about this: the leaderboard is points-based, so a trainer who signs up today and plays daily can pass someone who signed up on day one and stopped showing up.

Sign-up date decides your Monster Egg tier and nothing else. Every airdrop position is earned on points, and there is no sale and no way to buy in — the Monster NFTs are only ever awarded by leaderboard rank.

chunks.title: FAQ: What are the four Genesis Legendaries?
chunks.text:
Q: What are the four Genesis Legendaries?
A: They're the founding set of Legendary monsters, earned on leaderboard rank alone. Since the September docs update they also have utilities and supplies, and two of the names changed — the old "Legendary Egg A/B/C" labels are long retired, and so now is Tide:

Monster | Ranks | Airdropped | Total supply | Utility |

🌩 Storm | 1 – 50 | 50 | 75 | Yakkamon within range work 2× as fast (large AOE) |

⬜ Echo | 1–3, 51 – 250 | 203 | 275 | Yakkamon within range produce double resources (small AOE) |

👻 Ghost | 4–10, 251 – 500 | 256 | 400 | Always at maximum stamina on the farm (small AOE) |

🌸 Bloom | 501 – 2,000 | 1,500 | 2,000 | Regenerates a % of Max HP every combat turn |

Figures are from the official Yakkapedia. The airdrop totals 5,010 Monster NFTs across 5,000 trainers — the extra ten are the second monsters going to ranks 1–10. (The docs' 256 for Ghost is one short of the 257 the bands imply; we read it as a rounding slip.) The full breakdown, including free-mint and raffle copies →

chunks.title: FAQ: What happened to Tide?
chunks.text:
Q: What happened to Tide?
A: It was renamed. The 12 August ladder ran Storm / Echo / Bloom / Tide. The official Yakkapedia and airdrop table now run Storm / Echo / Ghost / Bloom: the 251–500 monster that used to be called Bloom is now Ghost, and the 501–2,000 monster that used to be called Tide is now Bloom. On the free-mint stream the team said the names don't change what the monsters do — "they're functionally the same things, they have the same boosts, we're just renaming them to match our types". If you were in line for a Tide, you are in line for a Bloom. Older articles on this site that say Tide are left as they were published, with the new name noted where it matters.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is Storm better than the others?
chunks.text:
Q: Is Storm better than the others?
A: Storm is the exception to the "all the same power level" rule. The team describes it as the newest monster in the set and the hardest to earn — it sits above everything else, and the only way to be airdropped one is to finish in the top 50. The Yakkapedia shows why: Storm's utility (Yakkamon within range work twice as fast) is the only one with a large AOE, covering a whole section of your farm, and only 75 exist.

Echo, Ghost and Bloom differ in role rather than raw strength. Echo doubles the resources of the few Yakkamon working beside it, Ghost keeps its neighbours at full stamina so they never sleep, and Bloom is the odd one out — a combat passive that regenerates HP every turn, which the team called "absolutely busted" on a tanky monster.

The top 10 get two. Ranks 1–3 receive Storm and Echo; ranks 4–10 receive Storm and Ghost. Everyone from 11 to 2,000 receives a single Genesis Legendary. Storm plus Echo is also the combo the team confirmed multiplies — twice the speed on double the output.

chunks.title: FAQ: Did anyone lose out in the 12 August change?
chunks.text:
Q: Did anyone lose out in the 12 August change?
A: No band did. Every rank either kept the monster it was in line for — with its utility lifted — or moved up into a better one. Storm was added above the ladder rather than pushing anyone down it, and the Legendary bracket doubled in size, running to rank 2,000 where it used to stop at 1,000.

The band that gained most is 1,001–2,000, which was in line for a Rare Egg and now receives a Genesis Legendary — called Tide at the time, renamed Bloom in the September docs. Our full analysis →

chunks.title: FAQ: How is this different from the sign-up egg tiers?
chunks.text:
Q: How is this different from the sign-up egg tiers?
A: Completely different systems, and they get confused constantly.

Sign-up egg tiers (Platinum, Gold, Silver, Bronze, Basic) come from when you registered, and the team has said they’re mainly cosmetic and early-collectible.

The four Genesis Legendaries (Storm, Echo, Ghost, Bloom) come from your points rank, are limited to the top 2,000 trainers, and are genuine Legendary monsters.

One is decided the day you sign up and matters least. The other is earned over months. The full rank ladder →

chunks.title: FAQ: What is the egg counter I keep seeing?
chunks.text:
Q: What is the egg counter I keep seeing?
A: It tracks Monster Egg tiers only — how many Platinum sign-up slots are left. That is all it tracks. It is not an early-access counter, and it is not counting down Genesis Monster NFTs. When a tier fills, the only thing you've missed is that egg type; everything that actually decides your rank is still wide open.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is my Monster Egg an NFT?
chunks.text:
Q: Is my Monster Egg an NFT?
A: No. It's an in-game item — nothing to mint, nothing to claim, no wallet needed. It simply appears on your farm the first time you log into Yakkamon.

chunks.title: FAQ: I signed up late. Am I out of the running?
chunks.text:
Q: I signed up late. Am I out of the running?
A: Not at all. A Basic egg holder who earns points every day will finish above a Platinum egg holder who signed up and never came back. Rank is earned, not reserved.

chunks.title: FAQ: How do referral points work — and can they be taken away?
chunks.text:
Q: How do referral points work — and can they be taken away?
A: Yes, they can. Referrals are reviewed before rewards are finalized, so referral points stay provisional until then. A referral only counts if the friend is a real, separate person with a verified account who actually takes part in pre-registration. Each counting referral is worth 75 points. Your first five referrals are instant. From the sixth onward, your friend must link a wallet and deposit 100 $FLOWER of their own before the points land — linking Discord and X no longer verifies a referral, because bot accounts cleared that bar in bulk. A sign-up alone pays nothing. The rule change →

These don't count:

Unverified accounts — sign-ups that never complete verification.

Multi-accounting — referring yourself with alt accounts, throwaway emails, or shared devices and wallets.

Bots and automation — bulk or scripted sign-ups.

Inactive sign-ups — accounts made purely to farm a referral bonus, with no real activity.

Removed referrals are deducted from your total, which can lower your trainer number and your tier. Serious or repeated abuse can disqualify an account from pre-registration rewards entirely.

chunks.title: FAQ: How does the reward track work?
chunks.text:
Q: How does the reward track work?
A: It runs on a 7-day cycle rather than fixed points milestones. Every week a new list of rewards appears for you to claim; claimed items go into your inventory and stay there, and you'll be able to claim them in-game once you have early access. Each new list replaces the last, so anything left unclaimed is gone — check back weekly.

chunks.title: FAQ: What exactly is a Genesis Monster?
chunks.text:
Q: What exactly is a Genesis Monster?
A: A Genesis Monster is one of 5,000 founding creatures handed out free when early access opens through the Genesis airdrop (the official docs also call this the Trainer Point airdrop or the NFT airdrop — all three names mean the same thing), as a thank-you to players who backed Yakkamon before launch. There is no sale, no second window, and no way to buy in afterwards. Once the leaderboard locks, the Genesis line closes permanently.

chunks.title: FAQ: Are they just collectibles, or do they actually do something?
chunks.text:
Q: Are they just collectibles, or do they actually do something?
A: They're playable creatures that sit at the top end of the power curve — not cosmetic items. Three things make them worth having:

Born with XP — each one arrives already carrying in-game experience, so you start ahead of anyone who caught their first creature on launch day.

Fully tradable — hold it, build your roster around it, or trade it on-chain. It's yours.

Specialized — and now named. Storm, Echo and Ghost carry farm auras (work faster, produce double, never tire, for Yakkamon within range); Bloom carries a combat passive (HP regeneration every turn). How utilities and auras work →

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I get to choose which one I get?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I get to choose which one I get?
A: No — your rank band decides the species, and the Yakkapedia now tells you which: Storm for ranks 1–50, Echo for 51–250, Ghost for 251–500, Bloom for 501–2,000, with the top 10 taking Storm plus a second. What you won't know until launch is the individual: at early access there's a Genesis Reveal Event where every Genesis Monster is unwrapped at once, with its own stat roll.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is the airdrop first come, first served?
chunks.text:
Q: Is the airdrop first come, first served?
A: No. The 5,000 Genesis Monster NFTs go to the top 5,000 trainers on the points leaderboard — not the first 5,000 to sign up. Registering on day one earns you nothing here; points do.

chunks.title: FAQ: So what decides whether I get one at all?
chunks.text:
Q: So what decides whether I get one at all?
A: Only your final leaderboard rank on points:

Leaderboard rank (by points) | Airdrop |

1 – 2,000 | Genesis Legendary (Storm, Echo, Ghost or Bloom by band) |

2,001 – 5,000 | Rare Egg |

5,001+ | Not eligible for the airdrop |

This is not first come, first served. Monster NFTs are awarded on points, not on how early you signed up. Signing up doesn't reserve one — you have to earn the rank and hold it until the leaderboard locks. There is no sale, no second window, and no way to buy in later.

Late to pre-registration? You're not locked out. A trainer who signs up today and grinds daily can pass someone who signed up on day one and stopped showing up.

chunks.title: FAQ: What is the free mint?
chunks.text:
Q: What is the free mint?
A: On 14 September a free mint of 10,000 hidden Genesis monster NFTs opens on the Ronin Launchpad. It runs in five whitelisted waves over five days, each open to a different slice of the leaderboard. Mint one and you're holding a sealed Yakkamon that is revealed on 14 October. It costs nothing beyond the network fee (gas, in RON) — there's no mint price. The full guide → · The wave table →

chunks.title: FAQ: When exactly, and what are the waves?
chunks.text:
Q: When exactly, and what are the waves?
A: One wave a day from 14 September, each with its own supply and its own list:

Wave | Date | Supply | Who |

1 | 14 Sept | 1,000 | Top 1,000 trainers — guaranteed, at your own pace |

2 | 15 Sept | 3,000 | Ranks 1–10,000 with a 5 $FLOWER minimum deposit |

3 (Ronin) | 16 Sept | 2,000 | Active Ronin gamers, on a list the Ronin team is building |

4 | 17 Sept | 5,000 | Ranks 1–20,000 with a 5 $FLOWER minimum deposit; ends early if the 10,000 sell out |

5 | 18 Sept, 00:00 UTC | Remaining | Ranks 1–50,000 |

A further 1,500 are sent manually as an ecosystem airdrop — 1,000 to top Ronin spenders, 500 to $FLOWER ecosystem players — probably a week after the mint and before the reveal. The dates after Wave 1 were described as tentative on the stream.

chunks.title: FAQ: How many are there?
chunks.text:
Q: How many are there?
A: 10,000 hidden NFTs — 68 Legendaries (3 Storm, 5 Echo, 10 Ghost, 50 Bloom), 50 Rares and 9,882 Uncommons. Each wave has a set supply and, as Adam put it, "there is usually more people than that supply", so outside the guaranteed top-1,000 wave it is fastest-click and not everyone gets one. The wave supplies add up to 11,000 against a 10,000 collection, so later waves only get what earlier ones left — Wave 4 may be where it sells out.

This is a change. The earlier docs described a verified whitelist with one mint per trainer and no race. The current plan is rank-gated waves with fixed supply, and speed matters in every wave except the first. Be online with gas in your wallet when your wave opens.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I need a good rank to take part?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I need a good rank to take part?
A: You need to be inside the top 50,000 on the leaderboard to be in any wave, and the higher you are the more waves you're on the list for, because the brackets nest. The rank that counts is your rank at the 10 September snapshot.

Rank on 10 Sept | Waves | Needs 5 $FLOWER? |

1–1,000 | 1, 2, 4, 5 — Wave 1 guaranteed | For Waves 2 and 4 |

1,001–10,000 | 2, 4, 5 | For Waves 2 and 4 |

10,001–20,000 | 4, 5 | For Wave 4 |

20,001–50,000 | 5 only | No |

50,001+ | None from the leaderboard — Wave 3 only if Ronin's gamer list includes you | — |

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I need to do anything before mint day?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I need to do anything before mint day?
A: Four things, all before 10 September:

Be pre-registered and verified — the whitelists are built from the leaderboard inside yakkamon.com.

Be at the rank you want. The snapshot on 10 September fixes which waves you're in.

Deposit at least 5 $FLOWER if you're counting on Wave 2 or Wave 4. It's withdrawable; it exists to make multi-accounting expensive.

Connect a Ronin wallet and hold some RON for gas.

Then be online when your wave opens on the Ronin Launchpad. Mint day, step by step →

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I mint more than once?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I mint more than once?
A: Yes — one NFT per wave per account, and you can mint in every wave you qualify for. A top-1,000 trainer with 5 $FLOWER deposited is on the list for Waves 1, 2, 4 and 5. The team said this directly: the higher up the leaderboard you are, the more chances you get.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does the 5 $FLOWER deposit do?
chunks.text:
Q: What does the 5 $FLOWER deposit do?
A: It's the eligibility condition for Waves 2 and 4, added at the Ronin team's suggestion to stop multi-accounting — free mints "get botted heavily" without a cost like this. The deposit stays yours: withdrawable, or spendable in the game whenever you want. More than 3,000 trainers in the top 10,000 had already met it when the stream aired.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I get to see what I minted?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I get to see what I minted?
A: Not straight away. You're minting blind — all 10,000 stay sealed until 14 October, when every one is revealed at once. That's before the leaderboard finalises, so you'll know what you're holding while you can still climb. Hidden NFTs are tradable before the reveal as well as after.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is there anything rare in there?
chunks.text:
Q: Is there anything rare in there?
A: Yes. Hidden in the 10,000 are 68 Genesis Legendaries — 3 Storm, 5 Echo, 10 Ghost and 50 Bloom — and 50 Rares; the other 9,882 are Uncommons, described in the Yakkapedia as normal working Yakkamon. That's roughly a 0.7% chance of a Legendary per mint. The old docs' figure of five Legendaries is out of date.

chunks.title: FAQ: Why bother if I'm already pre-registered?
chunks.text:
Q: Why bother if I'm already pre-registered?
A: Because it's a free NFT from the collection that is the Yakkamon collection — when new Yakkamon are released into the wild they appear in this same collection — and it's tradable from the day you mint it, seven weeks before early access. And minting earns 250 pre-registration points — more than three referrals for one click — so it feeds straight back into your airdrop band and early-access wave.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I need to mint to get my Monster Egg?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I need to mint to get my Monster Egg?
A: No — the two are completely unrelated. Your Monster Egg is already yours from signing up and appears on your farm automatically. The free mint is a separate, optional event for a different thing entirely: an NFT monster.

chunks.title: FAQ: What do I do with it once I've minted?
chunks.text:
Q: What do I do with it once I've minted?
A: Hold it, trade it on the Ronin marketplace, or wait for the 14 October reveal. A few weeks after that — or whenever you get game access — you can deposit minted monsters into Yakkamon and play with them.

The free mint and the Genesis airdrop are not the same thing. The mint is 10,000 hidden monsters, claimed by you in rank-gated waves from 14 September. The airdrop (also called the Trainer Point airdrop) is 5,010 monsters to the top 5,000 on final rank, landing automatically three days after the leaderboard locks. You can receive both — see section 4.

chunks.title: FAQ: What is the gas fee, and what is it paid in?
chunks.text:
Q: What is the gas fee, and what is it paid in?
A: It's on the Ronin blockchain, so gas is in RON. How much, and whether the Ronin team sponsors any of it, wasn't known on the stream — Craig explained that on the Ronin Launchpad it's Ronin's own contract that calls the mint, so the exact flow was still being confirmed with them. Hold a small amount of RON and check the Launchpad page when it goes up.

chunks.title: FAQ: I deposited on Base — do I need a Ronin wallet?
chunks.text:
Q: I deposited on Base — do I need a Ronin wallet?
A: Yes. Base is fine for deposits — the points count the same, and a 5 $FLOWER deposit on Base satisfies the Wave 2 and 4 condition — but the mint happens only on Ronin, through the Ronin Launchpad. If you plan to mint, connect a Ronin-compatible wallet and hold some RON before your wave opens; a Base wallet cannot mint, however verified the trainer behind it is.

chunks.title: FAQ: How do I actually mint on the day?
chunks.text:
Q: How do I actually mint on the day?
A: Buy a little RON for gas days ahead. On the day, open the Ronin Launchpad at marketplace.roninchain.com/launchpads yourself — not from a link in a DM or a reply — connect the Ronin wallet you linked to your Yakkamon account, and have the page loaded before your wave opens. Click mint, approve the transaction in your wallet, and the hidden NFT lands in that wallet once it confirms. Come back for every wave you qualify for. Only Wave 5 has a published opening time (00:00 UTC on 18 September); the others have dates but no clock time yet. The step-by-step guide →

chunks.title: FAQ: Is the 10 September snapshot the same as the leaderboard lock?
chunks.text:
Q: Is the 10 September snapshot the same as the leaderboard lock?
A: No, and this catches people out. The 10 September snapshot only builds the mint whitelists — it fixes which waves you can mint in and nothing else. The leaderboard lock that decides your Genesis airdrop monster, your trainer number and your early-access wave comes later: one week before early access, with the airdrop landing three days after that. So you can keep climbing after 10 September, and the 250 points from minting count towards that later lock.

chunks.title: FAQ: How do I know a mint link is real?
chunks.text:
Q: How do I know a mint link is real?
A: The mint is free, so anything asking for a price, a deposit or approval over your whole wallet is not Yakkamon. Mint only at marketplace.roninchain.com — bookmark it now, because look-alike launchpads appear around every popular free mint. The team will not DM you a link, an early mint or a "whitelist fix", and nobody legitimate ever needs your recovery phrase. If you are new to Ronin, keep only the RON you need for gas in the wallet you mint with, and read every wallet prompt before approving it.

chunks.title: FAQ: What is $FLOWER, and is it a new token?
chunks.text:
Q: What is $FLOWER, and is it a new token?
A: No, it isn't new. Yakkamon deliberately doesn't launch its own token — it reuses $FLOWER, the same one already running across the studio's other games. That means you can start building an in-game balance before early access even opens.

chunks.title: FAQ: What does depositing actually do for me?
chunks.text:
Q: What does depositing actually do for me?
A: Two things at once, and this is the part people miss:

It credits your in-game balance. The $FLOWER is held for you and waiting the moment you get access.

It earns leaderboard points. Two boosts stack. A weekly multiplier — 3× through the opening week, then 0.2× less every week until it settles at 1× — held at 2.8× for week 3 after the week-2 deposit pause. And a size bonus rated per deposit, doubling at each step from +10% at 50 $FLOWER to +80% at 50,000. Splitting one deposit into several smaller ones earns less, because each piece gets its own smaller bonus.

You aren't trading one for the other. You keep the $FLOWER and the points, and those points push you toward better trainer tiers, earlier access waves, and the Genesis airdrop.

chunks.title: FAQ: Are the points one-time, or do I keep earning while my $FLOWER sits there?
chunks.text:
Q: Are the points one-time, or do I keep earning while my $FLOWER sits there?
A: One-time, per deposit. Each deposit is scored once, in the week it confirms, and that’s the end of it — a deposit sitting in your balance doesn’t keep generating points.

But every deposit earns its own points, so several deposits each pay out. The catch is that each one is also scored on its own size: a single 5,000 $FLOWER transfer earns the +40% bonus, while ten transfers of 500 earn ten separate +20% bonuses instead. That’s why splitting costs you.

Two things are locked in at the moment you send, and neither changes afterwards:

The week you deposit in sets the multiplier — 3× in the opening week, falling 0.2× weekly to a 1× floor (week 3 held at 2.8×).

The size of that single transfer sets the bonus tier.

The full deposit guideline →

chunks.title: FAQ: When did deposits open, and why do the docs say 10 August?
chunks.text:
Q: When did deposits open, and why do the docs say 10 August?
A: Deposits opened on 9 August at 8:00 PM ET, which is when deposit addresses were issued. They’re live now. The official docs say 10 August because they quote the UTC date — 8:00 PM ET is midnight UTC, already the 10th in London and everywhere east of it. Same instant, two calendar dates. Minimum deposit is 5 $FLOWER on Base or Ronin, and points land in the week the deposit confirms.

chunks.title: FAQ: Should I deposit all at once or spread it out?
chunks.text:
Q: Should I deposit all at once or spread it out?
A: All at once, and as early as you can — both bonuses push the same way. The weekly multiplier is 3× in the opening week and falls 0.2× weekly to a floor of 1× (week 3 was held at 2.8× after the week-2 pause), and the size bonus is rated per deposit, so the full amount has to land in one transfer. Concretely: 5,000 $FLOWER sent once in the opening week earns 17,000 points; the same 5,000 sent as ten deposits of 500 once the multiplier bottoms out earns 6,000. The full breakdown →

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I get my $FLOWER back if I change my mind?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I get my $FLOWER back if I change my mind?
A: Yes. There's no lock-up and no penalty. You can withdraw with no withdrawal tax once you have game access.

chunks.title: FAQ: Where do I get $FLOWER in the first place?
chunks.text:
Q: Where do I get $FLOWER in the first place?
A: Two routes. You can earn it free by playing Sunflower Land — selling crops, deliveries, seasonal chapters — since $FLOWER is that game’s in-game token. Or you can buy it — $FLOWER is the same ERC20 token on both Base and Ronin, at one identical contract address, and Yakkamon accepts deposits on either. Neither chain needs bridging: you can swap for it on Base, or directly inside the Ronin Wallet. Use whichever chain your funds are already on.

For anything to do with acquiring or depositing it, work from the official Yakkamon deposits guideline — which now publishes the contract address and the buy links for both chains — and the deposit panel in your own trainer dashboard. Never take a contract address or deposit address from a reply or a DM, and check anything a swap interface shows you against the official docs page — fake tokens with the same name and ticker are a common way people lose money. Full breakdown →

chunks.title: FAQ: Which deposit week am I in right now?
chunks.text:
Q: Which deposit week am I in right now?
A: The rate steps down every week, so it depends when you read this. Week one (10–16 Aug) paid 3×, and it normally falls 0.2× each week — with one exception: depositing was paused during week 2, so week 3 (24–30 Aug) was held at 2.8× and the schedule shifted a week, resting at 1× from around 26 October. The deposit guideline carries the full week-by-week table with a live indicator showing the current rate.

chunks.title: FAQ: When can I actually withdraw — is it this year?
chunks.text:
Q: When can I actually withdraw — is it this year?
A: Yes, this year, but with two qualifications. The official guideline says your $FLOWER can be spent in-game or withdrawn once you gain access to the game, and early access opens in November or December 2026. Note that access is staged by wave, so your own unlock follows your wave rather than launch day — and Wave 4 has no confirmed timing yet.

Access is staged by wave, not a single date. Wave 1 is the top 1,000 on points, wave 2 runs to 5,000, and so on. If withdrawal follows access, a later wave waits longer than an earlier one. No exact dates have been announced for any wave.

And it isn’t instant even then — percentage-based limits apply for the first few weeks after launch, capping how much you can take out in a period. So "deposit now, withdraw everything on day one" isn’t a plan that’s available.

One honest flag: the docs say "once you gain access to the game" without spelling out whether that means your wave or the general launch. We read it as your wave, but that’s our inference rather than something stated — worth asking the team directly if the timing matters to you.

chunks.title: FAQ: What are the withdrawal limits I've heard about?
chunks.text:
Q: What are the withdrawal limits I've heard about?
A: For security, percentage-based limits may apply during the first few weeks after launch. These cap how much can be withdrawn in a given period — they don't stop you withdrawing. It's a standard safeguard while the game economy stabilises, and the limits are lifted as things settle.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is depositing risky?
chunks.text:
Q: Is depositing risky?
A: We're not financial advisors and can't tell you whether to deposit — that's your call. What we can say factually: $FLOWER isn't a new speculative token, deposits are held on-chain rather than in a company account, there's no lock-up, and withdrawal is tax-free. As with any on-chain asset, smart-contract and platform risk still apply, the same as with any blockchain system.

chunks.title: FAQ: Why didn't the multiplier drop in week 3?
chunks.text:
Q: Why didn't the multiplier drop in week 3?
A: Because depositing was paused during week 2, the team held the week 3 multiplier at 2.8× rather than dropping it to 2.6×. The usual 0.2× weekly step resumed from week 4, which pushes every later week — and the 1.0× floor — one week later than first scheduled: the floor now arrives from 26 October. The full corrected week-by-week table is on the Tips page and in the deposit guideline.

chunks.title: FAQ: When do $FLOWER deposits close?
chunks.text:
Q: When do $FLOWER deposits close?
A: The final deposit window ends on 16 November at 01:59 UTC. Weeks turn at 02:00 UTC each Monday, and the multiplier sits at its 1.0× floor from 26 October through to the close — so there is no scheduled moment after that where waiting earns you a better rate.

chunks.title: FAQ: Where can I see the live deposit leaderboard?
chunks.text:
Q: Where can I see the live deposit leaderboard?
A: Right here on this site — the Deposit Leaderboard ranks every address that has deposited $FLOWER, built from public blockchain data on both Base and Ronin. Paste your deposit address to find your rank, see how far the next reward band is, and plan what a climb would cost.

chunks.title: FAQ: Why is my leaderboard score lower than the game shows?
chunks.text:
Q: Why is my leaderboard score lower than the game shows?
A: Because the board can only see the blockchain. It counts deposit points — amount × (week multiplier + size bonus) — exactly as the game scores them. Your streak, referral and quest points live off-chain, so your real total in the game is higher than your on-chain row. Treat the board as your deposit ranking, not your full score.

chunks.title: FAQ: What's the difference between my wallet address and my deposit address?
chunks.text:
Q: What's the difference between my wallet address and my deposit address?
A: They are different addresses, and mixing them up is the most common lookup mistake. Every trainer gets their own deposit address, shown in the game, valid on both Base and Ronin — that receiving address is your identity on-chain. You can send $FLOWER to it from any wallet and it still counts to you. When searching the leaderboard, use the deposit address, not the wallet you sent from.

chunks.title: FAQ: How often does the leaderboard update?
chunks.text:
Q: How often does the leaderboard update?
A: Roughly every six hours. The page shows when it was last recalculated and a countdown to the next update, both next to the Full Ranking heading and under the table. Deposits confirm on-chain immediately — they just take up to one refresh cycle to appear in the rankings.

chunks.title: FAQ: Can any monster gather any resource?
chunks.text:
Q: Can any monster gather any resource?
A: No — and this single rule shapes the whole game. Every resource is gated to a type: a Grass type gathers Wood, and a Fire type is refused outright ("Fire type cannot harvest wood!"). So collecting more species literally unlocks more of the map's materials, and a narrow roster caps what you can produce no matter how well you play. Full write-up under type locking.

chunks.title: FAQ: Are rarer monsters always better?
chunks.text:
Q: Are rarer monsters always better?
A: No. Rarity is set at the species level — there's no rare version of a common monster — and the team has been specific that the best commons can beat middling rares and roughly match a low-end legendary on raw stats. What rares and legendaries have is higher potential as they level, plus scarcer, higher-impact utilities. And since the free-mint stream we know that Rare and Uncommon monsters roll their utility at random, independently of their stats — so a modest monster can carry exactly the boost you need. Utilities & auras →

chunks.title: FAQ: What do the Genesis Legendaries actually do?
chunks.text:
Q: What do the Genesis Legendaries actually do?
A: The official Yakkapedia names each utility. Storm (Stormcharged): Yakkamon within range work twice as fast, with a large area of effect. Echo: Yakkamon within range produce double resources, small area. Ghost (Unsleeping): Yakkamon within range are always at maximum stamina on the farm, small area. Bloom: regenerates a percentage of its Max HP every combat turn. Three farm auras and one battle passive — and the numbers behind them (radius, percentage) are still unpublished. The full table →

chunks.title: FAQ: What's the difference between a small and a large AOE?
chunks.text:
Q: What's the difference between a small and a large AOE?
A: Bryn defined it on the free-mint stream. A small AOE only touches the job the monster is standing on: assign an Echo to a tree and the two or three adjacent trees get the doubling, nothing else. A large AOE covers an entire section of your farm and every Yakkamon in that area doing that job. Storm is the only Legendary with a large AOE, which is a big part of why it sits above the other three.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do utilities stack?
chunks.text:
Q: Do utilities stack?
A: Yes — some add and some multiply. The team's words: "you can get ones that are additive, but you can find ones that are also multiplicative with each other". Storm plus Echo is the confirmed multiplying pair: twice the speed on top of double the output on the same jobs. The older rule still holds too — two copies of the same named boost don't stack, so breadth beats duplicates.

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I put gear on my Yakkamon?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I put gear on my Yakkamon?
A: No. "We're not doing wearable gear for this game. The Yakkamon have the stats." There may be a single held item in the Pokémon mould — one thing granting one passive — but no clothes and no equipment slots. Stats are set at generation from genetics and training values and improve through time invested, training and breeding. The buffs in this game come from the monsters themselves, not from what they wear.

chunks.title: FAQ: How many types are there, and can a Yakkamon have two?
chunks.text:
Q: How many types are there, and can a Yakkamon have two?
A: Thirteen types at launch — the familiar creature-collector set of fire, water, rock and so on, with the team's own spin — and every Yakkamon has exactly one type at release. Dual types are "definitely coming" later. For type locking that means thirteen buckets of resources, and one monster can only ever open one of them.

chunks.title: FAQ: Should I collect duplicates of my best monster?
chunks.text:
Q: Should I collect duplicates of my best monster?
A: No — the game is designed against it. Identically named boosts don't stack: two monsters with "Wood Gatherer I" give you the effect once. Differently named or higher-ranked boosts do stack. The stated intent is to reward breadth — a wide roster with one strong specialist per job beats five copies of your best monster. See boost stacking.

chunks.title: FAQ: How does the world expand?
chunks.text:
Q: How does the world expand?
A: In three layers, per the official Regions post. Your Region is made of tiles: you gather resources to unlock more of them (the starter one costs 10 Wood + 1 Stone), and each tile can hold fresh resources, room to build, or a hunting area — and raises how much you can run at once. Grow your starting Region far enough and you unlock entirely new Regions, each with its own resources and monster types. More Regions arrive in later Chapters, each bigger than the last. Regions, tiles & the world →

chunks.title: FAQ: What Regions are there?
chunks.text:
Q: What Regions are there?
A: Two are named officially: Grasslands, which appears in the in-game Updates panel and looks like the starter area, and a Water Region, named in the Regions post as the example of a place with water hunting areas full of Yakkamon you could not catch back home. Deserts, volcanoes and fire regions have been described on the dev streams without names. Each Region has its own resources and its own monster types, so reaching one is only half the job — you also need the right type to gather there.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I lose my old Region when I unlock a new one?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I lose my old Region when I unlock a new one?
A: No. You keep everything you have unlocked, and old Regions stay part of your operation. The team frames that as the reason you will need to automate and manage your Yakkamon across several Regions at once. Read it with plot degradation and bin caps in mind: a Region you stop visiting does not pause, it decays.

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I use resources from one Region in another?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I use resources from one Region in another?
A: Only by moving them, it seems. The Regions post says that moving and sharing resources between your Regions becomes a core part of the strategy and that "the trainers who master logistics get ahead" — which only makes sense if resources are held per Region rather than in one global inventory. What a transfer costs (time, stamina, a building, a fee) is not published. Logistics between Regions →

chunks.title: FAQ: Does my farm keep running while I'm offline?
chunks.text:
Q: Does my farm keep running while I'm offline?
A: Yes, and being away costs you less than we first thought. Monsters repeat their work cycles automatically while you're gone, their haul lands in storage bins that cap, and once the bins and job areas are full they simply stop and wait. The team was explicit on the free-mint stream: "it just pauses the progress. There is no punitive system for not logging in" — no decay, no neglect state. Plot degradation is a cost of using a plot, not of leaving it. So the only thing a long absence costs you is the production you didn't bank while the bins sat full.

chunks.title: FAQ: How many Yakkamon are there?
chunks.text:
Q: How many Yakkamon are there?
A: Twenty-two have been officially shown so far, on the roster sheet — you can see it on the Gameplay page — out of roughly 50–60 species at launch. The rest of the roster arrives after launch across chapter releases, each typically paired with a new region. No names, types or rarities have been attached to the portraits yet: what can and can't be read into the sheet.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do the Yakkamon have names yet?
chunks.text:
Q: Do the Yakkamon have names yet?
A: No — none are published, and the team has said monster names are not final and may be community-influenced. Any name you see circulating is a fan's guess, including ours.

chunks.title: FAQ: What are shinies?
chunks.text:
Q: What are shinies?
A: The official economy post mentioned them once: every monster NFT has unique traits, including collectible shinies. That's the entire published record — no odds, no mechanics, no pictures. They read as a collectability axis separate from the rarity tiers, but treat anything beyond that one sentence as speculation for now. Background in our economy breakdown.

chunks.title: FAQ: When can I battle other players?
chunks.text:
Q: When can I battle other players?
A: After launch — the PvP arena and tournaments are post-launch features, arriving once the core game has settled. Worth knowing early: the team expects the market to value gathering specialists first and shift toward battle-stat monsters once the arena establishes, and they've said they'll let that shift happen rather than intervene.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is combat a pure simulation, or do I get to do anything?
chunks.text:
Q: Is combat a pure simulation, or do I get to do anything?
A: You'll get to act. The team decided at the end of August that players can take actions inside combat, through a mechanic Bryn called "mechanic swapping" — influencing which mechanic is in play rather than pressing attack every turn. What that looks like on screen hasn't been shown. The rest is settled: lanes act top to bottom, each monster cycles through two or three abilities in a preset order, and who goes first is a coin flip unless one lane holds the type advantage, which overrides everything.

chunks.title: FAQ: How does a hunt actually work?
chunks.text:
Q: How does a hunt actually work?
A: Hunting is a job you assign, not a place you walk to — the game is the same top-down view as Sunflower Land. You send a Yakkamon out to passively roam a hunting ground while you run your farm, and it triggers encounters with the wild monsters living there; lures and baits, crafted from resources, tilt the roll toward a type, and choosing a specific area of the ground (a rocky outcrop, say) does the same. Which monsters are out depends on the time of day on the in-game clock. Wild Yakkamon have three temperaments: affectionate ones only come home if your hunter wins them over, greedy ones want resources first, and angry ones start a fight. There's no limit on hunts per Yakkamon; it's the ground that depletes as it's hunted out. Crafting & hunting →

chunks.title: FAQ: What are affectionate, greedy and angry Yakkamon?
chunks.text:
Q: What are affectionate, greedy and angry Yakkamon?
A: The three wild temperaments from the official Hunting post. An affectionate Yakkamon comes home only if the Yakkamon you sent wins it over — what it judges (type, level, a bait) isn't published. A greedy one wants resources and won't budge until you've paid, so bring the right goods if you're chasing a particular monster. An angry one turns the encounter into a battle, and a hunter that can't hold its own comes back empty-handed. In practice that makes a hunting squad three checks at once: strength, charm and stock. What the Hunting post means for players →

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I catch a Legendary by hunting?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I catch a Legendary by hunting?
A: Yes, according to the official Hunting post: Legendaries and Rares sporadically appear in the hunting grounds, with no schedule to memorise. The team's advice is to keep a strong, well-supplied team ready to go the moment one shows up — which reads as needing both a hunter that can win a fight and a stock of goods, in case the Legendary is greedy. How often they appear, and whether wild Legendaries draw on the same limited supply as the Chapter 0 batches, is unpublished. Our reading →

chunks.title: FAQ: Does the time of day matter for hunting?
chunks.text:
Q: Does the time of day matter for hunting?
A: Yes. Each hunting ground reveals different Yakkamon at different times of day — the post says what roams a ground at dawn won't be what you find at midnight. Two things to know: it's the sped-up in-game clock in the HUD, not your local time, so no timezone has an advantage; and the team frames "learning the clock" as the skill, which suggests the game won't simply show you the timetable. Keeping your own log of ground, in-game hour and what appeared is the cheapest edge in the game. Day, night & weather →

chunks.title: FAQ: Do hunting grounds run out, and what do I do about it?
chunks.text:
Q: Do hunting grounds run out, and what do I do about it?
A: They do. The more you hunt a ground, the less populated it becomes, and the regeneration rate isn't published. The official answer is to spread your hunts across grounds and Regions. Since a hunting area is a tile on your own Region, that means budgeting a second hunting tile before the first runs dry — and eventually a second Region. Future Seasons also change which Yakkamon are available and where, so the map you learn this Chapter won't be next Chapter's. Why depletion is now a reason to own more than one ground →

chunks.title: FAQ: Is there a limit on how many Yakkamon can work at once?
chunks.text:
Q: Is there a limit on how many Yakkamon can work at once?
A: No. If you can find the jobs for them and set their cycles up so they don't compete, as many Yakkamon as you have can be working at once. Jobs, not headcount, are the ceiling — every tile you claim adds jobs, and the pressure as you grow is to keep the whole farm staffed and the supply chains behind each processing building actually delivering.

chunks.title: FAQ: Are there evolutions?
chunks.text:
Q: Are there evolutions?
A: Confirmed, but not at launch. The reason is supply: launch with evolutions and the lower tiers gradually filter out as everyone evolves upward, until the population piles up at the top tier. The team wants to solve that before shipping the feature. Breeding has a limit for a related reason — bred Yakkamon are tradable, so commons breed above replacement, rarer species around it, and some Legendaries may breed only once.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is Yakkamon free to play?
chunks.text:
Q: Is Yakkamon free to play?
A: Yes — free-to-play is confirmed, and it runs as a browser web app with no download. A wallet only matters for the on-chain parts: the free mint, the airdrop, and trading. You can play the whole game without any of those.

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I earn real money playing for free?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I earn real money playing for free?
A: The free-mint stream answered this more directly than the economy post did. There is a completely free-to-play layer with no limit on what you can produce — but what it produces is not tradable. Making something tradable costs the game's Web2 currency, coins, and coins only come from VIP, from actions that help the economy (burning crops or other assets) and from contract hunts. So the honest answer is: a free player can reach the market, but only by feeding the free layer into the coin gate first. Bryn borrowed a phrase for it — "more free to try than free to play". The two-track economy →

chunks.title: FAQ: What are coins?
chunks.text:
Q: What are coins?
A: The in-game Web2 currency — "currently called coins", with a rename to something like "new yen" floated on the stream. They're the balancing lever on the tradable economy: you spend coins to produce tradable assets, and the faucets for coins are deliberately limited. Not to be confused with $FLOWER, which is the on-chain token; how the two relate hasn't been published.

chunks.title: FAQ: Where will I trade monsters?
chunks.text:
Q: Where will I trade monsters?
A: Two places, in order. The free mint and the trainer airdrop launch exclusively on the Ronin marketplace; an in-game marketplace follows after launch, running on $FLOWER with a percentage fee applied as a soft burn. Until launch, the Ronin marketplace is the only venue that will exist.

Timing: the official Important Dates page puts the in-game marketplace, auctions and $FLOWER withdrawals at Chapter 0, one month after early access opens. Free-mint NFTs are tradable on Ronin from 14 September.

chunks.title: FAQ: Can I sell any monster I catch?
chunks.text:
Q: Can I sell any monster I catch?
A: Not necessarily. Basic monsters have limited tradeability, and some must be hunted yourself rather than bought. The tiers behave differently on-chain: Legendaries are NFTs, rares are SFTs with supply set by how hard players hunt during their window, and commons are plain game assets. So you can't simply buy your way out of a gap — or sell your way out of every surplus.

chunks.title: FAQ: Is $FLOWER deflationary?
chunks.text:
Q: Is $FLOWER deflationary?
A: The team says the game is "built deflationary", with marketplace fees applied as a soft burn — burned or recycled into rewards. Worth being precise here: the fee percentage, the burn share and the emission schedule are all unpublished, so the claim can't be checked yet. Not false — just currently unfalsifiable, which is our standing note until numbers land.

chunks.title: FAQ: When does the game actually come out?
chunks.text:
Q: When does the game actually come out?
A: Early access opens in November or December 2026, and it rolls out in waves rather than all at once. Wave 1 enters on launch day, Wave 2 a week later, Wave 3 a week after that, and Wave 4 is confirmed closer to launch. A full public launch date beyond early access hasn't been announced. The full schedule →

chunks.title: FAQ: Is there a hard date?
chunks.text:
Q: Is there a hard date?
A: For the mint, yes: the Ronin free mint opens 14 September (whitelist snapshot 10 September) and the reveal is 14 October. For the game, not yet: the official docs narrow early access to November or December 2026, with Chapter 0 — the marketplace, auctions and $FLOWER withdrawals — one month after that. Our timeline shows the quarter rather than a specific day; check the News page for confirmation once one is set.

chunks.title: FAQ: Do I lose my place if I can't play on day one?
chunks.text:
Q: Do I lose my place if I can't play on day one?
A: No. Your wave decides when the door opens for you, not how long it stays open. Your trainer number is permanent, and your Genesis Monster is airdropped to you regardless of when you first log in.

chunks.title: FAQ: Does Yakkamon mean Sunflower Land gets less attention?
chunks.text:
Q: Does Yakkamon mean Sunflower Land gets less attention?
A: The team's answer is no, and they've published their reasoning in some detail. The short version:

Sunflower Land is still shipping. Over the same six months Yakkamon has been in development, Sunflower Land committed to a two-year roadmap, open-source contributors went up, and the release cadence kept climbing.

A creature collector doesn't belong inside a farming game. Bolting one onto Sunflower Land would have taken years and slowed both games down. Spinning it out lets each be built at its own pace.

Both games grow the same ecosystem. There's no new token — Yakkamon runs on $FLOWER, the same one used across the studio's games. More games means more places to use it.

The team is growing. They're actively hiring designers, developers, moderators and community managers.

Five years of shared foundations. The same team has worked together for over five years, so architecture, tooling and hard-won lessons carry directly from one game to the other rather than being rebuilt.

It's worth reading their full answer if this is a concern for you — and Sunflower Land is live today, so you can judge the release cadence yourself.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Two Halves, One Game
chunks.text:
Half of Yakkamon plays itself. The other half only moves when you do — and each half feeds the other.

Yakkamon is two games bolted together. The idle half runs around the clock: your monsters farm, gather and produce whether or not the game is open, so you log back in to a pile of resources waiting to be collected. The active half only moves when you're playing — hunting rare creatures in the wild, crafting gear, and fighting other trainers. The two are not separate hobbies: better hunts give you better monsters, better monsters farm faster, and faster farming buys the gear for harder hunts.

The team put a number on the balance on 21 August. They are not building a game where you spend most of your time in combat, the way an RPG does — they're aiming at roughly an even split, described as 50/50 or 30/30/30 across farming, combat and market activity. If you were expecting a battler with a farm attached, or a farm with a battler bolted on, it's meant to be neither.

Like this: Your farm is a slow cooker that keeps going all night. Hunting is the trip to the shops for better ingredients.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Core Loop
chunks.text:
Catch, work, collect, craft, maintain, level up — then go catch something rarer. Every system bolts onto this circle.

Six steps, repeated. 1. Catch — head into the wild and hunt Yakkamon; every one you catch joins your roster. 2. Work — send them out to gather resources, which they repeat automatically, including offline. 3. Collect — their haul stacks up in a storage bin, and you tap the bin to move it into your inventory. 4. Craft — turn raw resources into gear, items and buildings, including the gear that catches rarer monsters. 5. Maintain — feed and heal your monsters, and refertilise plots that have degraded, or output quietly falls off. 6. Level up — higher-level Yakkamon gather faster, and better gear plus a better team lets you go catch something rarer. Then back to step one.

Step five is new as of 21 August and it changes the rhythm of the loop: this is no longer a game you can set up once and leave. See Upkeep & Degradation.

Like this: It's a snowball. Small team, small resources, small upgrades, slightly bigger team. Do that twenty times and you have an empire — but you have to keep sweeping the path.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Your Yakkamon
chunks.text:
Around 50–60 species at launch — and four separate things decide whether an individual monster is worth keeping.

The team has said to expect roughly 50–60 Yakkamon at launch, with more arriving each chapter rather than all at once. Four things make one individual worth having. Its species decides what it can gather at all (see Type Locking) and also fixes its rarity tier. Its stats roll differently on every individual, so two of the same species won't be identical — it's worth hunting the same creature again to chase a better roll. Its traits are randomly rolled percentage-chance bonuses that change how it farms. Its skills decide what it does in combat.

Underneath sits more machinery than the marketing suggests: real genetics, species-specific stat curves, hidden initial values you can't see when a monster spawns, and training values that shift stats depending on how you raise it. That last part matters — a species that's naturally defensive but rolled a high genetic attack stat can be trained into an attacker, which is where individual build expression comes from.

One idea the team explored and dropped: age and weight affecting stats. Bryn called it a step too complicated and backed away from it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Your Yakkamon
chunks.text:
Crucially, your monsters are also your boost items. Rather than crafting a statue and placing it on your land the way Sunflower Land does, the buffs live on the creatures themselves — gathering multipliers, yield and speed bonuses. The team you farm with is the source of your bonuses, not a decoration you buy. The free-mint stream gave that a name: every monster carries a utility, named on Legendaries and randomly rolled on everything else.

Thirteen types at launch, one per monster. Bryn confirmed the type list is 13 to start — fire, water, rock and the other familiar creature-collector elements, "with our own spin" — and that every Yakkamon has exactly one type at release. Dual types are "definitely coming", later. For type locking that means thirteen buckets of resources and a monster can only ever open one of them.

No wearable gear. Asked about equipment and stat boosts, Bryn was flat: "We’re not doing wearable gear for this game. The Yakkamon have the stats." There may be a single held item in the Pokémon mould — one thing granting one passive — but no clothes and no equipment slots. Stats are baked in at generation from genetics and training values, and improve through time invested, training and, later, breeding. If you want a stronger monster, you raise one or you find one; you don’t dress one. Levelling comes from combat, training and food — "all of the above", with more systems to come.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Your Yakkamon
chunks.text: Like this: Think trading cards. Same picture on the front, better numbers on the back — and that's the one everybody wants.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Rarity & What It Actually Buys
chunks.text:
Rarity is fixed at the species level — and rarer does not simply mean stronger.

Two corrections landed on 21 August that change how the whole roster should be read.

Rarity is set at the species level. Every individual of a given species shares that species' rarity. There is no rare version of a common monster and no legendary variant of an ordinary one — if a species is Legendary, all of them are, and if it's Common, you will never roll a shiny exception. That kills a whole category of speculation about hunting commons for a lucky upgrade.

Rarer is not strictly better. Bryn was specific: rares and legendaries carry a slightly better statistical allotment, but the best commons can beat middling rares and roughly match a low-end legendary on raw stat outlay. What the rarer monsters have is higher potential as they level, plus scarcer and higher-impact utility. Some commons carry unique traits you will need and cannot get elsewhere.

The three tiers, with the team's working definitions:Legendary — pre-minted, fixed, scarce supply. Minted as NFTs. Carries traits no other tier can access. Obtained mainly through events, specific conditions and tournament wins.
Rare — time-limited or event-limited availability, with final supply set by how hard players hunt. Issued as SFTs. Can appear in any hunt.
Common — plain game assets with no token behind them.
Hunting is the primary route to any monster regardless of tier.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Rarity & What It Actually Buys
chunks.text:
Utilities are now out, as text. The Yakkapedia names what each Genesis Legendary does, and the free-mint stream confirmed that Rare and Uncommon monsters roll their utility at random, independently of their stats — so "rarer is not strictly better" now has a mechanism behind it: a Common can roll the boost you need. The Yakkapedia also splits the Genesis collection into Legendary / Rare / Uncommon lines (2,750 / 4,000 / 15,000 by supply), which is where the Uncommon label enters the vocabulary. See Utilities & Auras for how they work, and The Genesis Legendaries for the table. The numbers behind each utility are still unpublished.

Like this: A first-team squad player can outperform a bench-warming international. The badge tells you the ceiling, not the current form.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Type Locking
chunks.text:
Every resource can only be gathered by the right type — so your roster decides what you can gather at all.

This is the rule that makes collecting matter rather than just being a scoreboard. Each resource is gated to a type: a Grass type gathers Wood, and a Fire type cannot — the game refuses outright, with an in-game message reading “Fire type cannot harvest wood!”

The consequence is that collecting more species literally unlocks more of the map's materials. A narrow roster caps what you're able to produce no matter how well you play. Only the Grass→Wood pairing has been shown so far; the types behind Stone, berries and crops haven't been announced, and each region's materials are expected to follow the same pattern.

The official economy post makes this more expensive than it first looked: basic monsters have limited tradeability, so you can't simply buy your way out of a type gap. Every missing type is an expedition you fund yourself.

Like this: You wouldn't ask a fish to chop firewood. Same rule — except here the game enforces it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Work Cycle
chunks.text:
Gathering runs on a repeating work-and-rest cycle: assign, produce, tire out, sleep, restart — all by itself.

The engine room of the whole game. You assign a Yakkamon to a resource it's allowed to gather. Each work cycle runs for a set time before paying out, and working burns stamina — stamina is the limit on how much a monster can do in one stretch. The cycle finishes and drops its haul into a storage bin, then repeats automatically, so work continues while you're off hunting or battling. When stamina runs out the Yakkamon goes to bed, sleeps, recovers, and gets back to work on its own.

A sleeping monster isn't broken, it's recharging. There are two ways to raise output: level them up, since higher levels make them more efficient farmers, and collect more of them, since more monsters means more resource types unlocked and more gathering happening at once.

There is no cap on how many can work at once. Asked directly on the free-mint stream, Bryn said no: "if you can find the jobs for them and have them working, and set them up for cycles so they don’t compete with each other, as many Yakkamon as you have can be working at once". The limit is jobs, not headcount — every tile you claim adds jobs (see Regions, Tiles & The World), and every monster you catch is "a new action you can perform simultaneously". The pressure as you grow is to fully staff the farm and keep every job fed.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Work Cycle
chunks.text:
Processing is where the choices bite. Bryn’s example: one processing building can make X, Y or Z, but only one at a time, and X needs wood, Y needs crops, Z needs ore. So you choose what to run, and you make sure the supply chain behind it is actually delivering — "it’s an efficiency puzzle in that sense". Legendary auras are the levers on that puzzle: a Ghost next to a job removes the sleep half of the cycle for its neighbours entirely.

Cycle duration, stamina cost, yield per cycle and sleep recovery rate are all unpublished.

Like this: Each monster is a little worker with a battery. Work drains it, sleep charges it, and it clocks back on without being told.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Upkeep & Degradation
chunks.text:
Plots wear out as you farm them, and refertilising costs resources — a sink that doesn't exist in Sunflower Land.

Revealed on 21 August from Spencer's job-card screenshots, and one of the more consequential mechanics announced so far.

Farm plots degrade with use. The job card carries a degradation marker — the example shown read degraded 1.6×, meaning that plot now farms more slowly until you refertilise it. Making fertiliser costs resources, so upkeep is a genuine, permanent sink on your production rather than a cosmetic status.

Degradation comes from use, not from absence. That distinction was settled on the free-mint stream, and it corrects the way we first read this system. Asked what happens if a player is away for a week or a month, Bryn said: "It just pauses the progress. There is no punitive system for not logging in." Your Yakkamon work until the bins and job areas are full, then stop and wait. "There isn’t any decay. There is no neglect feature or anything like that" — with a hundred monsters on the farm, an attention system for each one would be too punishing. So a plot wears out because you farmed it, and a full bin is production you didn’t bank, but a farm you walk away from is a farm on pause. Bryn was equally explicit that the intent is not to punish players for going wide — upkeep is meant to be manageable.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Upkeep & Degradation
chunks.text:
Plot groups are non-linear, and that's deliberate. Growing tiles come in groups — three in the screenshot shown. Your first plot is free and requires upkeep; the second and third also require upkeep, but the upkeep cost scales more slowly than the production does. Filling out a group is therefore strictly better value per unit of upkeep than spreading thin, which is the team's way of pushing you to invest early and deep rather than wide and shallow.

No numbers beyond the 1.6× example have been published — not the degradation rate, not the fertiliser recipe, not the group size in the live build.

Like this: A vegetable patch, not a vending machine. Crop the same soil forever and yields drop until you feed it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Storage Bins
chunks.text:
Gathered resources pile into a capped bin that keeps filling offline — and stops paying once it's full.

Resources don't go straight into your bag. They stack in a storage bin that keeps filling on its own, including while you're offline, until you tap it to collect the haul into your inventory.

The catch is the cap. Screenshots show bins counting up as 84 / 120 and topping out at 120 / 120 MAX, with early-game bins capped at 20. Once a bin hits MAX it stops accepting, and every hour it spends full is production you never banked. That makes bin capacity, and how often you check in, a real strategic variable rather than a chore — the difference between a farm that runs all night and one that quietly stops at 2am.

A full bin is the only cost of being away. The free-mint stream confirmed there is no decay and no neglect penalty for not logging in — your monsters fill the bins, then stop and wait (see Upkeep & Degradation, which is about use, not absence). Two smaller notes from the same stream: the team has moved from many bins to one bin per resource, and shops now buy resources from you. And once you hold more than one Region, expect a bin in each — the Regions post makes moving resources between them a mechanic in its own right (see Logistics).

Like this: A piggy bank that fills itself. Once it's full, extra coins bounce off the top — so empty it before it overflows.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Looking After Them
chunks.text:
Your Yakkamon get hungry, hurt and tired — and a monster that needs something isn't earning.

Status icons float above a Yakkamon when something's wrong, and a notification feed calls it out by name — screenshots show messages in the form of “[name] is Hungry”. The states shown so far are hungry (needs feeding), hurt or knocked out, sleeping (recovering stamina) and needs an item. A Yakkamon can also ask for something directly with a speech bubble — one screenshot shows a stone icon with an exclamation mark.

An item bar sits along the bottom of the screen for exactly this: milk, flowers, mushrooms, a health item and others, ready to use on whoever's struggling. Since a monster in a bad state isn't producing, upkeep is part of the economy rather than flavour.

But nothing gets worse while you're gone. The free-mint stream drew the line clearly: a monster that needs something stops earning until you deal with it, and that is the whole penalty. There is no hunger clock that runs while you're logged out, no neglect state, no decay — "it just pauses the progress". Care is a cost of running the farm, not a tax on being away from it.

Each monster is also getting its own audio identity — a select sound, an idle sound, and separate relaxed and aggressive states. Craig's stated goal is that you'd recognise a monster by its noise without looking at the screen.

Like this: They're pets with jobs. Feed them, patch them up, let them nap — and they keep earning for you.

chunks.title: Gameplay: How Boosts Stack
chunks.text:
Two monsters with the same boost don't stack. Two with different boosts do — so breadth beats duplicates.
