A short rule with large consequences, answered directly on 21 August.

Identically named boosts do not stack. If two of your monsters both carry “Wood Gatherer I”, you get the effect once, not twice. Stacking a shelf of duplicates does nothing.

Differently named or higher-ranked boosts do stack. “Wood Gatherer” alongside “Extreme Wood Gatherer” is two separate effects and both apply.

The design intent was stated plainly: remove the reason to hoard duplicates of one good monster, and create a strong reason to collect a broad array of monsters with different skills so you can layer boosts on a single activity. Combined with type locking, the shape of an optimal roster is becoming clear — wide rather than deep, one excellent specialist per job rather than five copies of your best one.

This is also the single most useful thing published so far for anyone trying to plan a roster, because it rules out the strategy most players would default to.

Like this: Two identical umbrellas keep you exactly as dry as one. An umbrella and a raincoat is the upgrade.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Utilities & Auras
chunks.text:
A utility is a boost the monster carries around with it. Legendaries get a named one; everyone else rolls theirs at random.

The word the docs use is utility. It is the Yakkamon equivalent of a Sunflower Land boost item — except, as Bryn put it on the free-mint stream, "for Yakkamon, the boosts come from the Yakkamon themselves". There is no statue to craft and place. You put a monster on the farm and the monsters around it get faster, or richer, or never tire.

Legendaries have named utilities. The Yakkapedia lists them: Storm’s Stormcharged makes Yakkamon within range work twice as fast, Echo makes those within range produce double resources, Ghost’s Unsleeping keeps its neighbours at maximum stamina, and Bloom regenerates a share of its Max HP every combat turn. Three farm auras and one battle passive — see The Genesis Legendaries for the full table.

Small AOE versus large AOE. This is the number that decides how much a Legendary is worth, and Bryn defined it on the stream. A small AOE touches only the job the monster is standing on: assign an Echo to a tree and the two or three adjacent trees get the doubling, nothing else. A large AOE covers an entire section of your farm and every Yakkamon in that area doing that job. Storm is the only large-AOE Legendary, which is one reason 75 of them exist against 2,000 Bloom.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Utilities & Auras
chunks.text:
They stack — and some multiply. Bryn’s exact words: "you can get ones that are additive, but you can find ones that are also multiplicative with each other". The example the chat spotted and he confirmed is Storm plus Echo: twice the speed on top of double the output, on the same patch of trees. Building a farm team is meant to feel like building a combat team — complementary abilities working within range of each other. Read this alongside How Boosts Stack, which still holds: two copies of the same named boost don’t add up.

Rares and Uncommons roll theirs. The Yakkapedia lists no utility for either tier, and that is deliberate. When a Rare or Uncommon is generated — hunted, hatched, bred — it rolls a species, a stat outlay, and a utility, independently of each other. You can catch a monster with superb stats and a dud utility, or a weak monster with a boost you badly want. The ones worth keeping, or worth trading, are the ones that rolled both. This is the first confirmation that trait rolls and stat rolls are separate dice.

The numbers are not out. The September utilities reveal was expected to carry real figures per species; what shipped is descriptive text, because the values are still being playtested and, in Bryn’s words, "will probably still be balanced up until release". The radius of a small AOE, the size of a "section", Bloom’s regeneration percentage — all unpublished.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Utilities & Auras
chunks.text: Like this: A good foreman on a building site. He doesn't lay bricks himself — everyone within earshot just lays them faster.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Breeding & Genetics
chunks.text:
Bloodlines carry stats down the generations — now with a breeding limit that scales with rarity, and a stated one-to-three-year horizon.

Breeding is where the team expects the deepest optimisation to live. Genetics carry down the line: breed two strong individuals of the same species and their good stats and traits can propagate, letting you build a bloodline aimed at a specific result.

There is a breeding limit after all, and it scales with rarity. On 13 August the line was degradation with no hard cap. The free-mint stream replaced that with something firmer, because bred Yakkamon are tradable and the obvious follow-up was how to stop massive inflation. Bryn’s answer: "Yakkamon have a breeding limit." Commons can breed above replacement — two parents might make three — while rarer species breed at roughly replacement, two making two or one, and some Legendaries might only breed once. Offspring can breed in turn, but their own count "can narrow down further" each generation. Alongside that, the earlier idea survives as flavour rather than the cap: random noise still increases the more you breed out of one individual, so a heavily used line produces scruffier results even before it runs out of breeds.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Breeding & Genetics
chunks.text:
How predictable is it? Bryn's design principle is one RNG component plus one fixed component, and explicitly not stacking RNG on RNG. The stated outcome is that a player who understands the system should be able to estimate results within roughly 80–90% and build a sensible best-case/worst-case range before committing. There's still “a little bit of spice”, in his words.

The time horizon is unusual. The team is openly designing for one-to-three-year breeding projects — long-running attempts to move a specific trait set onto a perfect monster. Later goals include ways to carry traits across species and eventually across type groups, described as “sneaky ways” that are meant to be discovered rather than documented.

Advanced breeding is not in early access. It arrives in a chapter release after launch.

Ruled out: no forging. Combining ten commons into one rare was considered and rejected — Bryn described it as squashing your creatures into jam, tonally wrong for a cosy collector, despite conceding the economic upside.

Like this: Pedigree breeding. The champion only sires so many litters — and the ones it does get scruffier each time.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Evolutions
chunks.text:
Confirmed, handled monster by monster — but not at launch, for a supply reason the team spelled out.

Evolutions are confirmed and being designed for, and as of the free-mint stream they are explicitly not launching with the game. "Evolutions will be coming later. We will not be launching with evolutions."

The reason is supply, not time. A questioner put it to Bryn that the supply of each evolution tier would end up very low, and he agreed: launch with evolutions and the lower tier gradually filters out as everyone evolves upward, until the population piles up at the barrier of the highest tier — "that’s where the system will trend towards". It is a problem they want to solve before shipping the feature, not after. Read that with the new breeding limits: both systems are being tuned around how many of each thing should exist.

They are handled monster by monster rather than on one universal rule. The conditions vary: reaching a certain level, feeding a particular item, or fulfilling some other requirement specific to that species.

The notable part is that many conditions will be hidden. This is intentional black-box design — Bryn wants evolution triggers to be something the community works out and shares rather than reads in a wiki on day one. He was careful to say it won't be pure brute force: the game will give you hints that something is required, without telling you what.

Expect this to be one of the first genuine community research projects once the game opens.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Evolutions
chunks.text: Like this: A recipe with the last ingredient smudged out. You know there's a step missing, and finding it is the fun.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Your Base & Your Gym
chunks.text:
Land expansions, workstations, the Hunting Area — and a gym you decorate that other trainers come to challenge.

Your base is the place all of this runs from. Land expansion is tile by tile: each tile carries a resource price on the button — the starter one reads 10 Wood + 1 Stone — and a claimed tile can hold resource nodes, room for workstations and plots, or a hunting area. The Regions post adds that every tile also raises how much you can run at once, so land is a concurrency cap as well as floor space (see Regions, Tiles & The World). Buildings and stations shown so far include workbenches with their own storage counters, a workshop marked with an axe, houses with beds for sleeping monsters, crop plots and rock nodes. The Hunting Area is a dedicated zone with an entry cost on the sign (5 berries in the launch screenshot) — your doorway from farming into hunting.

The main menu carries six buttons: Squad (your active team), Items, Quests, Shop, Trade (the player market) and Log (notification history).

chunks.title: Gameplay: Your Base & Your Gym
chunks.text:
Customisation splits in two, confirmed on 21 August. Land customisation is unlikely at launch — revealed areas will mostly sit where the game puts them, though Adam expects to get there eventually. Your gym is the exception: the plan is full customisation of a core gym you decorate yourself. When other trainers visit to battle you, they see your gym, your layout and your monsters — which turns decoration into a social display rather than a private hobby. That's a direct lift of what worked in Sunflower Land with wearables, landscaping and trophy display.

Presentation note: the game is built for landscape orientation.

Like this: It's a workshop yard with a shopfront. More benches out the back, and one room you actually tidy up because people come and look at it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Regions, Tiles & The World
chunks.text:
The world opens in three layers — tiles inside your Region, then whole new Regions, then Chapters — and nothing you unlock ever closes.

The official Regions post (28 August) turned expansion from a vague “part the clouds” into a structure with three distinct layers.

Layer one: tiles. Your Region is made of tiles. You gather resources to unlock more of them — the starter expansion button reads 10 Wood + 1 Stone — and, in the team’s words, each tile you claim expands what you can do and how much you can run at once. That second clause is the important one: tiles are a cap on concurrency, not just square footage. A tile can hold fresh resource nodes, room to build, or a hunting area where wild Yakkamon roam — so every expansion is a choice between more gathering, more workstations, or more places to catch things.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Regions, Tiles & The World
chunks.text:
Layer two: Regions. Once you have grown your starting Region far enough, you unlock entirely new Regions, and each brings its own resources and its own monster types. The first named example is a Water Region, with water hunting areas full of Yakkamon you could not catch back home. Combine that with type locking and a new Region is a bootstrapping problem: its resources need a type you may not own yet, and the monsters of that type live in the Region’s own hunting areas. You arrive with lures and berries from home, catch the first local, and only then can the Region start working for you. Regions shown or described so far include grasslands, deserts, volcanoes, fire regions and water.

Layer three: Chapters. Regions get progressively bigger each time you expand, and more arrive in upcoming Chapters — the same cadence the team gave for new species, roughly a Region per Chapter across the first year.

Nothing sunsets. You keep every Region you have unlocked. Old Regions stay part of your operation, which the team frames as the reason you will need to automate and manage your Yakkamon across multiple Regions at once. Read that with bin caps in mind: a Region you stop visiting fills its bins and stops earning — it doesn’t decay, the team has since confirmed, but it doesn’t produce either. How you move things between Regions is its own system — see Logistics.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Regions, Tiles & The World
chunks.text:
How this squares with the dev stream. On 21 August the team drew a line between gathering regions you build on and hunting regions you explore. The Regions post puts hunting areas on tiles inside a Region instead. The most likely reading is that both are true — hunting areas are tiles you claim within a Region, and the “arrive at the beach” feeling Adam described is a new Region’s hunting areas rather than a separate map. We are flagging it rather than picking one.

The art: the studio has early access to an exclusive biome pack from Daniel Diggle, the designer behind the original Sunflower Land assets, covering multiple biome types, seasons and elements — the first hard evidence that Region variants are being built rather than discussed.

Like this: A shop that keeps adding aisles. You unlock shelves in the aisle you are in, then whole new aisles — and you still have to keep the old ones stocked.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Logistics Between Regions
chunks.text:
Resources belong to the Region they were gathered in. Moving and sharing them is, in the team’s words, “the real puzzle”.

The most consequential line in the Regions post is the one written most casually: as things get more complex, moving and sharing resources between your Regions becomes a core part of the strategy, and “the trainers who master logistics get ahead”.

That sentence only makes sense if resources are held per Region rather than in one global inventory. Wood gathered in the grasslands sits in the grasslands until something moves it. Which means a second Region is not simply more production — it is production that lands in the wrong place, plus a transport step to get it where it is needed.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Logistics Between Regions
chunks.text:
What that implies, if it holds:A new Region has to be fed before it feeds you — building materials, fertiliser and lures travel outward from home first.
Bin caps probably apply per Region, so an unvisited Region fills up and stops earning just like an unvisited bin.
Type-locked materials that only exist in one Region become something you ship, which is where specialisation — and a market — starts to look inevitable.
Any tool that plans production will need a transport cost in it, and that number does not exist yet.
What is not published: the transfer mechanic itself. Whether moving resources costs time, a monster’s stamina, a building, a fee, or nothing beyond a tap; whether monsters move between Regions freely; and whether the Trade menu doubles as the transport layer. The post promises a puzzle and gives none of the rules. Until it does, treat every cross-Region plan as a sketch.

Like this: Running two warehouses in two towns. Doubling the shelves is easy — the lorry between them is the business.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Day, Night & Weather
chunks.text:
A clock and a weather indicator run in the HUD, and both change what's out in the wild.

A clock sits in the corner of the screen with a sun or moon icon, and separate weather indicators sit next to it — sunshine and rain are both shown in the HUD. Day and night change which creatures are out, which resources are easiest to gather, and how regions look.

One thing worth knowing before you plan around it: the team confirmed on the 6 August stream that day and night run on a sped-up in-game clock, not real time. There is no timezone that gets a better night shift and no advantage to living anywhere in particular — the cycle comes to everyone equally.

A weather system proper is confirmed as wanted, and on 21 August a community suggestion got a warm reception from both Adam and Bryn: that legendary monsters are the in-world cause of seasonal and weather changes, in the manner of Pokémon's weather legendaries. Bryn's answer was that they want a weather system and special events anyway, so “there's a good home for it”. Not confirmed — but it is the first piece of Yakkamon lore to come from a player.

Like this: The world has its own little day that runs faster than yours. Nobody gets a head start on sunrise.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Seasonal System
chunks.text:
Seasons reshape the world, and new monsters drop into the wild on a schedule players race to claim.

Seasons change the world around you and each region shifts with them. On a three-month cadence, brand-new Yakkamon are released into the wild and players compete to hunt them down and claim them first. Being ready when a drop lands is a genuine advantage, and one of the better reasons to keep your farm and gear strong between seasons rather than coasting.

The cadence isn't settled. The docs describe the three-month cycle, but the team said on 6 August they are considering a Sunflower Land-style weekly season instead — a winter week, a summer week, different Yakkamon appearing week to week. That was still framed as current thinking rather than a promise as of 21 August.

The new biome pack includes season variants for each Region type, which is the first hard evidence that seasonal reskinning of regions is actually being built rather than just discussed.

Like this: New stock arrives on a known date and everyone queues. Turning up prepared beats turning up first.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Crafting & Hunting
chunks.text:
Hunting is a job you assign, on an in-game clock, in grounds that run dry — with affectionate, greedy and angry wild monsters, and Legendaries that turn up unannounced.

You refine gathered resources into the gear and items needed to track down and capture rarer, tougher monsters. Better gear opens harder regions and rarer spawns, and those rarer monsters gather better, which funds the next tier of gear. Crafting is worth watching as the thing that actually gates progress: raw gathering scales fairly easily once you have a roster, but turning that pile into the specific items a harder hunt needs is what limits most players.

How a hunt actually runs. You send one of your Yakkamon into a revealed hunting area carrying lures. It searches around and tries to draw wild monsters back onto your land, where you can keep them. You can walk in and look around yourself, but the monster does the hunting — you're the one deciding where it goes and what it takes with it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Crafting & Hunting
chunks.text:
Hunting is a job, and the hunting ground is a job system. The free-mint stream filled in the machinery. You are not walking around; it is the same top-down "god view" as Sunflower Land, and hunting is one more job you assign. Bryn’s description: "You assign a Yakkamon to a job. Hunting can be a job. It will roll for a Yakkamon. You can influence the outcome through use of resources." Spencer called the hunting ground "a separate job architecture" with its own food and upkeep, and it is the biggest thing to have landed in the build recently.

Grounds have areas, and lures pick the target. The ground shown had three areas — a rocky outcrop among them — with swamps and water areas to come. Send a monster to snoop around a specific area and you are far more likely to turn up that area’s type; let it wander and you may find anything. Lures and baits narrow it further — a rock-type lure draws rock types — and both are crafted from resources, which is what the recipe system Spencer is building is for — Bryn’s verdict on explaining recipe crafting out loud was "you’ll just have to play it".

chunks.title: Gameplay: Crafting & Hunting
chunks.text:
Two kinds of wild monster. An aggressive one shows up with a red alert on the hunting ground: something in there wants to fight you, most activity in the ground pauses, and it waits for you to act — this is where hunting hands off to combat. An ambient one just bops around, skittish, and never alerts you. Those you have to win over: send your hunter across with bait, watch a short emoji conversation play out, and see whether it decides to come along or runs off. Spencer called the mechanic "super cute" and still in flux.

Grounds deplete; monsters don’t. There is no limit on how many hunts one Yakkamon can perform — "they can keep hunting forever". The restriction sits at the ground level: as a hunting ground is progressively hunted out, its chance of producing anything drops. You can also start PvE with only one or two monsters, in a one-against-three.

Contract hunts are a coin faucet. A contract system will request specific Yakkamon to be found, paying out in coins — one of the few ways to earn the currency that gates the tradable economy. Bryn expects you to be "wanting to perform hunts very regularly" for that reason alone.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Crafting & Hunting
chunks.text: The official Hunting post (5 September) put the rest in writing. Each ground reveals different Yakkamon at different times of day — on the sped-up in-game clock, not yours — and the team frames "learning the clock" as the skill, which suggests the timetable is yours to discover. Wild monsters come in three temperaments: affectionate ones only come home if the Yakkamon you sent wins them over (the ambient encounter, renamed), greedy ones want resources and will not budge until you have paid — "bring the right goods" — and angry ones start a battle that a hunter who cannot hold its own will lose, sending you home empty-handed. Legendaries and Rares sporadically appear in the hunting grounds, with no schedule to memorise, so the post's advice is to keep "a strong, well-supplied team ready to go the moment one shows up". Depletion is confirmed and given its strategic half: spread your hunts across grounds and Regions. And future Seasons change which Yakkamon are available and where, so the map you master this Chapter will not be next Chapter's. Our reading of all eight points is in Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Crafting & Hunting
chunks.text:
Hunting is the primary route to any monster at any rarity — the post puts Legendaries as well as Rares in ordinary grounds, sporadically, alongside the events and tournaments the streams described. The exact mechanic is still moving — as of the free-mint stream the team was "still playing around with what this mechanic is like", and none of the rates (day length, regeneration, spawn odds, what a greedy monster charges) are published.

Like this: Sending the dog out to find rabbits. Some rabbits bite, some you have to coax out with a carrot, some want paying — and the field empties if you work it every day.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Battle System
chunks.text:
Lane-based 3v3 auto-battling — with a newly decided layer of player actions on top, so it isn't a pure simulation after all.

The 21 August stream turned combat from a one-line placeholder into the most thoroughly explained system in the game. The free-mint stream then changed one foundation of it.

You will act inside a fight. The open question from 21 August was whether the auto-battler would be a full simulation with no inputs. Bryn called the answer "a massive decision this week" and "a big architectural decision for us at the start": players can act inside combat, through a mechanic he described as mechanic swapping — influencing which mechanic is in play rather than pressing attack each turn. The architecture is deliberately flexible so that when player feedback starts, the team can "go any sort of way" on battle type rather than being locked into one dogma. What that swapping actually looks like on screen has not been shown.

Who goes first, and in what order. Initiative in PvP is a coin flip — unless one side holds the type advantage in a lane, which overrides everything: fire attacking grass goes first, full stop. Within your own team, lanes act top to bottom: lane one, then lane two, then lane three, every time, which makes lane one the slot where a type disadvantage hurts most. Each monster carries two to three abilities in a preset order and cycles through them — ability one, two, three, then back to one — each time it gets to act.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Battle System
chunks.text:
What goes into a fight: stats, level, type, abilities, passives and, potentially, a single held item. Dragons got a specific mention: they are weak to only two types where every other type is weak to three, and Bryn went straight from Bloom’s per-turn regeneration into dragon resistances in the same breath, which is as close as anyone has come to saying what species Bloom is. Put that regeneration on a monster with good defensive stats and it is "like a brick" — an anchor your opponent has to alpha-strike off the board in one turn or not at all. In the back pocket, and explicitly not for early access: lane effects, ground types, and weather events like a sandstorm, all of which can be triggered through the skill system without much extra code.

The format: lane-based 3v3 auto-battling, RPG-style. Monsters hold assigned lanes. You set positions before the fight and cannot change them mid-battle unless a specific skill does it for you. Positioning still matters, because monsters have AOE attacks and matchups.

Skills execute in a fixed order and the move list is visible in advance. That creates the tension the team is most interested in: type advantage versus skill-loop advantage. You might hold a favourable elemental matchup — water against fire — and still lose because their skill order absorbs your one big hit behind their one big shield. Currently under consideration: cutting each monster down to around two skills with more passives.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Battle System
chunks.text:
Pacing. Bryn's rule of thumb is three to five rounds, under a minute for a typical encounter. But he's deliberately building wide variance — the stated goal is that the “average” fight is less than 40% of all fights, with frequent one-turn solves and occasional long strategic grinds. Battles run on an animation timer that can be sped up but likely not skipped outright, because real-time interaction mechanics are in testing.

Skills can be respecced, expensively. The intended route is to find a monster carrying a skill you want, extract that skill and move it onto another. Ideally you find one with premium skills and premium stats and skip the process. The design goal is explicit: buildcraft should come out of breeding, not out of hot-swapping loadouts before every fight. Your team composition is a long-term project and combat executes the plan.

PvE and PvP share the system. What was demonstrated is PvE, but the same engine runs the arena.

Matchmaking is confirmed, with an anti-bot approach borrowed from Bryn's previous games: no meaningful rewards below an MMR cutoff. That's the band where low-skill human players sit, and it suppresses unsophisticated bots by making the low end worthless. Bots good enough to climb above it get flagged through event tracking and banned.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Battle System
chunks.text:
What was shown in the leaked screenshot is an internal dev gym, not the finished battle screen — placeholder backgrounds, rough layout. Matt L, the studio's game design intern, was singled out for most of the credit on this system.

Like this: You're a manager, not a player. You pick the squad and the formation — and now you get to shout one or two things from the touchline.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Arena, Quests & Trading
chunks.text:
PvP arena combat, an on-chain market, and the timing that decides when any of it is live.

You face other trainers in PvP arena combat and build your own gym. Because rarity and stat rolls both feed into power, the team you build on the farm is the team you fight with — the two halves of the game aren't separable here either. See The Battle System for how a fight actually resolves, and Your Base & Your Gym for what visitors see when they arrive.

Every core resource and creature is tradable on-chain, with a Trade button in the main menu — though the official economy post narrows that considerably, walling easily-farmed free-to-play resources off from the tradeable economy and giving basic monsters only limited tradeability. There are still two valid routes to an empire: grind it yourself, or trade your way there.

Quests appear in a feed with names like “Capture the Spikemon” and a counter for how many are waiting, and timed events run on a countdown with a milestone bar filling toward marked rewards.

Timing: the team confirmed on 6 August that PvP is not in early access. Early access (November or December 2026) ships gathering, monsters, hunting and combat, with the PvP arena, tournaments and advanced breeding arriving after launch in chapter releases. Guilds and alliances were addressed on 21 August and pushed further back still — acknowledged as popular, described as a lot of work, and explicitly behind core functionality.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Arena, Quests & Trading
chunks.text: Like this: The farm is practice, the arena is the match — and the market is there if you'd rather buy a good player than raise one.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Two-Track Economy
chunks.text:
An infinite free-to-play layer that can't be traded, and a tradable layer gated by coins. The gate is the whole design.

The official economy post said assets come in two classes. The free-mint stream explained the mechanism, and Bryn was frank that it is early — "we’ve sort of settled on a model, or at least we’ve started working on a model".

Track one: the free-to-play layer. You never have to put anything in. Your monsters gather, your farm produces, and there is no limiter on how much untradable resource you can make. The catch is the word untradable: what this layer produces stays in your game. Bryn described it as "essentially infinite" for free players, but designed so that it is not heavily impactful on the rest of the economy.

Track two: the tradable layer, gated by coins. Producing something you can sell costs the game’s Web2 currency — currently called coins, with a rename to something like "new yen" floated on the stream. Coins are "the balancing lever for tradable assets": there is a limiter on how much tradable resource you can produce, and that limiter is how many coins you can get your hands on.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Two-Track Economy
chunks.text:
Coin faucets are deliberately scarce. Outside of VIP, coins come from actions that are good for the economy — the examples given were burning other assets and burning crops, and the contract hunt system, which pays coins for finding a requested Yakkamon. So the loop for a free player who wants to reach the market runs: produce untradable resources for free, burn some of them for coins, spend the coins to produce something tradable. Every coin is a sink somebody else paid.

What this settles from the economy post. The "two classes of asset" are not two kinds of item; they are the same items with and without a tradable flag, and the flag costs coins. It also confirms what our economy article inferred: the free layer buys progress, not income. Free-to-play is, in Bryn’s phrase borrowed from Sunflower Land, "more free to try than free to play" — "it is to sort of require people to put in to get out as well".

Unpublished: the coin cost of a tradable unit, the burn rates, whether coins themselves can be bought, and where $FLOWER sits relative to coins. Trading itself, along with the marketplace, auctions and $FLOWER withdrawals, is a Chapter 0 feature — one month after early access opens.

Like this: A hobby farm with a licence to sell at market. Grow all you like for your own table — selling needs the permit, and permits are rationed.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Progression & Endgame
chunks.text:
Infinite levels, chapter releases, and a meta that's expected to move from farming to fighting.

Infinite levels and expansions. The team intends to launch with plans and sinks already in place for an endless endgame, though those specific features arrive after early access once the core has been tested. Bryn named seasonal PvP, scaling difficulty content and other infinite-play patterns as fitting the studio's kind of game.

Not all monsters ship at launch. Around 50–60 species open the game and the rest arrive across chapter releases, each typically paired with a new Region — framed internally as roughly the first year of content, and confirmed in the 28 August Regions post, which says more Regions roll out in upcoming Chapters and that each one is bigger than the last. Once the roster is established, a more permanent replayability system takes over, which Adam pointedly declined to call “ascension” the way Sunflower Land does.

The meta is expected to move. This is the most useful strategic statement of the 21 August stream. Early on, the valuable monsters are the gathering and hunting specialists, because you need resource throughput to fund everything else. Once the PvP arena and tournaments establish, the team expects demand to shift toward battle-stat monsters. They're aware of it, they're letting community demand decide the pace, and they're not planning to intervene — which means anyone reading the market early has a genuine window.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Progression & Endgame
chunks.text:
No hard cap on specialisation. There is no enforced limit stopping a producer from also being a fighter. The split is meant to emerge naturally from opportunity cost: focus on fighting and you'll buy from the market, focus on production and you'll trade for combat monsters. Top-end players will comfortably do both.

No resets, ever. Bryn is explicitly against total economy resets — mistakes get worn and fixed. Inflation is treated as normal and healthy in any live economy, attacked with hard sinks and new content that absorbs old, following the infinite XP sink pattern Sunflower Land shipped in its last chapter.

Like this: A long-running league rather than a season that wipes. The table never resets — they just keep adding divisions.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Playing It — Platform & Access
chunks.text:
Free to play, email login, browser first, landscape — and an open-source client.

Free to play, free sign-up. Same strategy as Sunflower Land: get as many players in as possible, then let NFTs and wallets be an optional layer on top. You can play the entire game without ever connecting a wallet, and earn NFTs through play if you decide to go down that path.

Email is the primary login method, confirmed 21 August. You do not need a wallet to get in.

Browser first. Yakkamon launches as a web app. There's no native mobile app planned yet — the position as of 13 August was web first, assess later — and no app store or console release, with the team citing prior experience of app store friction. Not ruled out permanently.

The PWA is back, and recommended. On 21 August Adam described installing the PWA to your home screen as noticeably more performant than playing inside a wallet's embedded browser. Wallet in-app browsers do work, and support portrait, but the team suggests playing outside them. The game itself is built for landscape.

The client will be open sourced — reversing the 6 August position, which was that the game was changing too fast to accept contributions. The team credits AI with making community contribution viable, citing 30 community features, patches and fixes shipped to Sunflower Land in a single recent week.

chunks.title: Gameplay: Playing It — Platform & Access
chunks.text:
Discord is being built into the game. Adam is integrating Discord announcements and communication directly into the client, plus a light role system bridging the two, so Discord members get extra in-game capabilities.

No plaza at early access. Asked whether the game will have MMO aspects like Sunflower Land’s plaza, Bryn said it is wanted but not being worked on yet — the focus is the initial onboarding and "the first island". The MMO layer comes later, and he thinks it works especially well for battling. Fishing, for the record, hasn’t been designed for early access either.

Like this: It's a website you can pin to your phone. No download, no store, no wallet unless you want one.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Genesis Legendaries
chunks.text:
Storm, Echo, Ghost and Bloom — the four founding Legendaries now have utilities, supplies and a home in the official Yakkapedia.

The official docs opened a Yakkapedia at the end of August — pushed live minutes before the free-mint dev stream — with the first hard data on the Genesis set: a supply figure, an ability and a distribution note for each of the four Legendaries, plus the Rare and Uncommon lines that fill out the rest of the collection. Everything in the table below is quoted from it.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Genesis Legendaries
chunks.text:
Yakkamon | Supply | Ability | Where the copies go |
🌩 Storm
#0–75 · Legendary | 75 | Stormcharged — Yakkamon within range work 2× as fast (large AOE) | 50 trainer airdrop · 3 in the free mint · 1 trainer raffle · rest for future events |
⬜ Echo
#75–350 · Legendary | 275 | Yakkamon within range produce double resources (small AOE) | 203 trainer airdrop · 5 in the free mint · 1 trainer raffle · rest for future events |
👻 Ghost
#350–750 · Legendary | 400 | Unsleeping — always at maximum stamina on the farm (small AOE) | 256 trainer airdrop · 10 in the free mint · 1 trainer raffle · rest for future events |
🌸 Bloom
#750–2,750 · Legendary | 2,000 | Regenerates a % of Max HP every combat turn | 1,500 trainer airdrop · 50 in the free mint · 1 trainer raffle · rest for future events |
Rare
#2,750–6,750 | 4,000 | Normal working Yakkamon | 3,000 trainer airdrop · 50 in the free mint · rest for future events |
Uncommon
#6,750–22,000 | 15,000 | Normal working Yakkamon | 11,882 in the free mint · rest for future events |

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Genesis Legendaries
chunks.text:
Who is airdropped which. Unchanged in shape: the top 2,000 on the pre-registration leaderboard receive a Legendary and ranks 2,001–5,000 a Rare Egg. Storm goes to ranks 1–50, Echo to 51–250, Ghost to 251–500 and Bloom to 501–2,000; ranks 1–3 take Storm plus Echo and ranks 4–10 Storm plus Ghost. Add the airdrop counts up and they match: 50 + 203 + 256 + 1,500 Legendaries and 3,000 Rares for 5,000 trainers, the extra ten being the second monster for the top 10 (the docs’ 256 for Ghost is one short of the 257 that 4–10 plus 251–500 implies, which we read as a rounding slip rather than a missing monster).

Tide is gone, and two names moved. The 12 August ladder ran Storm / Echo / Bloom / Tide. The Yakkapedia and the airdrop table now run Storm / Echo / Ghost / Bloom: the 251–500 monster that used to be called Bloom is Ghost, and the 501–2,000 monster that used to be called Tide is Bloom. On the free-mint stream Adam called the Ghost entry a typo that would be fixed in the docs, and Bryn added that the names don’t change what the monsters do — "they’re functionally the same things, they have the same boosts, we’re just renaming them to match our types". As of 2 September the docs still say Ghost, so that is the name we use. If you were in line for a Tide, you are in line for a Bloom.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Genesis Legendaries
chunks.text:
What the abilities mean in play. Three of the four are farm auras, not battle skills: Storm speeds up every Yakkamon in a large radius, Echo doubles the output of the few working next to it, and Ghost removes the stamina cycle for its neighbours entirely. Only Bloom is a combat ability — and on the stream Bryn called per-turn HP regeneration "absolutely busted" on a monster with good defensive stats, an anchor the opponent has to remove in a single turn or not at all. How small and large AOE differ, and how these auras stack with each other, is its own system: Utilities & Auras.

Four ways to get one. The trainer airdrop is still the overwhelming majority (2,009 of the 2,750 Legendaries), but it is no longer the only route: 68 Legendaries are hidden in the 14 September free mint (3 Storm, 5 Echo, 10 Ghost, 50 Bloom — about a 0.7% chance per mint), one of each is set aside for a trainer raffle with no published rules, and the remainder is held for future game events. Storm is scarcer than it looks: 75 exist in total, and only 50 are being airdropped.

chunks.title: Gameplay: The Genesis Legendaries
chunks.text:
Read the fine print. The Yakkapedia carries two caveats of its own: the ID ranges are an internal numbering system that may differ from the NFT IDs, and "codenames, descriptions, images and utility will be tweaked to fit the finalised gameplay". The portraits are still silhouettes. And the numbers behind each ability — the actual radius, what "within range" counts — are unpublished; Bryn said on the stream that the utilities are descriptive text for now because the values are still being balanced, and will keep being tuned up to release. One more wrinkle: the Yakkapedia says 11,882 Uncommons appear in the free mint, while the free mint page says 9,882, which is the figure that adds up to 10,000. We show the docs’ number and flag it.

Like this: The founding members' badge — and now the badge has a job description printed on the back.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon Dev Stream 9-1-26 Recap — Free Mint, Game Updates & Launch Calendar
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 17 (4:05): Yakkamon Dev Stream 9-1-26 Recap — Free Mint, Game Updates & Launch Calendar. The free-mint stream in four minutes: 10,000 hidden Yakkamon on the Ronin Launchpad from 14 September, five waves gated by your rank at the 10 September snapshot, one NFT per wave, 68 Legendaries in the pool and a 14 October reveal — plus the game updates that landed alongside it (utilities as economic auras, absence pauses the farm, no gear, no evolutions at launch) and the calendar from here to Chapter 0.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon Dev Stream 8-21-26 Recap and Game Economy
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 15 (5:04): Yakkamon Dev Stream 8-21-26 Recap and Game Economy. The third dev stream in five minutes, plus the economy post that landed the same day. Combat turned out to be a lane-based 3v3 auto-battler, farm plots now degrade and need refertilising, identical boosts don't stack, and rarity is fixed at species level — so a good common can out-stat a middling rare. The economy half covers the split between free-to-play gathered resources and the tradeable layer, and what that does to the Wave 1 argument.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon — Your Rank Buys Less Than You Think
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 13 (4:40): Yakkamon — Your Rank Buys Less Than You Think. Your wave is a market position, not a head start. Everything is tradable from day one, so Wave 1 walks into a market with no sellers, while a later wave arrives to cheaper, deeper stock and two weeks of everyone else's mistakes already priced in. What rank actually buys you — and the four assumptions that would overturn the whole argument.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon Airdrop: Legendary Supply Just Doubled — And The Rule Nobody's Reading
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 11 (7:33): Yakkamon Airdrop: Legendary Supply Just Doubled — And The Rule Nobody's Reading. The four Genesis Legendaries named, the ladder change explained band by band, and the odds recalculated against 77,763 trainers. Includes the correction to EP 10 below, and the rule that decides whether you keep the rank you're sitting on.

chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 09 (22:11): I Graded Yakkamon's First Dev Stream (6 Aug) — One Decision Gets a C. Nine decisions from the 6 August dev stream, graded A to C — what the team got right, and the one call that makes the top of the leaderboard purchased rather than contested.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon Leaderboard Is Live
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 14 (4:33): Yakkamon Leaderboard Is Live. The deposit leaderboard is now on this site, scored from on-chain Base and Ronin transfers on the published point rules. What it shows once you look: roughly 3,000 addresses have deposited against 5,000 airdrop places, and the weekly multiplier drops 0.2× every Monday whether or not the timing ever feels right.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon $FLOWER Deposits: Week One Pays 3× — Then It Drops
chunks.text: YakkamonWorld video, episode 05 (2:29): Yakkamon $FLOWER Deposits: Week One Pays 3× — Then It Drops. Everything about deposits before you send anything: the decaying weekly multiplier, the per-deposit size bonus, and the trap that costs people points.

chunks.title: Video: Yakkamon Regions Explained — How to Expand Your World

Privacy

Official docs ↗

We are not the Yakkamon team. This is a fan-run site with no connection to Thought Farm. We can’t see your account, change your points, or fix anything inside the game. For that you need the official site.

chunks.title: About — WHAT THIS IS
chunks.text:
WHAT THIS IS

YakkamonWorld exists because the rules of this game are scattered. Some of it is in the official docs, some is said once on a dev stream and never written down, and some of it — the deposit maths, the rank ladder, what a streak is actually worth — only becomes clear when somebody sits down and works it out.

So that is what this site is: the published rules, in plain language, plus the arithmetic nobody else has bothered to do. Guides for the things people keep asking about, news when something genuinely changes, and a deposit leaderboard built from public blockchain data because the numbers were there for anyone to read.

It is free, it needs no account, and there is nothing to sign into.

chunks.title: About — WHO WRITES IT
chunks.text:
WHO WRITES IT

Yakkamon players. We pre-registered like everyone else, we deposit like everyone else, and we have exactly the same information you do — no insider line to the studio, no early access, no private briefings.

That is worth stating plainly, because it cuts both ways. It means nothing here is authorised or approved by anyone. It also means nobody is telling us what to write.

Plenty of what ends up on the site starts with a reader. Tips that hold up get published with the sender’s name on them, and a fair few corrections have come in from people who spotted something before we did.

chunks.title: About — HOW WE WORK
chunks.text:
HOW WE WORK

Published sources first. The official documentation, the team’s own announcements and dev streams, and the game itself. When something comes from a stream rather than the docs, we say so — spoken answers get revised more often than written ones.

Chain data where it exists. Deposits are public transfers on Base and Ronin, so they can be read and added up rather than guessed at. That is where the leaderboard comes from.

We test before we publish. The deposit points formula went up only after we rebuilt a real account’s deposits from chain data and the total matched the game exactly, to the point.

Our own reasoning is labelled as ours. Where we are working something out rather than reporting it — what a rank is likely to cost, whether waiting is worth it — it is marked as our reading, not the rules.

We say when we don’t know. Dates that haven’t been confirmed, numbers nobody has published, mechanics that have only been hinted at. An honest gap is more useful than a confident guess.

We have been critical of the game, and expect to be again. A fan site that only ever cheers is not much use to the people reading it.

chunks.title: About — WHEN WE GET IT WRONG
chunks.text:
WHEN WE GET IT WRONG

We do, and the rules move underneath us as well — a referral change or a schedule shift can make a page wrong overnight without anybody touching it.

When that happens we fix the page and say what changed, rather than quietly editing it and hoping nobody noticed. If you find something wrong, tell us. Corrections go to the front of the queue, and we would much rather hear it from you than leave it up.

chunks.title: About — CONTENT AND IMAGE USAGE
chunks.text:
CONTENT AND IMAGE USAGE

Yakkamon, its artwork, its characters and its game content belong to Thought Farm. Game details, screenshots and images used on this site come from the official docs.yakkamon.com, the team’s public announcements and the game itself, and are used here for reference, commentary and player guidance.

We claim no ownership of any of it, and this site is not endorsed by or affiliated with Thought Farm in any way. Where we are quoting or describing something official, the official source is the one to trust — and it is always linked so you can check it yourself.

Our own writing, the calculations and the leaderboard are our work. Quote them, argue with them, use them in your own guides — a link back is appreciated but not demanded. If you are from Thought Farm and want something here changed or taken down, write to us and it will be.

chunks.title: About — HOW IT PAYS FOR ITSELF
chunks.text:
HOW IT PAYS FOR ITSELF

Barely, is the honest answer. Links to yakkamon.com carry our access code, YAKKA-UDBVPX, which gets you a Gold Box in game and earns us leaderboard points. It costs you nothing, you can ignore it entirely, and it is the only thing this site earns.

What we don’t do: take payment for coverage, accept anything in exchange for a favourable write-up, or let any of it change what goes on the page. The privacy page spells out the rest — including that analytics only run if you say yes.

chunks.title: About — WHAT WE CAN’T DO
chunks.text:
WHAT WE CAN’T DO

Anything inside your account. Recover it, restore a streak, chase missing points, change a rank. Only the official team can.

Tell you whether to deposit. We will show you the arithmetic. The decision is yours, and we can’t give financial advice.

Promise the rules will hold. This game is still in development. Everything here describes the rules as they stand today.

We will never ask for your seed phrase, private key, password or wallet access, and we will never ask you to connect a wallet. Nobody legitimate ever will. Anyone claiming to be us and asking for that is a scammer.

chunks.title: About — SAY HELLO
chunks.text:
SAY HELLO

Corrections, tips, scam reports, or just an argument about the deposit maths — the contact form reaches us, or email yakkamonworld@gmail.com directly. We are also on Telegram, X and YouTube.

Last updated 20 August 2026.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›The Game That Starts the Next Morning

Guideline
The Game That Starts the Next Morning

Aug 18, 2026

Every serious piece written about Yakkamon so far — ours very much included — has been about the same eleven weeks. Points. Multipliers. Streak timing. Which rank band gets Tide instead of a Rare Egg. It's the right obsession, because the leaderboard finalizes one week before early access and everything it decides is permanent.

But it does end. Somewhere in November or December the board locks, three days later the airdrop lands, and four days after that the doors open. At that point every optimization anyone has made stops mattering and a completely different game begins — one that almost nobody has planned for, because we've all been staring at a scoreboard.

This is an attempt at that plan. Not predictions about unreleased content, but what the published mechanics already commit the opening weeks to looking like, and the strategic conclusions that follow from them. Some of these run against the instincts a creature-collector normally trains into you.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — First: be honest about what your rank actually bought
chunks.text:
First: be honest about what your rank actually bought

Your leaderboard finish buys you exactly three things.

A monster, if you land top 5,000 — a Genesis Legendary in the top 2,000, a Rare Egg from 2,001 to 5,000.

A trainer number, which is cosmetic bragging rights and nothing else.

An entry date, via your wave.

That's the whole list. It does not buy you resources, land, gear, crafting progress, or any in-game currency. Your $FLOWER deposit isn't a war chest waiting in an account — it's a balance that unlocks when your wave gets access, and until then it's inert.

This matters because a lot of people are treating rank as a proxy for "how strong I start." It isn't. A rank-800 trainer and a rank-15,000 trainer both begin with an empty base, one starter creature, and the same tutorial. One of them has a Tide and a two-week head start. That's real, but much narrower than the leaderboard's emotional weight suggests.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis one: breadth beats depth, and it isn't close
chunks.text:
Thesis one: breadth beats depth, and it isn't close

Here is the single most under-discussed rule in the game.

Type locking. Each resource is gated to a monster type. A Grass type gathers Wood. A Fire type cannot — the game refuses outright, with an in-game message reading "Fire type cannot harvest wood!" It isn't a penalty or an efficiency loss. It's a hard block.

Now stack that against two other published facts: there are roughly 50–60 species at launch, and the world splits into regions — deserts, volcanoes, oceans — each holding materials found nowhere else.

The conclusion follows immediately, and it's the opposite of what creature-collectors train you to do. Your roster's breadth, not its quality, sets the ceiling on what you can produce at all. A player with twelve mediocre monsters of twelve different types can gather twelve resource lines. A player with four exceptional monsters of two types can gather two, no matter how good those four are. The second player has better numbers and a smaller game.

In practice, for opening week:

Catch widely before you catch well. A common of a type you don't have is worth more than a better roll of a type you already run.

Treat each new type as a key, not a unit. The question isn't "is this one strong," it's "does this one open a door."

Re-hunting the same species for a better stat roll is a later activity. It's real — individual stats vary and traits change how a monster farms — but it optimizes a lane you've already opened.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis one: breadth beats depth, and it isn't close
chunks.text: The natural instinct, especially for anyone arriving with a Genesis Legendary, is to build around the good monster. That's a trap in week one. Your Legendary is one type. It cannot harvest what it isn't.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis two: your storage bin is your real output ceiling
chunks.text:
Thesis two: your storage bin is your real output ceiling

Gathering doesn't flow into your inventory. It stacks in a storage bin that keeps filling while you're offline — and caps. Screenshots show early bins capped at 20 and later ones at 120, displaying "MAX" when full.

Once a bin hits MAX it stops accepting. Every hour it sits full is production that simply never happened. That turns a chore into the central scheduling problem of the idle half of the game, and produces a counter-intuitive result: past a certain point, adding monsters to a job doesn't increase your output — it fills the bin faster and wastes more of it.

Think about the shape of it. If you check in twice a day and your bin fills in four hours, you're banking a third of your theoretical production and burning the rest. Adding a second monster to that job doesn't help; it fills the bin in two hours and wastes even more. What helps is a bigger bin, an earlier check-in, or spreading those monsters across different jobs with their own separate caps.

Priority | Why it beats the obvious alternative |

Bin capacity upgrades | Lifts the ceiling rather than pushing harder against it — probably the highest-value early investment in the game |

Spread across jobs | Separate bins mean separate caps, so a long overnight gap wastes proportionally less |

Match assignments to your routine | A once-a-day player wants slow jobs with big bins; a frequent player can run fast jobs and empty them |

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis two: your storage bin is your real output ceiling
chunks.text:
Nobody can calculate the exact break-even yet, because cycle duration, yield per cycle and stamina cost are all unpublished. But the shape of the trade-off is already fixed by the rules, and that's enough to plan around.

Update, 28 Aug 2026. The official Regions post puts a ceiling above the bin: your Region is made of tiles, and each tile you claim raises "how much you can run at once". The bin argument still holds within a tile — but tile count decides how many bins you have, and tiles are bought with what the bins hold. It also says moving resources between Regions is a core mechanic, which is a second scheduling problem this piece didn’t know about. Neither changes the priority order above; both make "spread across jobs" a tile budget rather than a free choice.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis three: your wave is a market position, not just a head start
chunks.text:
Thesis three: your wave is a market position, not just a head start

Update, 21 Aug 2026. The official economy post says easily gathered free-to-play resources are kept separate from the tradeable economy. That undercuts the argument below where it concerns ordinary materials — if wood and berries aren’t tradeable, there is no Wave 1 scarcity premium on them, and later waves can’t buy their way to parity on basics either. The reasoning still holds for monsters, rares and crafted goods, which are the tradeable layer. Left in place rather than rewritten, so the correction is visible.

This is the one I think will surprise people most.

Waves enter a week apart: Wave 1 on launch day, Wave 2 seven days later, Wave 3 seven days after that, Wave 4 "confirmed closer to launch." The obvious reading is that Wave 1 gets a two-week head start on progress.

But every core resource and creature is tradable on-chain, and there's a marketplace in the game from day one. That changes what a head start is.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis three: your wave is a market position, not just a head start
chunks.text:
Update, 2 September 2026. The free-mint stream retires the "market with no sellers" detail below as written. Hidden free-mint NFTs are tradable on Ronin from 14 September, seven weeks before early access, so a monster market exists before anyone enters the game. Separately, the official Important Dates page now puts the in-game marketplace, auctions and $FLOWER withdrawals at Chapter 0, one month after early access — so for ordinary materials the wave-timing argument is weaker still, and for monsters the market opens before the waves rather than with them. The broader point — that later waves buy into deeper, better-informed markets — survives; the seven-day monopoly does not.

Wave 1 doesn't primarily enter a game two weeks earlier. Wave 1 enters a market with no sellers. For seven days, the only Wood, Stone and berries in existence are held by the first cohort, and demand arrives in waves after them. Whatever the early scarcity premium turns out to be, Wave 1 is the only group positioned to capture it.

By the same logic, later waves enter a progressively cheaper, deeper market. A Wave 3 player starts two weeks behind on progress — but starts in a world where basic materials already have sellers, prices have found a level, and the gear that gates the first serious hunts can potentially be bought rather than farmed.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis three: your wave is a market position, not just a head start
chunks.text:
If you're Wave 1, your scarce window is measured in days and applies to ordinary materials, not just rare ones. Deciding in advance what you'll sell and what you'll hoard is worth more than any tutorial optimization.

If you're Wave 3 or 4, the "I'm behind" framing is mostly wrong. You're behind on progress and ahead on information — you'll enter knowing which types are bottlenecked, what things cost, and which strategies the first cohort already disproved. That's a real asset if you use the intervening weeks to watch.

Wave 4 has no confirmed date at all, and it covers a very large share of everyone who gets in. If you've deposited $FLOWER, your balance unlocks with your access, not with launch day — so an undated Wave 4 is an undated lockup on real money. That's the strongest practical argument for pushing your rank above the Wave 4 line, and it has nothing to do with monsters.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — Thesis four: upkeep is a tax nobody has priced
chunks.text:
Thesis four: upkeep is a tax nobody has priced

Monsters get hungry. They get hurt. They sleep to recover stamina and restart on their own. They can ask for a specific item with a speech bubble, and there's an item bar of milk, flowers, mushrooms and health items to answer with.

The consequence is easy to state and easy to underestimate: a monster in a bad state isn't earning. Upkeep is not flavor, it's a running cost on your entire production base, and it scales with roster size.

Which means the breadth strategy above has a natural limit. Every type you add is another mouth. The optimum is not "catch everything," it's "catch one of everything you can keep fed." Where that line sits depends on food economics nobody has seen yet, but anyone planning a sprawling roster should expect a feeding bill to arrive with it.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — What launch morning should actually look like
chunks.text:
What launch morning should actually look like

Do the tutorial, then immediately go wide. Get into the Hunting Area — 5 berries to enter in the launch screenshot — and prioritize catching unfamiliar types over better versions of what you have.

Expand land early. The first expansion reads 10 Wood + 1 Stone. Land is what lets you run more stations and more jobs at once, and more jobs means more separate bins.

Find out what your bins hold, and time your check-ins to that number rather than to habit. This single measurement should shape your whole schedule.

Don't build around your Legendary. Use it — but it's one type, and week one is about opening lanes.

Watch the market from hour one, whether or not you intend to trade. Prices are the fastest available signal for which types are bottlenecked.

Don't chase perfect rolls yet. Traits and genetics are real and will matter enormously later. They matter far less than having a second Fire type.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — What would overturn any of this
chunks.text:
What would overturn any of this

Being straight about the load-bearing assumptions:

Cycle and stamina numbers are unpublished. If work cycles turn out to be very long relative to bin caps, the overflow problem largely dissolves and thesis two weakens considerably.

The full type chart is unknown. Only Grass→Wood is confirmed. If types map many-to-one onto resources, breadth matters much less than argued here.

Utilities land in September. What each Genesis Legendary actually does could easily make building around it correct after all.

PvP isn't in early access, so none of this weighs combat viability. When PvP arrives, the calculus around stats and traits changes sharply.

Market behavior is a guess. The wave economics above are reasoned from the fact that trading exists and entry is staggered. Real markets do surprising things.

Every one of these is a place where we'd expect to be partly wrong. The reasoning is laid out so you can see exactly where it breaks when the numbers arrive, rather than having to take it on trust.

chunks.title: The Race Ends in November — Here's the Game That Starts the Next Morning — The point
chunks.text:
The point

The pre-registration race has been a fair, well-documented contest with clear rules, and it's been worth playing carefully. But it's a qualifier, not the tournament. It decides which monster you're handed and which morning you walk in.

What you do on that morning is a separate skill, and right now it's an unpracticed one for everyone — including the people at the top of the leaderboard. There's an unusual window where someone who has thought carefully about bin capacity and type coverage can outplay someone who out-deposited them by a factor of ten.

That window closes about a week after launch, when everyone has learned the same lessons the expensive way.

This is our own reasoning from published mechanics — not official, not insider information, and not a prediction of unreleased content. Every mechanic referenced is documented with its source in the field guide.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›What Actually Changed in the Airdrop

Community
What Actually Changed in the Airdrop

Aug 14, 2026 · Odds updated for a field of 77,763 trainers

Update, 2 September 2026. Two of the names used below have changed. The official Yakkapedia and airdrop table now run Storm / Echo / Ghost / Bloom: the 251–500 monster this article calls Bloom is now Ghost, and the 501–2,000 monster it calls Tide is now Bloom. The team says the monsters and their boosts are unchanged — the names were swapped to match their types. The utilities are also published now: Storm makes Yakkamon within range work 2× as fast (large AOE), Echo doubles the resources of those within range (small AOE), Ghost keeps those within range at maximum stamina (small AOE), and Bloom regenerates a share of its Max HP every combat turn. Total supplies are 75 / 275 / 400 / 2,000, with 68 of them hidden in the 14 September free mint. The rank bands below are unchanged. The full table →

Yakkamon rewrote the Monster NFT airdrop on 12 August and published the monster names on the 14th. Between the two, the picture only became legible this week — and it’s a bigger change than the first announcement suggested.

This is the full breakdown: what moved, the supply maths, your actual odds, and where the change creates problems nobody is discussing.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 1. The mapping that explains everything
chunks.text:
1. The mapping that explains everything

The old ladder used placeholder labels. The new one uses monster names, and one line in the team’s own comparison table is the key to reading the whole change:

"Echo is the old Legendary A." Bloom was Legendary Egg B. Tide was Legendary Egg C. And Storm is entirely new — it was added above the existing ladder rather than inserted into it.

Once you have that, every band becomes comparable:

Rank | Was in line for | Now receives | Effect |

1 – 3 | Legendary Egg A | 🌩 Storm + ⬜ Echo | ⬆️ gains a second monster |

4 – 10 | Legendary Egg A | 🌩 Storm + 🌸 Bloom | ⬆️ gains a second monster |

11 – 50 | Legendary Egg A | 🌩 Storm | ⬆️ upgraded to the new top tier |

51 – 100 | Legendary Egg A | ⬜ Echo | same monster, utility lifted |

101 – 250 | Legendary Egg B | ⬜ Echo | ⬆️ moved up a tier |

251 – 500 | Legendary Egg B | 🌸 Bloom | same slot, utility lifted |

501 – 1,000 | Legendary Egg C | 🌊 Tide | same slot, utility lifted |

1,001 – 2,000 | Rare Egg | 🌊 Tide | ⬆️ Rare becomes Legendary |

2,001 – 5,000 | Rare Egg | Rare Egg | unchanged, utility lifted |

1,200 ranks improved. 3,800 held their slot with utility lifted. Zero moved down. That’s the whole change in one line, and it’s why the team’s "nothing has been nerfed" claim survives scrutiny.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 2. The supply maths
chunks.text:
2. The supply maths

| Before | After | Change |

Genesis Legendaries | 1,000 | 2,010 | +1,010 |

Rare Eggs | 4,000 | 3,000 | −1,000 |

Total Monster NFTs | 5,000 | 5,010 | +10 |

The individual counts are official: Storm 50, Echo 203, Bloom 257, Tide 1,500. The airdrop totals 5,010 Monster NFTs across 5,000 trainers — the extra ten are the second monsters going to ranks 1–10.

The composition shift is the striking part. Legendaries went from 20% of all airdropped NFTs to 40%. The same number of trainers are rewarded; twice the proportion receive a Legendary.

Nobody was diluted by this. Worth stating plainly, because "doubling supply" normally means existing holders lose out. Here nothing has been minted yet — the airdrop happens at early access. Doubling the supply of an asset nobody holds costs nobody anything. It simply moves a thousand trainers from Rare to Legendary.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 3. Your actual odds
chunks.text:
3. Your actual odds

Against the current field of 77,763 registered trainers:

Outcome | Ranks | Share of registered trainers | Or roughly |

🌩 Storm | 1 – 50 | 0.06% | 1 in 1,555 |

Any Genesis Legendary (before) | 1 – 1,000 | 1.29% | 1 in 78 |

Any Genesis Legendary (now) | 1 – 2,000 | 2.57% | 1 in 39 |

Any Monster NFT | 1 – 5,000 | 6.43% | 1 in 16 |

So the practical effect for an individual trainer is that the chance of finishing with a Legendary roughly doubled, from about one in 78 to about one in 39.

And you can now watch this decay in real time. We first ran these numbers against a field of 68,700 trainers. The field has grown 13% in the days since, and every one of these percentages fell with it — a Legendary slipped from 2.91% to 2.57% without a single rule changing. The reward bands are fixed in number; the queue for them is not. That is the argument for climbing now rather than later, and it gets stronger every day you wait.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 4. Storm changes the design, not just the ladder
chunks.text:
4. Storm changes the design, not just the ladder

Until this week the site’s position — taken from the team’s own statements — was that the Genesis Legendaries are equal in power and differ in species and role rather than strength. Some battle monsters, some farm utility.

Storm is the stated exception. It’s described as the newest monster in the set and the hardest to earn, and the only route to one is a top-50 finish.

That matters beyond the reward table, because it fixes something structural. Under the old ladder, ranks 1 through 100 all received an identical reward — meaning the difference between finishing first and finishing ninety-ninth was worth precisely nothing. We flagged that as a real design weakness after the first dev stream.

Adding a scarcer monster above the ladder solves it without breaking the rest. The team couldn’t steepen the curve by making Echo beat Bloom — that would contradict the same-power-level design the other three rest on. Adding a fourth monster above them creates the gradient while leaving that design intact. It’s a neat solution and worth crediting.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 5. The leaderboard locks — and that’s the part to plan around
chunks.text:
5. The leaderboard locks — and that’s the part to plan around

New terminology arrived with this update, and it’s the most consequential thing in it for anyone currently sitting in a good position.

The team’s wording: you have to earn your rank and hold it until the leaderboard locks. Once it does, the airdrop is closed for good.

A rank you occupy today is not a rank you own. Sitting at 1,800 now means nothing if two hundred people pass you before the lock.

There is no second chance. No later window, no follow-up airdrop, and — the team is explicit — no sale and no way to buy in.

The lock is now dated relative to launch. The official Important Dates page puts it one week before early access, with rewards three days later — and early access itself is now given as November or December. The exact day is still to be announced. The full schedule →

Combine that with the hidden leaderboard and a common plan stops working. The team said on the first dev stream that the board will be hidden as launch approaches, to stop last-day gaming. So "coast now, sprint at the end" fails twice over: you won’t know where the line is, and you won’t know whether you’ve crossed it.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 6. Where climbing actually pays
chunks.text:
6. Where climbing actually pays

Most of this ladder is flat, and points spent inside a band buy nothing at all.

Band | Ranks inside it | Everyone receives |

11 – 50 | 40 | 🌩 Storm |

51 – 250 | 200 | ⬜ Echo |

251 – 500 | 250 | 🌸 Bloom |

501 – 2,000 | 1,500 | 🌊 Tide |

2,001 – 5,000 | 3,000 | Rare Egg |

5,001 – 100,000 | 95,000 | Early access only |

Climbing from rank 1,900 to rank 600 gains you nothing — both receive Tide. Climbing from 2,100 to 1,999 moves you from a Rare Egg to a Genesis Legendary. The value is entirely at the edges: ranks 10, 50, 250, 500, 2,000, 5,000 and 100,000.

The widened Tide band is a double-edged thing. It made a Legendary far more reachable — and it created the largest flat zone in the Legendary bracket, 1,500 ranks deep. If you land inside it, further effort is wasted unless you can realistically reach 500.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 7. The problem this update makes worse
chunks.text:
7. The problem this update makes worse

One consequence nobody has raised, and it follows directly from the widening.

We wrote previously about a wallet-splitting incentive in the deposit design: because the deposit size bonus is rated per deposit and the rewards are granted per account, a large depositor can split across wallets, lose around 10% of their points, and multiply their reward slots.

Extending the Legendary band to rank 2,000 makes that more attractive, not less. More split wallets now land inside Legendary territory.

Wallets occupying the top ranks | Old ladder | Now |

1 | 1 monster | 2 monsters |

10 | 10 monsters | 20 monsters, all Legendary |

100 | 100 monsters | 110 monsters, all Legendary |

That assumes each split wallet carries enough points to occupy a top rank, which for a large depositor in the opening deposit week is plausible rather than certain. But the direction is unambiguous.

The fix is the team’s own precedent. They already require the friend to link a wallet and deposit 100 $FLOWER before a referral counts. Applying the same test to airdrop eligibility — requiring a minimum of points earned from non-deposit sources — would make a hundred split wallets need a hundred aged accounts and a week of daily play each. It costs honest players nothing.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 8. What this tells you about the team
chunks.text:
8. What this tells you about the team

Three things worth reading from how this was handled.

They expanded rather than reshuffled. The easy version of this update would have moved rewards around within a fixed pool. Instead they added a monster and widened the Legendary bracket — that costs them scarcity, and they did it anyway.

They published a before-and-after table. Most studios announce the new state and let players work out what moved. Publishing a band-by-band comparison, including the bands that only held their slot, is a choice that invites scrutiny.

But the naming came two days late, and that gap caused real confusion — including ours. The 12 August table used labels like "Rare Egg A" for a band that turns out to receive a Genesis Legendary. We read that as a downgrade and published an analysis that was wrong. Announcing the names and the bands together would have prevented every misreading we’ve seen this week.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — 9. What’s still unknown
chunks.text:
9. What’s still unknown

The utilities. Due in September. Everything about what these monsters actually do — and what "utility lifted" amounts to in practice — is unverifiable until then.

The lock date. Not announced. It decides how long you have.

Whether the two monsters at ranks 1–10 are separate creatures or one reward described in two parts. The phrasing points at separate, and the 5,010-across-5,000 total supports that.

Where Storm sits against the others in practice. "Hardest to earn" is a statement about scarcity. Whether it’s also stronger is a September question.

chunks.title: What Actually Changed in the Airdrop — A Full Breakdown — The short version
chunks.text:
The short version

Legendary supply doubled — 1,000 to 2,010, now 40% of all airdropped NFTs.

The Legendary line moved out from rank 1,000 to rank 2,000. If you’d written a Legendary off, reconsider.

Nobody moved down a band. 1,200 ranks improved, 3,800 held their slot.

Storm is new, top 50 only, and it gives the leaderboard a gradient it badly needed.

You have to hold your rank until the leaderboard locks — and you won’t be able to see the line when it happens.

The wallet-splitting hole got wider, and the fix already exists in their referral rules.

chunks.text:
