chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced

Community
First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced

Dev stream: Aug 6, 2026 · Published Aug 7 · Updated Aug 14, 2026

Thought Farm ran their first Yakkamon-only Discord stream on August 6th. A lot changed, and some of it reverses advice that was correct last week — including ours. Here's everything that matters, grouped by what it affects.

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 1. The $FLOWER deposit system has been rebuilt
chunks.text:
1. The $FLOWER deposit system has been rebuilt

This is the big one, and it lands two days before deposits open. There are now two separate bonuses, and both reward depositing early and in larger single transfers.

Bonus | How it works |

Weekly multiplier | 3× through the opening week, then −0.2× every week until it rests at 1×. |

Size bonus | Rated per deposit, doubling at every step: +10% at 50 $FLOWER, +20% at 500, +40% at 5,000, +80% at 50,000. |

The size bonus is per transfer. Craig was explicit: depositing 25 $FLOWER and then another 25 does not reach the 50 tier. It has to be one transaction. You keep your $FLOWER either way — the multiplier applies to points only.

The stated intent is to stop a last-minute rush before launch. They want points earned early, rather than everyone piling in on the final day.

This reverses our own tip. We previously advised splitting deposits weekly, because the bonus appeared to follow your cumulative deposited total. It doesn't any more, and the decaying multiplier makes later slices worth less than earlier ones. Our tip has been rewritten to match.

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 2. The official X account, and 10 free points
chunks.text:
2. The official X account, and 10 free points

The compromise of @playyakkamon is confirmed — a phishing link was posted from it. X support was slow enough that the team stopped waiting and created a new account, @yakkamon_game.

Two things matter for you. First, the game itself was never compromised — you don't need to re-register or change anything about your account. Second, there are 10 bonus points waiting in the trainer dashboard.

Go and reconnect X. Anyone who connected the old account keeps those points and earns more, for 20 total. New connections earn the usual 10. It shows as "reconnect" in the dashboard if you'd connected before.

Three or four fake Yakkamon websites have already been taken down. Treat any Yakkamon link you didn't type yourself with suspicion.

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 3. The numbers, and the crackdown
chunks.text:
3. The numbers, and the crackdown

45,000 pre-registered trainers at the time of the stream. Around 10,000 arrived through private codes distributed via Sunflower Land and Ronin, and another 8,000–9,000 tried to sign up before referrals opened to everyone.

Roughly 4,500–5,000 bot accounts banned. Referrals will be double-verified before the leaderboard is finalized, so suspicious entries you can see now are expected to be cleaned up.

Discord points are switched off. The emoji reward system turned into reaction farming — chat hit ten messages a second — so they pulled it. It returns later as a manual weekly reward rather than an automated one.

The leaderboard will be hidden as launch approaches, to stop last-day gaming. Only the top 100 is visible now.

Worth acting on: the leaderboard going dark means the earlier you start climbing, the better a read you'll have on where you'll finish. Once it's hidden, you're flying blind.

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 4. What early access will actually include
chunks.text:
4. What early access will actually include

Early access in Q4 ships the fundamentals only: gathering, monsters, hunting, and basic combat.

PvP is not in early access. Neither is advanced breeding. Both were described as post-launch, arriving through Sunflower Land-style chapter releases rather than all at once on day one.

Two other design notes worth knowing. The day/night cycle runs on a sped-up in-game clock, deliberately not tied to your real-world time — they've played games that do that and found it oppressive. And the season system may be weekly rather than quarterly: they're considering a Sunflower Land-style model with a winter week, a summer week, and different Yakkamon appearing week to week.

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 5. What the game is turning into
chunks.text:
5. What the game is turning into

The clearest description yet: idle farming, plus automation, plus creature collecting. Named influences were Pokémon, Palworld, and Zachtronics — that last one being the automation-puzzle lineage, which tells you a lot about the depth they're aiming for.

Hunting is the third pillar, and the part they think other web3 games get wrong. You'll place snacks, send monsters to search, and combine the day/night and seasonal systems to find specific creatures. Legendaries are meant to be hunted, not bought.

Monsters have hidden genetics. Each spawns with stat ranges and initial values you can't fully see, and training shapes what it becomes. A defensive species with a high attack roll, trained into attack, produces something distinct.

Breeding and bloodlines are planned as a specialization you could build an entire playstyle around.

Your monsters are the specialization, not separate boost items — the team you farm with and the team you fight with are the primary source of bonuses.

No forging. No combining ten commons into one rare; the designer dislikes the mechanic in creature collectors.

Mobile is confirmed, as a PWA you save to your home screen rather than an app store download, at least initially.

Want our opinion on all this? We graded every decision from the stream A to C in a separate piece — what the team got right, and the one call we’d change. Read the graded breakdown →

chunks.title: First Yakkamon Dev Stream (6 August): Everything They Announced — 6. Take all of it with a grain of salt
chunks.text:
6. Take all of it with a grain of salt

The team said this repeatedly, so it's worth repeating here. They're running hundreds of experiments and anything discussed can change before launch. Nothing above is a promise — it's where the project stands on August 7th.

chunks.text:

What the new multiplier means for timing, with the numbers worked through.

OPEN TIPS →

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August)
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August)

Community
We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August)

Dev stream: Aug 6, 2026 · Published Aug 11 · Updated Aug 14, 2026

We’ve already published the factual recap of Thought Farm’s first Yakkamon dev stream. This is the other half: what we think of it.

Nine decisions, graded. Some of this is critical — that’s the point. This is a team with five years of live-game experience shipping a second title, and they’ve earned a serious read rather than a hype post.

One note on the stream itself. The team asked people not to screen-record it, because things will change. We’ve respected that — no footage, quotes kept short, and everything below treated as where the project stood on 6 August rather than as a promise. They said "grain of salt" repeatedly, and they meant it.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — The scorecard
chunks.text:
The scorecard

Nine decisions, graded. Eight came out of the stream itself; the ninth predates it but underpins everything else.

Decision | Grade |

Specialization through monsters, not items | A |

New X account, made fast | A |

Reusing $FLOWER instead of launching a token (predates the stream) | A |

Referral rule change | A− |

Chapter-based rollout, PvP after launch | A− |

Decaying deposit multiplier | B |

Black-box genetics | B |

Hiding the leaderboard | B− |

The doubling size bonus | C |

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — What they got right
chunks.text:
What they got right

Specialization comes from your monsters

The designer said the primary way you specialize will be the monsters you have — your farming team and your combat team — rather than separate boost items. That’s the best decision of the stream, and it’s the one that makes everything else cohere.

It means the creatures are the game. In a lot of web3 games the creatures are skins and the real power sits in equipment, which quietly makes the collection meaningless. Putting power in the monsters means hunting matters, breeding matters and trading matters — three pillars reinforcing each other instead of competing. Their stated lesson from Sunflower Land was blunt: players only collect things with utility, and nobody wants cosmetic PFPs.

Abandoning the compromised X account

Their official account was compromised and a phishing link went out. They chased malicious domains through the night, then stopped waiting for X support and started a new account.

Correct, and the speed is the impressive part. Every hour that account stayed compromised it was a weapon pointed at their own community, with their verification badge on it.

The recovery move was smart too. Rather than just asking people to follow the new handle, they wired it into the dashboard: reconnect X and previous connectors keep their points and earn more, for 20 in total. That converts an administrative chore into a reward, so the migration actually happens.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — What they got right
chunks.text:
The cost: everyone still following the old handle now follows a compromised account and may never learn there’s a new one. The new account needs to be findable from every official surface, not just announced once.

No new token

Not from this stream, but underpinning all of it. In a space where a new project almost always means a new token to sell, choosing to reuse $FLOWER is the strongest signal of intent they’ve given.

Shipping narrow

Early access in Q4 ships the fundamentals only: gathering, monsters, hunting and basic combat. PvP and advanced breeding come after launch, in chapter releases.

Right call, and they’ve run this playbook for five years on Sunflower Land. But there’s a marketing tension worth naming: the airdrop is sold on Legendary monsters described as top of the power curve and built for combat. If combat is "basic" at launch, the headline reward is partly a promise about a system that doesn’t exist yet. Not dishonest — but someone chasing a Legendary should know they may hold it for months before the system that showcases it arrives.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Where we’d push back
chunks.text:
Where we’d push back

The doubling size bonus — our only C

The size bonus doubles at every step, up to +80% at 50,000 $FLOWER. Stack that on the opening week’s 3× multiplier and a single 50,000 deposit produces 190,000 points.

For comparison: grind every free action perfectly for two months, with no referrals, and you land near 900.

That’s roughly 190 to 1. Which means the top of this leaderboard isn’t competitive — it’s purchased. And the doubling structure specifically rewards concentration of capital rather than participation.

What we’d do instead: taper the size bonus rather than double it. Reward larger deposits with diminishing returns rather than accelerating ones, so the curve flattens at the top. You keep the incentive to deposit meaningfully while leaving the upper reaches reachable by effort.

To be fair: deposits are withdrawable and spendable in-game, which is genuinely unusual and far better than the lockups this space normally runs. And the team has never claimed the top 100 was reachable free. The early access cutoff is the top 100,000, and that is reachable free.

The wallet-splitting hole

This one came out of a reader conversation after the stream, and it’s the sharpest criticism of the deposit design we’ve seen.

Because the size bonus is rated per deposit, splitting a large sum across several wallets costs surprisingly little — while multiplying your leaderboard slots.

Same 50,000 $FLOWER, opening week | Points | Reward slots |

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Where we’d push back
chunks.text:
One wallet | 190,000 | 1 egg + 1 NFT |

Ten wallets of 5,000 | 17,000 each — 170,000 total | 10 eggs + 10 NFTs |

Splitting costs 10.5% of your points and turns one reward slot into ten. A 17,000-point account should land comfortably inside the top 5,000, so the trade is: give up one top-100 finish, gain roughly ten top-1,000 finishes, for about a tenth of your points. If the NFTs are tradable, that’s obviously worth doing.

Three fixes, in order of how well they’d work:

Apply the referral fix to the airdrop. They already require the friend to link a wallet and deposit 100 $FLOWER before a referral counts. Make the same thing a condition of airdrop eligibility — an account qualifies only with a minimum of points earned from non-deposit sources. Ten split wallets would each need a distinct aged Discord, a distinct X account and a week of daily play. Expensive at scale, and it costs honest players nothing.

Announce wallet-clustering checks in advance. Wallets funded from a common source are trivially detectable on-chain, and referrals are already double-verified before the leaderboard is finalized. Saying so beforehand deters more than catching people later.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Where we’d push back
chunks.text:
Cap reward slots per verified trainer. The exploit pays because ten Legendary Egg Cs are worth more than one Egg A — and since the team has since confirmed A, B and C are all the same power level, differing only in species and scarcity, steepening the curve isn’t available as a fix without breaking that design. Capping slots per verified identity is.

The blunt fix — making top rewards non-tradable — would end it instantly but breaks the tradability promise. Not worth it.

Hiding the leaderboard

As launch approaches they’ll hide the leaderboard so people can’t game it on the final day. The reasoning is sound — a visible board near a deadline becomes a bidding war.

But the cost lands on the wrong people. A visible leaderboard is how a free player knows whether their effort is working. Take it away and you’re asking people to grind daily toward a threshold they can’t see. Some will simply stop.

Our suggestion: hide the exact rank, show the band. Tell someone they’re in the top 5,000, or between 5,000 and 20,000, without showing the precise number or the threshold. You keep the motivational feedback and remove the sniping target.

Black-box genetics

Asked whether there would be formal design proposals, the designer said he wants to hide base-level systems — especially genetics — so the community back-solves how they work.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Where we’d push back
chunks.text:
We love the instinct. Games that publish every formula get solved in a week and then you’re playing a spreadsheet. Hidden systems create the discovery culture that keeps games alive for years.

The nervousness is about the market. Monsters are tradable on-chain, so when the underlying stats are hidden and the assets are tradable, information becomes an asset too — captured by whoever can datamine hardest or buy enough monsters to infer the distributions.

Our suggestion: publish the ranges, hide the rolls. Tell people a species has an attack range and that training shifts it. Don’t tell them the exact numbers on their monster. You keep the discovery and remove the scraping advantage.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — The thing nobody mentioned
chunks.text:
The thing nobody mentioned

This is inference rather than fact, so treat it as such.

By the team’s own description, the Yakkamon core is roughly one developer at ninety percent, one at fifty-fifty, and a twelve-week game design intern working on combat. The rest of the studio is still mainly on Sunflower Land.

That is a small team for a Q4 early access. It isn’t a criticism of competence — this is a studio that has run a live game for five years with over a hundred open source contributors, and they were open about the allocation rather than pretending otherwise.

But it means the Q4 window is tight, and "fundamentals only" starts to look less like philosophy and more like necessity. It also means a bus-factor risk they demonstrated on the stream itself: one developer got ill and the deposit launch moved five days. A minor slip, handled well — and a preview of what a bigger disruption looks like.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Four questions for the next stream
chunks.text:
Four questions for the next stream

What’s the rough chapter order after launch? Not dates — just whether PvP is early or late.

What’s the sink for common monsters, and when does it ship? Contracts were mentioned; details weren’t.

Will the hidden leaderboard show bands, or nothing at all?

Will stat ranges be published even if individual rolls aren’t?

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s First Dev Stream (6 August) — Our overall read
chunks.text:
Our overall read

The design instincts on this team are genuinely good. Power in the creatures rather than in items. No forging, for tonal reasons. Sped-up clocks so real life isn’t punished. Narrow launch, expand by chapter. Those are decisions made by people who have watched games fail and understand why.

The economy is where we’d push back, and specifically the acceleration of the size bonus — which turns the top of the leaderboard into something you buy rather than something you contest, and opens the wallet-splitting hole above.

And the biggest risk isn’t anything they decided. It’s bandwidth.

They’re being unusually honest about all of it — the bot numbers, the illness, the things they don’t know yet. That doesn’t guarantee anything. But it’s a better starting position than most projects in this space ever manage.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn’t What You Thought

Community
Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn’t What You Thought

Aug 21, 2026

The third dev stream ran an hour with Adam, Craig and Bryn — Spencer was off sick, so his work got narrated rather than demoed. It was the most mechanically dense hour the team has done, and unlike the last two it was almost entirely about the game rather than the pre-registration race.

Four things changed how you should plan a roster. Our Gameplay section has gone from 14 systems to 22, and the field guide poster has been redrawn around them.

The revised sheet — five new panels and a six-step core loop. Tap to open it full size, or read the guide if you’re on a phone.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — 1. Combat is a lane-based 3v3 auto-battler
chunks.text:
1. Combat is a lane-based 3v3 auto-battler

Until this week, "basic combat" was a bullet point. Now it has rules. Monsters hold assigned lanes in a 3v3 formation, you set positions before the fight, and you cannot move them mid-battle unless a skill does it for you. Skills fire in a fixed, visible order. Battles run on an animation timer you can speed up but probably not skip outright.

The tension Bryn named is type advantage versus skill-loop advantage: you can hold a favourable elemental matchup and still lose, because their shield lands before your one big hit. Target pacing is three to five rounds — under a minute — but with deliberate variance, such that the "average" fight is meant to be under 40% of all fights. Expect frequent one-turn solves and the occasional long grind.

The part that matters most for planning: respeccing is deliberately expensive. The intended route is to find a monster carrying the skill you want and extract it onto another. Buildcraft is supposed to come out of breeding, not out of swapping loadouts before every fight. This is explicitly not a game where you re-optimise per encounter — your team composition is a long-term project and the battle executes the plan.

Full detail: The Battle System →

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — 2. Your farm now wears out
chunks.text:
2. Your farm now wears out

The single most consequential mechanic revealed, and it arrived almost in passing from a job-card screenshot. Farm plots degrade as you use them. The example on screen read degraded 1.6× — that plot farms slower until you refertilise it, and fertiliser costs resources.

Read that against the storage bin cap and a long absence now costs you twice: you stop banking output at MAX, and your soil quality decays so that what does run, runs worse. Bryn was clear the intent isn’t to punish going wide — but an unattended Yakkamon farm decays rather than simply pausing, which is a real departure from Sunflower Land.

There’s a second half to it. Growing tiles come in groups of three, and upkeep scales more slowly than production does. Filling out a group is strictly better value per unit of upkeep than spreading thin — a deliberate push toward investing deep rather than wide.

No numbers were published. Not the degradation rate, not the fertiliser recipe, not the live group size. Only the single 1.6× example figure is public, and it came off a mock-up job card.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — 3. Identical boosts do not stack
chunks.text:
3. Identical boosts do not stack

Asked directly whether two monsters with a wood boost both contribute, the answer was no. Same-named boosts don’t stack. Two copies of "Wood Gatherer I" give you the effect once. Differently named or higher-ranked boosts do stack — "Wood Gatherer" alongside "Extreme Wood Gatherer" is two separate effects and both apply.

The stated intent is to remove any reason to hoard duplicates and create a strong reason to collect breadth. Combined with type locking, the shape of an optimal roster is legible for the first time:

Wide, not deep. One excellent specialist per job beats five copies of your best monster. That rules out the strategy most players would have defaulted to, and it’s the most actionable thing published all month.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — 4. Rarity is fixed at species level — and rarer isn’t simply stronger
chunks.text:
4. Rarity is fixed at species level — and rarer isn’t simply stronger

Two corrections that reframe the whole roster. First: rarity is set at the species level. Every individual of a species shares its tier. There is no rare version of a common monster and no legendary variant of an ordinary one. A whole category of speculation — grinding commons hoping for a lucky upgrade roll — is dead.

Second, and more surprising: the best commons can beat middling rares and roughly match a low-end legendary on raw stat outlay. What rarity actually buys is a higher ceiling as the monster levels, scarcer and higher-impact utility, and traits no other tier can access. Some commons carry unique traits you will need and cannot get anywhere else.

That should temper how the airdrop bands get read. A Genesis Legendary is a ceiling and a set of exclusive tools, not an automatic win — and the utilities still don’t land until September.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — What else moved
chunks.text:
What else moved

Gyms get full customisation; land probably doesn’t. Land layout is unlikely to be player-controlled at launch, but you’ll decorate a core gym that visiting trainers see when they arrive to battle you. Decoration becomes a social display rather than a private hobby.

Evolutions are per-monster and deliberately hidden. Triggers vary by species — a level, an item, some other condition — and many will be undocumented by design. The game hints that something is required without saying what.

Matchmaking is confirmed, with an anti-bot design. MMR-based, with no meaningful rewards below a cutoff — the band where weak human players sit, which makes the low end worthless to unsophisticated bots. Better bots get flagged through event tracking.

The meta is expected to move, and the team isn’t going to stop it. Early on, gathering and hunting specialists are the valuable monsters because throughput funds everything else. Once the arena and tournaments establish, demand should shift toward battle-stat monsters. They know, and they’re letting community demand set the pace.

An exclusive biome pack. Daniel Diggle, who designed the original Sunflower Land asset pack, has finished the UI HUD and given the studio early access to a biome pack covering biome types, seasons and elements — exclusive to Yakkamon. Adam described the result as a "V2" of the Sunflower Land look.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — What else moved
chunks.text:
Email login, PWA recommended, landscape. Email is the primary login method — no wallet needed to play. The PWA installed to your home screen is described as noticeably faster than a wallet’s embedded browser.

Guilds are pushed back. Acknowledged as popular, described as a lot of work, explicitly behind core functionality.

Player lore, warmly received. A community pitch that legendary monsters cause the weather and seasons got a yes-in-principle from both Adam and Bryn. Not confirmed — but the first piece of Yakkamon lore to come from a player.

100,000 pre-registered trainers, up from 45,000 two weeks ago.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — The honest caveats
chunks.text:
The honest caveats

The battle screenshot that circulated is an internal dev gym, not the finished battle screen — placeholder backgrounds, rough layout. Skill counts aren’t settled; the team is considering cutting to around two per monster with more passives. Real-time interaction during battles is in testing, not confirmed. The hunting mechanic itself is still described as not 100% locked. And the team repeated its standing disclaimer: everything is pre-launch and subject to change.

Most of the credit for the combat system went to Matt L, the studio’s game design intern, who has been on the team a matter of weeks.

chunks.title: Third Dev Stream: Combat Has Rules, Farms Wear Out, and Rarity Isn't What You Thought — What we’d do with this
chunks.text:
What we’d do with this

Stop planning around duplicates. Plan a wide roster with one strong specialist per resource type, because that’s what boost stacking rewards and type locking demands. Assume you’ll need to log in regularly rather than weekly, because degradation punishes absence in a way bin caps alone did not. And treat a Genesis Legendary as an access pass to exclusive traits rather than a guaranteed stat advantage — the September utility drop is still the thing that decides its real worth.

None of this moves your rank. Knowing the mechanics doesn’t change the leaderboard, and it still locks one week before early access launch. If you’re choosing where to spend the next hour, the schedule matters more than the meta. The tips that actually move rank →

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September

Community
Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September

Dev stream: second Yakkamon broadcast · Published Aug 14, 2026

Thought Farm ran their second Yakkamon-only stream, with Adam, Craig, Spencer and Bryn all on the mic for about an hour. It opened with an apology, closed with a request for more memes, and in between it moved two dates, put a number on how much money is sitting in the deposit pool, and explained for the first time what your monsters will actually do.

Here's everything that matters, ordered by how much it should change what you're doing this week.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 1. The airdrop change: the team's own account of it
chunks.text:
1. The airdrop change: the team's own account of it

Adam went straight at it. He described being put to the sword by the player base over the reward table update, and put the blame on the announcement rather than the change: he did a poor job writing it and conveying what had actually happened.

The reasoning behind the change was simple. Sign-ups exploded, and the top of the leaderboard started moving fast as deposits came in. So the team did two things: extended a solid reward down to the top 2,000 instead of the top 1,000, and added a brand new Legendary above the existing top tier as a thank-you to the players who had committed the most.

His summary of the outcome: in every case you are still getting the same monster, and in a lot of cases you're now getting something better.

And the band that caused the confusion is confirmed as Legendary. Adam said directly that the rare tier running up to 2,000 supply will be a Legendary as well — because the feedback made clear players wanted a real shot at one. That is exactly the reading our correction settled on after we initially got it wrong, and it's now confirmed out loud rather than inferred from a table.

What it means for you: nothing to do. If you were at rank 1,500 and panicking on the 12th, you weren't demoted, and the utility attached to your band went up rather than down. The panic was a communication failure, not a reward cut.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 2. What "Legendary" and "Rare" actually mean — and why it matters
chunks.text:
2. What "Legendary" and "Rare" actually mean — and why it matters

This is new information, and it's more consequential than it sounds. The team explained the internal definitions:

Tier | What defines it |

Legendary | Scarcity. Pre-minted, supply-limited, fixed. Once the supply of that monster exists, that's all there will ever be. |

Rare | Time. Catchable only during limited windows. The supply isn't fixed — it depends on how much players hunt during that window. |

Then the detail worth circling: Legendaries will have traits that only Legendaries can have. Not a bigger number on the same trait — abilities no other monster gets access to.

This doesn't contradict the "same power level" framing. That framing was about the Genesis Legendaries relative to each other — Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide differ by species and role, not strength. What's new is the gap between Legendary and Rare, which is now clearly a capability difference and not just a scarcity label.

Full utilities for each Genesis monster land in September. Until then the team's own request is to wait rather than trade on assumptions — they're still tuning drop rates, yields and even the art.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 3. The free mint may move to mid-September
chunks.text:
3. The free mint may move to mid-September

This is the single biggest scheduling item in the stream, and it wasn't framed as an announcement — it came out while Adam was answering a question about the leaderboard lock. The sequence he described:

Step | Timing given on stream |

Ronin free mint | "Likely" mid-September |

Mint reveal | Mid-October |

Leaderboard finalised | After the reveal — weeks, a month, possibly longer |

Rewards distributed, then early access | Q4 2026 (internal date exists, not shared) |

Update, 14 August — this one landed. The official docs have since moved the free mint to mid-September, with the reveal in mid-October. The caution below was written before that page went up. The published schedule →

Treat this as a signal, not a new date. The published date is still October 1st, and Adam said "likely" rather than announcing a change. But if the mint does land in mid-September, every verification deadline you've mentally filed under "end of September" moves up by roughly two weeks. Get your Discord and X verification done now rather than in late September — it costs you nothing to be early, and being late costs you the mint entirely.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 3. The free mint may move to mid-September
chunks.text:
Two more mint details came out of the FAQ round. The supply is no longer firmly 10,000: the team is working with Ronin and it may land between 10,000 and 15,000. And the whitelist will deliberately hold more addresses than there are NFTs — possibly 20–30% over capacity in the early waves — because a wave that doesn't mint out looks bad. Later waves are explicitly not restricted to top-ranked trainers.

What it means for you: if you're an ordinary trainer with a modest point total, the free mint remains the most accessible NFT in the whole programme. It's the one reward where being early and verified matters more than being rich.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 4. The leaderboard lock finally has a shape
chunks.text:
4. The leaderboard lock finally has a shape

We've been flagging for two weeks that the lock had no announced date. It still doesn't have one — but it now has a position in the sequence, which is nearly as useful.

The leaderboard runs until the game launches, ending roughly a week before early access begins, possibly a little less. It will be finalised after the mint reveal, and the team says it will announce a specific end date in advance so trainers can prepare.

The practical read: you have more runway than the word "locks" suggested — likely into late Q4. But two things still bite. You must hold your rank until the lock, and the leaderboard goes dark as launch approaches. A late sprint is a plan you can't measure.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 5. 2.5 million $FLOWER is already in the deposit pool
chunks.text:
5. 2.5 million $FLOWER is already in the deposit pool

Craig put a number on deposits for the first time, and it's a big one. Roughly 2.5 million $FLOWER has been deposited into Yakkamon so far — which he estimated at a fifth to a quarter of the circulating $FLOWER in Sunflower Land.

Adam's response was that the team consistently underestimates how hard players will push, and that this level of commitment is both motivating and slightly terrifying on the delivery side.

What it means for you: the paid bracket at the top of the leaderboard is being contested harder than most people assume, and points-per-rank at the top will keep inflating. It doesn't change the free route — the top 100,000 early-access cutoff is still comfortably reachable without spending — but if you were eyeing a Legendary band on deposits alone, the price of a given rank is rising every week.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 6. OG status: the exact requirement, and how fast it gets harder
chunks.text:
6. OG status: the exact requirement, and how fast it gets harder

OG has a precise number now. It's 50,000 points inside a single week, and Craig gave the current cost: about 15,000 $FLOWER this week at the 3× multiplier.

It's a weekly milestone, and it's permanent once claimed — if you hit it this week and never come close again, you're still OG. And because the multiplier decays, the $FLOWER cost of that same 50,000 points climbs every week:

Week | Multiplier | Roughly what OG costs in one transfer |

1 (now) | 3.0× | ~15,000 $FLOWER |

2 | 2.8× | ~15,600 |

4 | 2.4× | ~17,900 |

6 | 2.0× | ~20,800 |

11+ | 1.0× | ~35,700 |

Our calculation, assuming a single transfer in the +40% size-bonus band. Craig's 15,000 figure for week one matches this maths. Check your own deposit panel before acting on it.

One deliberate design note: the team discussed attaching a large reward to OG and decided against it, settling on a title only — specifically to avoid incentivising the wrong behaviour and setting expectations of some enormous payout. If you were depositing for OG on the assumption a prize is coming later, that assumption has now been explicitly denied.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 7. The multiplier may never actually reach 1.0×
chunks.text:
7. The multiplier may never actually reach 1.0×

A sharp question from chat: if the leaderboard locks before the multiplier finishes decaying, does the schedule change? Craig's answer was that the rate simply keeps stepping down weekly — and he acknowledged, apparently for the first time, that deposits may close while it's still around 1.2×. If it does reach 1.0×, it stays there rather than dropping further.

What it means for you: nothing about the advice changes — earlier is still worth more, always. But the tail end of our published schedule may be theoretical. There may be no such thing as a 1.0× deposit week.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 8. They would rather you spent that $FLOWER than withdrew it
chunks.text:
8. They would rather you spent that $FLOWER than withdrew it

Adam was refreshingly direct about a problem the team can see coming: a large amount of $FLOWER has been parked in Yakkamon by people who can simply withdraw it at launch.

Their answer is carrots rather than sticks. Expect discounts on hard-currency items, VIP offers, hunting events and possibly auctions during the opening weeks of early access, designed to give you something worth spending on before you think about withdrawing.

Read this next to the withdrawal limits. Percentage-based limits already apply during the first few weeks after launch. Now add a wave of limited-time offers landing in exactly that window. If your plan was "deposit for points, withdraw on day one," expect the game to be actively designed to change your mind — and expect the exit to be metered while it tries.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 9. What your monsters actually do — the answer to "why collect these?"
chunks.text:
9. What your monsters actually do — the answer to "why collect these?"

Bryn, the lead game designer, spent the middle of the stream on this, and it's the best explanation of the collection loop we've had so far.

Monsters are workers, and they're tradable. The team is positioning them as the equivalent of the big chapter items in Sunflower Land — the things that define a build.

Traits are randomly rolled on a percentage chance, and rares and legendaries carry significant farming buffs. Which monsters you hold determines how you build your farm.

Genetics and base stats are real systems. Breed two of the same species with good stats and traits and you carry that line forward. Bryn described deliberately designing for one-to-three-year breeding projects, including sneaky routes to move traits between species and between type groups.

Breeding degrades, but isn't capped. Keep breeding from the same monster and random noise increases, so results get progressively worse. There's no hard limit on attempts.

RNG is bounded. Bryn doesn't like stacking RNG on RNG — if you understand the system you should be able to predict an outcome within 80–90% and plan best and worst cases.

Evolutions are planned. Confirmed as something they're interested in and designing for.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 9. What your monsters actually do — the answer to "why collect these?"
chunks.text:
On what becomes an NFT — and Bryn was careful to say this isn't a promise — the current structure is Legendaries as NFTs (close to one-of-ones or extremely scarce), Rares as SFTs, and commons as plain in-game assets. Adam added that this is deliberate: not every monster becomes an NFT, precisely so the NFTs stay rare and worth trading.

And there's a sink. Contract deliveries for monsters will consume commons using progression coins — described as "hungrier" than your generation rate — so the common population gets burned rather than inflating endlessly.

What it means for you: rank isn't just a trophy. A Genesis Legendary is a permanent, buff-bearing, breedable asset with traits nobody else can obtain, entering an economy explicitly designed to keep it scarce. That's the strongest case yet for the points you're grinding now.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 10. A new idea: export limits tied to how much you actually play
chunks.text:
10. A new idea: export limits tied to how much you actually play

Bryn floated a concept — his words were that it's an idea, not a system yet — for handling extractive players without Sunflower Land's hard limits. Your export limit would grow with your in-game activity: play and burn resources legitimately and your ability to trade out expands, while someone farming purely to extract hits the ceiling almost immediately. VIP accounts would be treated as legitimate and uncapped.

Very early, explicitly beta, and aimed at one of the genuinely hard problems in web3 gaming. Worth watching rather than planning around.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 11. Gameplay: the first two hours are being built now
chunks.text:
11. Gameplay: the first two hours are being built now

Spencer is building the vertical slice — roughly the first couple of hours of the game. How it works:

You start on a small revealed patch of world with your first monster. It bounces around gathering berries and wood. You use what it gathers to part the clouds and reveal more land, and some of that new land contains hunting areas. The hunting mechanic isn't locked yet, but the shape is: you send a monster in with lures to try and draw wild monsters back to your land, and you can go in and look around yourself. Sometimes an aggressive monster turns up and challenges you to a battle.

A short clip did make it out on X during the stream — a monster (Spencer used the name "Wadler", unconfirmed) moving around gathering resources, with one expansion already revealing a lumber yard and a hunting area.

Also confirmed, with some amusement: the monster art that leaked earlier came through a developer backdoor used to avoid testing on production. Someone found it. That backdoor is now closed.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 12. The sound is being generated with AI, and they said so up front
chunks.text:
12. The sound is being generated with AI, and they said so up front

Craig has taken on audio in his first week on Yakkamon, and volunteered without being asked that he's using AI to generate the game's sounds. His reasoning: stock libraries can't deliver the specificity they want — his example was trying to find an existing sound that captures a chunky, Humpty-Dumpty-ish mouse monster.

Music, ambient beds and effects all exist already, though a technical hitch meant none of it could be played on stream. The plan is per-monster voices and personalities, with shared sounds for generic actions by body type — and one delightful production idea of recording the team making noises into a mic and modulating them per monster. Bryn: every time a monster faints, it's one of them screaming.

Community sounds are on the table, provided they match the recording fidelity and characteristics of the rest of the game. And the audio tech is planned to be back-ported into Sunflower Land.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 13. Why Discord went quiet: a three-day restriction
chunks.text:
13. Why Discord went quiet: a three-day restriction

If you noticed the Discord acting strangely, here's why. The bot ban waves cleaned up thousands of low-intent accounts on the Yakkamon side, but not before those accounts hit Discord — which placed a roughly three-day restriction on the server. Images couldn't be posted and invite links stopped working, which is also why this stream had almost no visual leaks. The restriction was expected to lift at the end of the day. Discord support hadn't responded.

Adam's framing is worth repeating, because it explains the run of rule changes: the tightening of verification and point rules isn't arbitrary — it's protecting the economy and, at this point, the server itself.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 14. Quick answers from the FAQ round
chunks.text:
14. Quick answers from the FAQ round

Can Storm and Echo be caught in-game later? A very small amount goes into the rewards pool, but the overwhelming majority only ever come from the trainer airdrop. Occasional special events may release a few more.

Platform: browser web app at launch. No mobile app, no console. Not ruled out forever, but not planned.

Free to play: confirmed. No NFT and no wallet needed to play; the web3 layer is opt-in.

Changing your linked wallet: being looked into after several people linked the wrong one. No ETA.

In-game marketplace: confirmed. Monster NFTs mint on Ronin before early access and can be traded on the Ronin marketplace immediately; once early access opens you deposit them into the game and can use the in-game market too.

Seasonal resets: not happening. Bryn is against them — mistakes get fixed rather than wiped. Inflation gets handled with hard sinks and new content, including an infinite XP sink of the kind Sunflower Land just shipped.

Open source: the client will be open sourced. Adam credits AI tooling for the recent surge in community contributions — 30 community features, patches and fixes shipped to Sunflower Land in seven days.

Monster names: not finalised. Bryn wants a naming framework that makes them feel distinctly Yakkamon, but is open to community suggestions inside it — and the team is watching the memes, because they're shaping the personalities. Meme creators, in Adam's words, have more influence than they think.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — 14. Quick answers from the FAQ round
chunks.text: Discord points: Adam said they're not doing Discord points any more, offering "personal points" for memes instead. Whether this cancels the manual weekly reward mentioned after the first stream wasn't spelled out.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — What we're changing on this site
chunks.text:
What we're changing on this site

Two things need flagging honestly. The free mint date is published across this site as October 1st, and it still is officially — but a mid-September mint was spoken about as likely, so we'll be carrying that as a caveat until the team confirms one way or the other. And our deposit multiplier schedule runs to a 1.0× floor in week 11; that floor may never arrive if deposits close first, so the table gets a note.

Everything else in this stream confirmed rather than contradicted what's here — including, gratifyingly, the Legendary status of the 501–2,000 band that our correction hinged on.

chunks.title: Second Yakkamon Dev Stream: The Airdrop U-Turn Explained, and a Free Mint That May Move to September — Verification is the deadline that moved
chunks.text:
Verification is the deadline that moved

If the mint lands in mid-September, being verified late costs you the whole thing.

FREE MINT GUIDE →

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Yakkamon Just Split Its Economy in Two

Event
Yakkamon Just Split Its Economy in Two

Aug 21, 2026

The Yakkamon team has published an economy and trading guide, and it is the most consequential thing they've released since the reward ladder changed. Seven numbered points, most of them a paragraph long. One of them quietly rewrites how the first month of the game will work — and, we think, breaks one of the arguments we published three days ago.

Here's what it says, what follows from it, and what it costs you if you plan around the wrong half.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — The seven points, in plain terms
chunks.text:
The seven points, in plain terms

# | What the post says | New? |

1 | The economy is player-driven and peer-to-peer. Expect trainers to specialise — gathering, building, hunting, battling — and trade for what they don't produce. | Framing |

2 | Assets are split into two classes. Easily gathered free-to-play resources are kept separate from things that take real effort. The stated reason: gathering loops can be automated, so cheap resources are walled off from the tradeable economy. | New |

3 | Basic monsters have limited tradeability. Some you'll have to hunt yourself. | New |

4 | Legendaries and rares release in limited supplies or windows, and become tradeable once that window closes. | New |

5 | Every monster NFT carries unique traits — including collectible shinies. | New (shinies) |

6 | Free mint and trainer airdrop launch on the Ronin marketplace. Once the game is live you deposit monsters in and use the in-game market. | Confirms |

7 | The in-game market runs on $FLOWER with a percentage fee acting as a soft burn — removed from circulation or recycled into rewards. The design intent is deflationary. | New |

Point 6 isn't news to anyone who watched the second dev stream; we reported that mint-on-Ronin-then-deposit sequence weeks ago. Points 2, 3, 4 and 7 are the ones worth reading twice.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — The headline: two economies, not one
chunks.text:
The headline: two economies, not one

Point 2 is the load-bearing one. Yakkamon is not building a single market where everything you touch has a price. It is building a walled free-to-play layer and a tradeable layer above it, deliberately separated.

The reasoning given is anti-bot, and it's honest in a way studios usually aren't: the team says outright that the gathering loops can be automated. That is a notable admission. It means they expect scripts to run the idle half of the game, they have decided not to fight that with detection, and they have instead removed the incentive by making automated output economically inert.

What this almost certainly means in practice. Wood, stone, berries and the other things your monsters pile into a storage bin overnight are unlikely to be sellable to other players for real value. They feed your own base. The things that are tradeable will be the ones a script can't farm: hunted monsters, rare drops, crafted goods, and NFTs. The post doesn't draw that boundary explicitly — which is exactly the thing to ask them to publish.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — The headline: two economies, not one
chunks.text: This also lines up with something already on the record from the dev streams: Legendaries are NFTs, rares are semi-fungible tokens, and commons are plain in-game assets with no token behind them at all. That three-tier structure and this two-class asset split are the same design seen from two angles. Point 3 — basic monsters having limited tradeability — is that structure stated in gameplay terms rather than token terms.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — This breaks one of our own arguments
chunks.text:
This breaks one of our own arguments

Three days ago we argued in The Game That Starts the Next Morning that your wave is a market position rather than a head start: that Wave 1 enters a market with no sellers and captures a scarcity premium on ordinary materials, while later waves arrive to a cheaper, deeper market where basic gear can be bought instead of farmed.

That reasoning rested on an assumption we stated at the time — that every core resource and creature is tradable from day one. Point 2 says otherwise. So:

The Wave 1 scarcity premium on ordinary materials probably doesn't exist. If wood and berries aren't tradeable, there is no seven-day window in which the first cohort is the only supplier of them. That part of the argument was wrong.

The Wave 3 and 4 consolation is weaker too. "You can buy your way to parity on basics" only works if basics have a market. Later waves keep their information advantage, but they do have to farm the free-to-play layer themselves, from scratch, the same as everyone.

The argument survives where it points at monsters. Hunted creatures, rares and crafted goods are the tradeable layer. Wave position still determines who is selling those first, and to whom.

Net effect: waves matter for the monster and item market, not for the resource market. That is a narrower claim than we made, and we'd rather correct it in public than let it sit. We've flagged the same note on the original piece.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — And it reinforces another one
chunks.text:
And it reinforces another one

The same piece argued that type locking makes roster breadth, not quality, the ceiling on what you can produce — and that catching one of everything beats perfecting a few.

Point 3 makes that argument stronger, not weaker. If basic monsters have limited tradeability, you cannot buy your way out of a type gap. A Fire type isn't a purchase, it's an expedition. Every missing type is a lane you personally have to go and open, using berries and squad stamina you also need for gathering. Breadth just got more expensive and more valuable at the same time.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — Rares unlock late — and everyone's unlock at once
chunks.text:
Rares unlock late — and everyone's unlock at once

Point 4 is the one with a date attached to it, even if the date isn't given. Legendaries and rares drop in limited supplies or limited windows, and only become tradeable once that availability period ends.

Two consequences, and they pull in opposite directions:

You may not be able to sell your airdrop monster when you get it. Anyone treating a top-5,000 finish as a liquid asset they can flip on reveal day should plan for a lockup of unknown length. The airdrop pays out three days after the board locks; nothing says the trading window opens then.

When it does open, it opens for everyone simultaneously. A supply cliff is the predictable result: 5,010 monsters, all of which become sellable on the same day, held by people who have been waiting to sell. If you intend to exit, being early in that queue is worth more than holding out for a headline price.

The flip side is that a window-gated supply is a genuinely scarce one. Storm at 50 units, Echo at 203, Bloom at 257 aren't numbers that get diluted later — unless breeding dilutes them, which is the open question below.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — Shinies: a rarity axis nobody can price yet
chunks.text:
Shinies: a rarity axis nobody can price yet

Point 5 confirms per-monster unique traits and adds one word that wasn't in any previous material: shinies. Collectible variants, presumably visual, presumably rare.

This creates a second rarity axis running crosswise to the first. Your monster's tier — Legendary, rare, common — is set by the airdrop ladder and by supply caps. Its traits and shininess are rolled. That means a common can be worth more than a rare, which is normal for this genre and is the single most reliable way for new players to find value that money didn't already claim.

The caveat that matters. The dev streams described breeding lines with genetic degradation and no hard cap on breeding. Trait scarcity and shiny scarcity are only real if the roll can't be farmed. If breeding lets a large operation grind for shinies, the supply of them is limited by patience rather than by design, and today's collector premium won't hold. Nothing published tells us which it is.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — The fee, the burn, and the word "deflationary"
chunks.text:
The fee, the burn, and the word "deflationary"

Point 7 is where to be most careful, because it's the point most likely to be quoted as an investment thesis by people who didn't read it closely.

What it actually commits to: the in-game market is denominated in $FLOWER, and it takes a percentage fee. What it describes that fee as: a soft burn, which either removes $FLOWER from circulation or feeds it back into rewards. And the stated design goal is that the game is built so there is "more taken out than given out".

Those two halves of the fee description are not the same mechanism at all. A burn destroys supply permanently. Recycling into rewards moves supply from traders to players — that's redistribution, and it's mildly inflationary in the hands of anyone who then sells. The post reserves the right to do either, and gives no split between them.

To judge the deflation claim you'd need | Published? |

The marketplace fee percentage | No |

What share of the fee burns vs. recycles | No |

$FLOWER emission into the game per day | No |

Expected market volume | Unknowable pre-launch |

Other sinks — the contract-delivery burn from the dev streams | Mentioned, not sized |

So the claim isn't false; it's currently unfalsifiable. "Deflationary" is a statement of intent about net flows, and every number needed to check it is unpublished. Treat it as a design goal the team is stating in good faith, and not as a fact about what $FLOWER will do.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — Ronin first, game second
chunks.text:
Ronin first, game second

Point 6 restates the sequence: free mint in mid-September, monsters live on the Ronin marketplace immediately, in-game market only once early access opens in November or December.

Two practical things fall out of that. First, if you deposited on Base, you still need a Ronin wallet — the mint and the airdrop land there regardless of which chain your $FLOWER went in on. Set that up well before mid-September rather than on the day.

Second, there is a two-to-three month stretch where Yakkamon monsters trade on a public marketplace with no game attached to them. No utilities are live, no gameplay proves what a trait is worth, and the reveal isn't until mid-October. Prices in that window are pure narrative. If you're buying then, you're buying a story; if you're selling then, you're selling to someone who is.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — What's genuinely good here
chunks.text:
What's genuinely good here

The bot problem was addressed head-on. Walling off automatable output is a structural answer, not a detection arms race, and it's the approach with the better track record.

Free-to-play is protected. The gathering loop stays available to everyone and can't be strip-mined by capital, because its output has no resale value to capital.

Effort is where the value is. Hunting, rares and traits are the tradeable layer — things time and skill produce, not things a wallet produces.

A real sink exists. A fee on every trade, plus the contract-delivery burn from the dev streams, is more sink design than most games this size ship with.

Specialisation is a stated goal. A game that wants you to be a hunter or a builder rather than everything at once has more interesting trade than one where everyone farms the same thing.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — What to be wary of
chunks.text:
What to be wary of

The free-to-play layer may have no earning path at all. If gathered resources can't be sold, the honest read is that free play buys progress, not income. Anyone pre-registering on the expectation of grinding into value should hear that clearly.

"Limited tradeability" is undefined. It could mean untradeable, bound-on-catch, cooldown-gated, or capped per week. Those have wildly different consequences and the post picks none of them.

The boundary line is unpublished. Nobody outside the team can currently say which resources sit on which side. That's the single most useful thing they could add.

Window-gated tradeability creates a synchronised sell. See above.

The deflation claim has no numbers behind it. See above.

Liquidity concentrates on one chain. Ronin-only launch is simpler for the team; it's an extra step and an extra bridge risk for Base depositors.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — What to actually do
chunks.text:
What to actually do

Get a Ronin wallet ready before mid-September. Cheapest possible action, hard deadline, and the free mint doesn't wait.

Don't budget around selling your airdrop monster. Assume it's locked until an unannounced window closes, and that everyone else's unlocks the same morning.

Stop planning to buy your way to type coverage. Basic monsters are yours to hunt. Plan berries and squad stamina for a catching campaign in week one, not a shopping trip.

Pick a lane early. The post is telling you specialisation is intended. Deciding now whether you're a hunter, a builder or a battler shapes which types you chase on day one.

Don't pay a premium for shinies yet. Until breeding rules are published, nobody knows whether shiny supply is capped or grindable.

Nothing here changes the deposit maths. The multiplier still steps down 0.2× a week and the board still locks a week before early access. The economy post is about the game after the race, not the race.

chunks.title: Yakkamon's Economy Explained: Two Asset Tiers, Shinies and a FLOWER Burn — The four questions we'd put to the team
chunks.text:
The four questions we'd put to the team

Which specific resources are on the tradeable side of the line, and which aren't?

What does "limited tradeability" mean mechanically for a basic monster?

How long is the availability window before Legendaries and rares become tradeable?

What is the marketplace fee, and what proportion of it is burned rather than recycled?

All four are answerable today without revealing anything competitive, and all four change how a careful player spends the next three months.

Source and standing. This is our reading of an official Yakkamon economy post, published on the team's own channels. The seven points above are summarised in our words; the analysis, the corrections and the criticisms are ours and are not endorsed by anyone. Where we've been wrong before we say so on the page it happened, and this piece contains one such correction.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained

Guideline
The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained

Aug 10, 2026 · Updated Aug 14, 2026

Yakkamon has published a dedicated $FLOWER deposits page in the official docs. It sets out what a deposit actually does, what happens to your money at launch, and one safeguard that hasn’t been widely discussed.

This is the whole thing in one place — the official guideline, plus the live rate schedule from your trainer dashboard, which the docs page doesn’t include.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 1. A deposit does two things, not one
chunks.text:
1. A deposit does two things, not one

This is the part people most often get wrong, and the docs are unambiguous about it. Every deposit credits your in-game balance and earns you leaderboard points. You are not trading one for the other.

The $FLOWER is held for you and waiting the moment you get access. The points are separate, and they push you toward trainer tiers, earlier access waves and the NFT airdrop.

Worth saying plainly: you are not spending your $FLOWER to buy points. You keep both.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 2. What you get back, and when
chunks.text:
2. What you get back, and when

Once early access opens, your deposited $FLOWER is yours to use:

Spend it in-game — gear, crafting, hunting supplies, and the rest of the economy.

Withdraw it with no withdrawal tax. The docs are explicit: no lock-up, no penalty for taking it back out.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 3. The safeguard nobody’s talking about
chunks.text:
3. The safeguard nobody’s talking about

Buried in the guideline is the detail most worth knowing before you deposit anything.

Percentage-based withdrawal limits may apply for the first few weeks after launch. The team describes it as a standard safeguard while the project stabilises — it caps how much can be withdrawn in a given period, not whether you can withdraw. Limits are lifted as things settle.

That’s a reasonable measure and a common one — it protects the economy from being drained in the first days. But it does mean your deposit isn’t instantly liquid on day one. If you were planning to deposit now and withdraw the moment access opens, plan for that taking longer than a single transaction.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 4. The rates: what the docs don’t tell you
chunks.text:
4. The rates: what the docs don’t tell you

The guideline says bigger deposits earn exponentially more, which is accurate but vague. The actual numbers live in the deposit panel in your trainer dashboard, and there are two bonuses stacked on top of each other.

The weekly multiplier — it decays

Every $FLOWER earns points, at a rate set by which week you deposit in. The opening week pays 3×, and the rate falls 0.2× every week until it settles at 1× and stops dropping.

Week | Dates | Rate |

1 | 10 – 16 Aug | 3.0× |

2 | 17 – 23 Aug | 2.8× |

3 | 24 – 30 Aug | 2.8× — held |

4 | 31 Aug – 6 Sep | 2.6× |

5 | 7 – 13 Sep | 2.4× |

6 | 14 – 20 Sep | 2.2× |

7 | 21 – 27 Sep | 2.0× |

8 | 28 Sep – 4 Oct | 1.8× |

9 | 5 – 11 Oct | 1.6× |

10 | 12 – 18 Oct | 1.4× |

11 | 19 – 25 Oct | 1.2× |

12+ | 26 Oct onward | 1.0× — the floor |

Updated 24 August — week 3 stays at 2.8×. Depositing was paused during week 2, so rather than dropping to 2.6×, the team held the week 3 multiplier at 2.8×. The 0.2× weekly step resumes from week 4, which pushes every later week — and the 1.0× floor — one week later than originally scheduled.

Rates are official — including the week-3 hold at 2.8×. The week boundaries are our calculation from the 10 Aug opening — check your own deposit panel if a date is borderline for you.

On the second dev stream the team acknowledged deposits may close while the multiplier is still around 1.2×, so the 1.0× floor may never actually be reached. What else changed →

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 4. The rates: what the docs don’t tell you
chunks.text:
The size bonus — it’s per deposit

Separately, larger deposits earn bonus points, and the rate doubles at every step. This is what the docs mean by exponential.

Single deposit | Bonus rate | Points in the opening week |

50 $FLOWER | +10% | 150 +5 bonus |

500 $FLOWER | +20% | 1,500 +100 bonus |

5,000 $FLOWER | +40% | 15,000 +2,000 bonus |

50,000 $FLOWER | +80% | 150,000 +40,000 bonus |

The full amount must land in one transfer. Depositing 25 $FLOWER and then another 25 does not reach the 50 tier — each piece earns its own smaller bonus instead.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 5. What that means in practice
chunks.text:
5. What that means in practice

Both bonuses push the same way: deposit early, and in single larger transfers.

Same 5,000 $FLOWER | Total points |

One transfer, opening week | 17,000 |

One transfer, week 6 | 13,000 |

Ten transfers of 500, opening week | 16,000 |

Ten transfers of 500, after the floor | 6,000 |

Same money, and a 65% swing between the best and worst way of sending it. The full tactical breakdown →

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 6. Where to get $FLOWER
chunks.text:
6. Where to get $FLOWER

Worth saying, since a guide about depositing is not much use if you don’t hold any. There are two routes, and one of them is free.

Earn it by playing

$FLOWER is the in-game token of Sunflower Land, the studio’s other game. You earn it by playing — selling crops, completing deliveries, competing in seasonal chapters. It’s free to start, and it means you can build a deposit without spending anything.

Slower than buying, obviously. But if you’re playing the free-to-play route anyway, it’s the only way to get deposit points without opening your wallet.

Buy it

$FLOWER already exists and trades today — Yakkamon didn’t launch a new token, so there’s nothing new to wait for. The official guideline has since been expanded on this point, and it changes the practical advice: $FLOWER is the same ERC20 token on both Base and Ronin, at one identical contract address on both chains. Deposits are accepted on either. Neither chain needs bridging — on Base you swap for it as normal, and on Ronin you can swap for it directly inside the Ronin Wallet.

Which chain you use is therefore down to where you already hold funds, not to which is the shorter route. If your money is on Ronin — where you’ll want a wallet anyway for the October mint — there’s no longer a reason to move it to Base first.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 6. Where to get $FLOWER
chunks.text:
For anything to do with acquiring and depositing it, work from the official source: the Yakkamon $FLOWER deposits guideline ↗, which now publishes the contract address alongside the swap and block-explorer links for each chain, and the deposit panel in your own trainer dashboard, which carries the current rates and your deposit address.

Never take a contract address or a deposit address from us, from a reply, or from a DM — check the official docs page instead, every single time. Fake tokens using the same name and ticker are one of the most common ways people lose money in this space, and a token that looks identical in a swap interface can be worthless. The docs give one address that should match on both Base and Ronin; if what your swap interface shows doesn’t match it exactly, stop.

One more thing worth knowing: $FLOWER is designed as an in-game currency rather than an investment, and Sunflower Land’s own docs say so plainly. It has a fixed supply, the team took no allocation, and its value moves. Buying it to chase leaderboard points is a decision only you can make.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — 7. The honest part
chunks.text:
7. The honest part

We’re not financial advisors and we won’t tell you whether to deposit — $FLOWER is real money, the game hasn’t launched, and that call is yours alone. Everything in pre-registration works without depositing anything, and the top 100,000 early-access cutoff is reachable free.

What we can tell you is what the rules are, and that a large deposit made early is worth tens of thousands of points, which no amount of free play matches. That’s why the very top of the leaderboard is effectively a paid bracket.

Your deposit address comes from your own logged-in account on yakkamon.com. It never comes from a post, a reply, a DM or a link somebody sends you. If anyone gives you an address to send $FLOWER to, it’s a scam — every time.

chunks.title: The Official $FLOWER Deposit Guideline, Explained — Timing is the whole game
chunks.text:
Timing is the whole game

What waiting costs, what splitting costs, and the week-by-week schedule.

OPEN TIPS →

Every points value in one place on the leaderboard guideline, and the free route to early access in the free-to-play guide. For background: what deposits do and the day they opened.

Event
$FLOWER Deposits Open Sunday, August 9 at 8:00 PM ET

Aug 5, 2026 · Updated Aug 10, 2026

$FLOWER deposits open on Sunday, August 9 at 8:00 PM ET. That's when your deposit address is issued, and when deposited $FLOWER starts converting into leaderboard points.

chunks.title: $FLOWER Deposits Open Sunday, August 9 at 8:00 PM ET — What you can do from that moment
chunks.text:
What you can do from that moment
Send any amount of $FLOWER to your deposit address on Base or Ronin, minimum 5 $FLOWER. Every $FLOWER earns a point, and your deposited total unlocks bonus rates on top:

Bonus | How it works |

Weekly multiplier | 3× through the opening week, then falling 0.2× every week until it rests at 1× |

Size bonus | Rated per deposit, doubling at every step: +10% at 50 $FLOWER, +20% at 500, +40% at 5,000, +80% at 50,000 |

Points land in the week the deposit confirms. It's the single biggest points lever in pre-registration — a large deposit is worth tens of thousands of points, which no amount of daily nurturing will match. We're not telling you to deposit; we're telling you what the numbers say.

chunks.title: $FLOWER Deposits Open Sunday, August 9 at 8:00 PM ET — Why the docs say "10 August"
chunks.text:
Why the docs say "10 August"

Because they're quoting the UTC date. 8:00 PM ET on Sunday Aug 9 is midnight UTC, which is already Monday Aug 10 in London and everywhere east of it. Same instant, two calendar dates — if you're in the Americas, the evening you want is Sunday the 9th.

chunks.title: $FLOWER Deposits Open Sunday, August 9 at 8:00 PM ET — Deposit early, and in one transfer
chunks.text:
Deposit early, and in one transfer

The instinct is to wait — watch the leaderboard, see where you stand, and deposit near the end to secure a rank. The deposit system is built specifically to punish that.

Two bonuses stack, and both reward moving early. The weekly multiplier pays 3× through the opening week and falls 0.2× each week after. The size bonus is rated per deposit rather than on your running total, so 25 $FLOWER followed by another 25 does not reach the 50 tier — the full amount has to land in one go.

Concretely: 5,000 $FLOWER sent as one transfer in the opening week earns 17,000 points. The same 5,000 sent as ten deposits of 500, after the multiplier bottoms out, earns 6,000. The full week-by-week schedule →

The team said plainly why it works this way: they want points earned early, not a stampede on the final day before launch. The full breakdown is here →

chunks.text:
