chunks.title: Free Mint Goes Live October 1st
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Free Mint Goes Live October 1st

Event
Free Mint Goes Live October 1st

Jul 29, 2026

Superseded — the date moved. This post was published when October 1st was the announced date. The official docs now give the free mint as mid-September, with the reveal in mid-October rather than at early access launch. Everything below about the whitelist, the supply and the five Legendaries still stands — only the timing changed, and your verification deadline moved up with it. The revised schedule →
On October 1st, the Genesis Monster NFT free mint goes live on Ronin. The mint is open to pre-registered trainers only, so signing up before that date is the only way to take part.

chunks.title: Free Mint Goes Live October 1st — What you need to know
chunks.text:
What you need to know
It's free — you only cover a small network fee, called gas. Only 10,000 can be minted, and it's first in, first minted — when the last one goes, the free mint closes for good. The mint runs on a secure, verified whitelist: only verified pre-registered trainers can mint, one each, and a wallet that isn't on the list is blocked at the contract no matter how fast it moves. Complete your verification before October 1st. Seeded into that supply are 5 Legendary monsters, the same top-of-the-power-curve creatures handed out in the Trainer Point airdrop. Five out of ten thousand.

chunks.title: Free Mint Goes Live October 1st — Why it's worth doing
chunks.text:
Why it's worth doing
Minting also earns pre-registration points toward your trainer tier, on top of the mint itself. Once you have game access, you'll be able to deposit whatever you mint straight into Yakkamon.
Full breakdown, including source details, is on the Early Access page.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline

Community
We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline

Dev stream: end of August 2026 · Published Sep 1, 2026

▶ Prefer to watch? The free-mint stream recap in 4 minutes ↗
The latest dev stream was the one the trainer chat has been waiting for: the Ronin free mint finally has a date, a structure and a snapshot deadline. Adam ran the session, Bryn took the gameplay questions at a sprint, Spencer walked through hunting, and Craig joined from the contract side. Around 160 trainers were in the chat, and the docs got a major update ten minutes before the stream started.

We graded every decision from the first dev stream back in August. This is the same treatment for this one: sixteen decisions, graded A to F. Nothing scored an F — but nothing scored lower than this team's distribution mechanics, either, and that pattern is becoming the story of the project.

One note on the stream itself. As always, the team asked for grain-of-salt treatment and no screen grabs, because everything is still in development. We’ve respected that — no footage, quotes kept short, and everything below treated as where the project stood at the end of August rather than as a promise.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — The scorecard
chunks.text:
The scorecard

Sixteen decisions. The first eight are about the mint; the second eight are about the game. The gap between those two halves is the whole review.

Decision | YakkamonWorld Score |

Guaranteed mint for the top 1,000 trainers | A |

The two-track economy: infinite free layer, coin-gated tradable layer | A |

No punishment for logging off | A |

No wearable gear — power stays in the monster | A |

Shipping the mint through the Ronin Launchpad | A− |

Legendary utilities as economic auras | A− |

Skill expression inside combat, on a swappable architecture | A− |

Breeding caps scaled by rarity | A− |

The five-flower minimum as bot protection | B+ |

Random-rolled utilities on rares and uncommons | B+ |

No evolutions at launch | B+ |

The Ronin wave: 2,000 mints to players from other Ronin games | B |

Announcing the snapshot date with the leaderboard fully visible | B |

Hidden mints, tradable from day one, one ongoing collection | B |

Reserving 1,500 mints for a manual airdrop | B− |

Fastest-click-wins inside every other wave | C+ |

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — The dates, before the opinions
chunks.text:
The dates, before the opinions

Because this is the part you act on, here it is without commentary.

10 September — the leaderboard snapshot. The rank you hold on the leaderboard that day is the rank the mint waves are built from. The team said it plainly: if you’re thinking of climbing, now is the time.

14 September — the free mint goes live on the Ronin Launchpad, running as waves over a few days. You pay nothing but gas, in RON.

About a week after the mint — 1,500 reserved Yakkamon are airdropped manually, before the reveal.

14 October — the reveal. Until then every minted Yakkamon is hidden. They are NFTs and tradable the whole time, before and after.

A few weeks later — whenever your access wave opens, you deposit them into the game and play.

The waves themselves, as presented on stream — the team stressed that dates after the first wave are tentative, and that they want feedback on time zones and durations:

Wave | Who’s eligible | Supply | Extra condition |

1 | Top 1,000 trainers | Guaranteed — one each, mint at your own pace | — |

2 | Top 10,000 trainers | 3,000 | Five-flower minimum deposit (withdrawable) |

3 — the "Ronin wave" | Active players from other Ronin games, list built by the Ronin team | 2,000 | — |

4 | Trainers ranked 1–20,000 | Whatever remains — the team expects the full 10,000 may sell out here | — |

5 | Trainers ranked 1–50,000 | Only if any supply survives wave 4 | — |

Reserve | Manual airdrop, criteria unpublished | 1,500 | — |

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — The dates, before the opinions
chunks.text:
You can mint in every wave you qualify for, so a high rank means multiple chances. Inside the mint sit some very good pulls: 3 Storm, 5 Echo, 10 Ghost and 50 Bloom legendary-tier Yakkamon are spread through the collection — 68 out of 10,000, or roughly a 0.7% chance per mint. And this collection is not a side promotion: it is the Yakkamon collection, the one every future wild release will join.

One naming wrinkle we can’t resolve yet. The docs and the stream had a mid-session mix-up around the "Ghost" tier — the team called it a typo, said the tiers are "functionally the same things" with the same boosts, and that they’re renaming tiers to match the type system. Whether Ghost is the tier previously published as Tide, or something new, wasn’t made explicit. We’ll update when the docs settle.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
Part one: the mint

1. A guaranteed mint for the top 1,000

If you’re in the top 1,000 trainers at the snapshot, you get a whitelist spot you can use at your own pace. No race, no refresh-clicking at 3am, no gas war. The team framed it as a thank-you, and it works as one — but it’s better than that: it converts months of leaderboard effort into a calm entitlement rather than yet another speed contest.

When we graded the first stream we complained that the deposit economy rewarded capital over effort. This is the counter-example: rank, earned however you earned it, buying you certainty instead of a lottery ticket. More of this.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A — the best community decision the team has made since the referral fix.

2. Shipping through the Ronin Launchpad

The mint runs on Ronin’s own launchpad, with the Ronin team reviewing contracts, contributing extra whitelists, and helping design the anti-bot protections. Jiho from the Ronin side has reportedly been helping personally. The stated purpose of the whole exercise is exposure — every player minting anything else on that launchpad walks past Yakkamon on the way.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
That’s the right platform and the right reason. The deduction is for how much of it the team couldn’t answer: asked who pays gas, how much it is, and whether Ronin sponsors it, Craig openly said he wasn’t sure how the process works yet — only the Ronin team can call the mint function, and the contracts were still in review at stream time. Honest, and two weeks is time to fix it. But "how much does it cost me" is the first question every minter asks, and it shouldn’t be answered with a shrug on the announcement stream.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A− — right platform, real support, one unanswered question that should have been answered.

3. The five-flower minimum

Wave 2 adds a condition: a minimum deposit of five $FLOWER, which stays yours — withdraw it or spend it in-game whenever you like. The team was refreshingly blunt about why: free mints get botted heavily, whoever spams gas fastest across the most addresses wins, and the Ronin team suggested this as a civil-attack filter. Requiring the minimum plus a top-10,000 rank means the mint targets provable players. More than 3,000 of the top 10,000 already qualify.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
Two small pushbacks. First, a "free" mint now has a wallet-plus-deposit prerequisite — trivial for anyone reading this site, a real hurdle for the strictly-free player the FAQ keeps promising is welcome. Second, five flower is a price, not an identity check: a bot farm with capital clears it at five flower per wallet. It’s a speed bump, and paired with the rank requirement it’s probably enough — but the protection is the rank, not the deposit.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B+ — sensible, cheap, honest about the bot problem; just don’t call the result fully free.

4. Fastest-click-wins inside every other wave

Outside the guaranteed top 1,000, every wave is a set supply and a starting gun. The team said it themselves, answering a chat question: yes, fastest to click gets it; there are usually more people than supply; be online, have gas, be prepared; not everyone gets one. Wave 2 is 3,000 mints for 10,000 eligible trainers — by construction, at least 7,000 people who earned eligibility walk away with nothing, sorted mostly by who was awake.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
This is our lowest grade of the stream, and it’s the same critique we’ve made twice before, wearing a new coat. The first stream’s deposit design sorted the top of the leaderboard by capital; this sorts mint access by latency and time zone. Both take a thing the team says they value — months of earned effort — and hand the last mile to something else. And a click race is the known-bad pattern of this genre: it manufactures 7,000 disappointed people on a night that was supposed to be a celebration, and it hands an edge to exactly the gas-spamming behaviour the five-flower minimum exists to stop.

The fix is boring and proven: within each wave, take the eligible wallets that opt in during a window — say 24 hours — and raffle the supply among them. Same scarcity, same excitement, zero latency advantage, works in every time zone. The team asking for time-zone feedback shows they feel the problem; asking people which hour they’d like to lose the race in isn’t the answer. To their credit: multi-wave eligibility gives high ranks several retries, and missing out entirely still leaves the open market, since these are tradable from day one.

YakkamonWorld Score is: C+ — a click race is a choice, and there were better ones on the table.

5. The Ronin wave

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
Wave 3 sets aside 2,000 mints — a fifth of supply — for players from other Ronin games, on a list the Ronin team is building of active and top players across their ecosystem. It has nothing to do with the Yakkamon leaderboard, and the team was upfront that this is the price of exposure: the launchpad publicises the game to the whole chain.

Reasonable people can dislike this — it dilutes the trainers who did the grinding, and the list is controlled by a third party. But 2,000 mints is a cheap user-acquisition spend if it works, and every new player it converts is future demand for the things existing trainers will be selling. We’d have liked the list criteria published, and we’d note the irony that "active players against all the existing Ronin games" describes exactly the professionalised airdrop-farming class most likely to flip these at reveal. Call it marketing with a leak in it.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B — a defensible spend of 20% of supply, bought with someone else’s list.

6. The 1,500-mint manual reserve

1,500 Yakkamon — 15% of the collection — are held back to be "sent out manually as an airdrop to players", about a week after the mint and before the reveal. That’s the entire published detail. No criteria, no recipient categories, no process.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
There are perfectly good uses for a reserve like this: creators, community contributors, make-goods for people the click race burns, partners. Doing it before the reveal at least keeps it blind — nobody can steer a Storm to a friend. But discretionary distribution without published criteria is how healthy communities curdle, because every unexplained wallet becomes a conspiracy theory at reveal time. This is a one-sentence fix: say who qualifies and roughly how many go where. Until then it’s the largest single unexplained allocation in the mint.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B− — flexibility is fine; opacity at 15% of supply is not.

7. Announcing the snapshot with the leaderboard visible

The snapshot is 10 September, announced two weeks out, with the full leaderboard live at yakkamon.com and exact ranks showing. The team even said the quiet part cheerfully: if you want to climb, now is the time.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
Fair warning is genuinely player-friendly — nobody can say they didn’t know. But cast your mind back to the first stream, where the team told us they’d hide the leaderboard near deadlines precisely so the final days didn’t become a bidding war, and we graded the instinct B− while suggesting bands instead of blackout. What’s actually shipping is the opposite of both: a hard deadline, ten days’ notice, and a fully visible board with exact ranks — a textbook sniping setup around the 1,000 and 10,000 lines, during a week when the deposit multiplier still pays 2.6× falling to 2.4×. Expect the lines to move late. If you’re sitting at rank 950 or 9,800, your rank today is not your rank on the 10th, and margin is the only defence.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B — transparency chosen over their own earlier anti-sniping logic; good for fairness of information, rough on anyone camped near a boundary.

8. Hidden mints, tradable immediately, one ongoing collection

Every mint is a hidden Yakkamon until 14 October, and tradable the entire time. And the collection is permanent: as new Yakkamon are released into the wild, they appear in this same collection.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part one: the mint
chunks.text:
Take those separately. The one-collection decision is quietly excellent — no "genesis collection" orphaned on a marketplace while the real game happens elsewhere, one floor price that means something, provenance that stays legible for years. On its own it’d be an A−. The month of blind trading is more casino than game: a market pricing a hidden 0.7% legendary chance is a lottery-ticket market, and it only stays fair if the hidden metadata is provably unknowable — by everyone, including insiders — until reveal. The team says the contracts are being reviewed with Ronin’s help and "pretty diligent" is the standard; for a blind market, diligence isn’t a vibe, it’s a commitment scheme. We’d like one sentence in the docs on how the reveal is secured.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B — the permanent collection earns it; the blind month spends it.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
Part two: the game

9. Legendary utilities as economic auras

The Yakopedia went live in the docs with the first legendary utilities, and they’re not stat sticks — they’re economic infrastructure. Storm-charged: Yakkamon within range work twice as fast. The design language is Sunflower Land’s farm boosts, but the boosts come from the monsters themselves, so building a farm team is now a placement-and-synergy puzzle, with additive and multiplicative combinations — the team specifically flagged Storm plus Echo as a production combo worth chasing.

This is the right identity for legendaries in a farming game: a Storm doesn’t just win fights, it accelerates everything around it. Our one structural worry: those auras sit almost entirely with the top of the leaderboard — the airdrop’s roughly 2,000 legendaries go to the highest ranks, the mint’s 68 mostly to the same crowd — and a multiplicative production advantage compounds. The people who deposited the most will also, literally, produce twice as fast. The balancing lever is that every number is still unpublished and in playtesting; where those numbers land decides whether this is flavourful or feudal.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A− — legendaries as engines, not trophies; watch the compounding.

10. Random-rolled utilities on rares and uncommons

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
Rares and uncommons don’t have fixed utilities: the bonuses are rolled when you get the monster, independently of its stats. You can catch great stats with a dull utility, or a mediocre body carrying a brilliant passive — and the ones with both are the ones you hold or trade.

This creates exactly the kind of depth a hunting game wants — every catch is a slot machine with four quadrants, and the trade market gets a second axis of value beyond species and stats. The honesty was also on display: Bryn called the regenerate-percentage-of-max-HP trait "absolutely busted" on a well-statted dragon (dragons being weak to only two types), live, unprompted. Designers who say that before launch usually fix it before launch. The deduction is the usual one for variance on tradable assets: RNG plus a marketplace equals lottery dynamics, and the difference between spicy and predatory is in numbers we haven’t seen.

YakkamonWorld Score is: B+ — good depth, honestly discussed, judged finally by the odds table.

11. The two-track economy

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
The biggest game decision of the stream got the least fanfare. The team has settled on an economy model with a completely free-to-play layer: you can generate assets from it without putting anything in, but those assets are not tradable — and there is no limit on how many untradable resources you can produce. Tradable production, by contrast, is throttled by the game’s soft currency ("coins", possibly "new yen" later), whose faucets are deliberately limited and tied to things that help the economy — burning assets, burning crops, VIP.

This is the cleanest answer we’ve seen from this team to the question that kills most web3 games: how do you let a million free players play infinitely without their output crushing the market? Answer: give them an infinite game that is economically airtight, and meter the door between it and the market. It also finally squares the official economy post’s two-class asset split with the gameplay we’ve been mapping. The standing caveat from our economy analysis is still standing: untradable output means free play is progress, not income. Free players get a real game — they don’t get an earning path, and nobody should pretend otherwise. Bryn himself described Sunflower Land as "free to try" more than free to play, and said Yakkamon follows similar guardrails.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A — the separation of concerns most of this genre never figures out.

12. Skill expression inside combat, on a swappable architecture

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
The "massive decision" of the week, in the team’s own words: combat will not be a fully simulated auto-battler. Players will be able to act inside the fight, influencing mechanic swapping, and the architecture underneath is being built so it can support "any sort of battle type" — explicitly so the team isn’t dogmatic when player feedback arrives. In the back pocket: lane effects, ground types, weather (they name-checked Pokémon’s sandstorm) that can trigger through the skill system without rewriting the codebase.

We like both halves. Pure auto-battlers age into spreadsheets; a little in-fight agency is where attachment to individual monsters comes from, and it stacks cleanly on the lane system from stream three — initiative from type advantage, lanes acting top to bottom, preset skill orders. The A− rather than A is because "flexible enough to support anything" is also "not yet decided": the battle showcase keeps sliding one stream further out, and at some point flexibility has to collapse into a fight we can actually watch. The team says the next showcase should be the battle itself. We’re holding them to that.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A− — the right architecture call; now show us the fight.

13. No punishment for logging off

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
Asked what happens when a player disappears for a week or a month: it pauses. Yakkamon do their jobs until the bins fill, then stop. No decay, no neglect mechanic, no guilt tax. The reasoning was explicitly humane — with a hundred monsters on a farm, an attention system per monster would be "a bit too punitive".

Two things worth saying. First, this is consistent with the sped-up day/night clock decision from earlier streams — this team keeps choosing not to weaponise real-world time, which remains rare and remains right. Second, it does not contradict stream three’s plot degradation, and the distinction matters for planning: farms wear out with use, not with absence. Playing costs upkeep; living your life costs nothing but opportunity. That’s exactly the right way round.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A — respect for the player’s time, structurally, not as a slogan.

14. No wearable gear

Settled flatly on stream: no wearable gear, no equipment slots. Stats are baked into the monster at generation — genetics, training values, your time investment, and breeding down the line are what produce a good Yakkamon. At most there may be a single Pokémon-style held item carrying a passive trait.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
This is the first stream’s best decision — specialisation lives in the monsters, not in items — defended a second time under direct questioning, which is what you want from a design principle. The moment gear slots exist, the gear becomes the game and the creatures become mannequins; the team clearly knows it. It also concentrates all trading value in the monsters themselves, which keeps the collection — and the mint you’re about to participate in — meaningful.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A — a principle held under pressure is worth more than one announced.

15. Breeding caps scaled by rarity

Bred Yakkamon will be tradable — and the team answered the inflation question before the chat finished asking it. Every Yakkamon has a breeding limit: commons can breed above replacement (a pair making three or more), rarer species sit near replacement, and some legendaries may breed exactly once. Offspring can breed too, but the count can narrow further down the line.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
This is monetary policy written into biology, and it’s elegant: supply growth is fastest exactly where assets are cheapest and slowest where scarcity carries the value. It also quietly answers a question we raised in the economy analysis — whether shiny scarcity was grindable through unlimited breeding. With per-monster breed caps, it isn’t, or at least not freely. What we still don’t know: whether caps are visible before purchase (a "two breeds left" counter changes a monster’s price completely), and how caps interact with genetics inheritance. Both answers belong in the docs before the marketplace opens.

YakkamonWorld Score is: A− — inflation control at the asset level, where it actually works.

16. No evolutions at launch

Evolutions are coming, but not at launch — and the reason given was economic rather than technical. Launch with evolutions and the lower evolution tiers eventually filter out of the population, players pile up at the barrier to the higher tier, and the supply of evolved forms is structurally tiny. The team called it "an interesting thing to try and fix" and chose to address it properly rather than ship it broken.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Part two: the game
chunks.text:
Deferring a beloved feature for a supply-dynamics reason most studios wouldn’t even model is the mature call, and saying the real reason out loud is worth something too. The grade isn’t higher because evolutions have been on the promise list since the airdrop era, levelling is already built around "all of the above" (combat, training, food), and at some point the roadmap owes this a chapter number rather than a "later".

YakkamonWorld Score is: B+ — right call, honestly explained, still undated.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — What we’re not grading
chunks.text:
What we’re not grading

A stream this dense leaves a pile of facts that are context rather than decisions. Briefly: launch brings 13 types, one type per Yakkamon, multi-types later. Hunting grounds now have two kinds of encounters — aggressive monsters that flag the ground with a red alert and wait for you to act, and ambient ones you court with bait through a little emoji conversation until they join or bolt. Grounds deplete as they’re hunted out, lures and crafted baits weight what appears, and a contract system will pay coins for requested hunts — one of those limited faucets from the economy model. There’s no walking around: it’s the Sunflower Land god view, and the appeal of a bigger roster is running more actions at once. The Yakopedia is live in the docs and moves in-game at launch. MMO-ish plaza features are wanted but post-early-access; onboarding’s first island comes first. Fishing: "ends up in every game", designed for nothing yet. And the team is using an AI tool to draft animations from still art — placeholder quality, openly labelled as such, and the reason the monsters have started ambling, sniffing and head-butting rocks instead of sliding around.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — What we’re not grading
chunks.text: One process note that does deserve a sentence: the docs got a big update ten minutes before the stream, a tier-naming typo was caught by chat and a fix was pushed during the stream. That’s a team that treats docs as a product. It’s also a team that ships typos into them. Both things are true; on balance we’ll take it.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — What this does to our own calls
chunks.text:
What this does to our own calls

Our wave-strategy analysis argued that your access wave is a market position, and that Wave 1 "enters a market with no sellers". That second part now has a date on its tombstone: from 14 September, roughly seven weeks before early access, there will be a live market of up to 10,000 tradable Yakkamon — blind until 14 October, revealed thereafter. By the time Wave 1 logs in, the market will be a month old, with price discovery already done on commons and a reveal behind it. That strengthens the core thesis — information and market timing beat raw earliness — while retiring the no-sellers detail.

And one small satisfaction: the team said more than 3,000 of the top 10,000 trainers already meet the five-flower minimum. Our own deposit leaderboard has tracked roughly 3,200 depositing trainers for a fortnight. The numbers agree, which is nice to know when one of them is ours.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Three things to do before 10 September
chunks.text:
Three things to do before 10 September

Find out where you actually stand. Log in at yakkamon.com and check your rank, or see the live picture on our leaderboard. The lines that matter are 1,000 (guaranteed mint) and 10,000 (wave 2 with the five-flower minimum); 20,000 and 50,000 are the outer rings.

If you’re near a line, move early, not on the 9th. Expect boundary sniping in the final days — the snapshot was announced with the board fully visible. The deposit window running to 6 September pays 2.6×; from the 7th it’s 2.4×. Per the deposit guideline, one larger single transfer beats several small ones because the size bonus rates per transfer.

Get mint-ready. A Ronin wallet with some RON for gas, the five-flower minimum deposited if you’re playing wave 2, and be genuinely online when your wave opens — every wave past the first is a race. If you miss out, the fallback is the open market, blind until 14 October.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Questions for the next stream
chunks.text:
Questions for the next stream

Who pays mint gas, how much is it, and is any of it sponsored?

What are the criteria for the 1,500 manual-airdrop reserve?

Is Ghost the tier previously published as Tide, renamed — or a new tier?

Would the team consider a raffle-within-window instead of fastest-click for waves 2–5?

How is the reveal secured — can anyone, including the team, read the metadata before 14 October?

Can a strictly free player earn enough coins to touch the tradable layer at all?

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Our overall read
chunks.text:
Our overall read

Sort the scorecard and a pattern falls out that’s been stable across three graded months: when this team designs the game, they earn A’s; when they design distribution, they import the genre’s bad habits. The economy model, the no-gear principle, the pause-don’t-punish stance, breeding caps — that’s a group of people who’ve watched games die and understand why. The click races, the discretionary reserve, the snapshot announced over a fully visible board — that’s the standard web3 launch kit, adopted mostly unexamined, softened only by the genuinely good top-1,000 guarantee.

The encouraging part is that the game half is the hard half, and it’s the half they’re good at. Distribution mechanics can be fixed with a paragraph in the docs and a raffle contract; a broken economy can’t be fixed at all. And they remain unusually honest — about bots, about busted traits, about what they haven’t decided. Two weeks out from the mint, that honesty is still the best predictor this project has.

chunks.title: We Graded Every Decision From Yakkamon’s Free-Mint Dev Stream — Sixteen Grades, and a 10 September Deadline — Where do you stand?
chunks.text:
Where do you stand?

The snapshot is 10 September. Check your rank against every reward line before it locks.

Home›News›The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access

Guideline
The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access

Aug 5, 2026 · Updated Aug 14, 2026

You can reach early access without spending anything. You cannot reach the top of the leaderboard without spending — a 50,000 $FLOWER deposit is worth 70,000 points, which is more than a hundred days of perfect free play. This guide is about playing the game that's actually winnable: hitting the thresholds that matter, on a routine that costs about two minutes a day.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — The two thresholds
chunks.text:
The two thresholds

Everything between them is a question of which wave you get in, not whether you get in at all.

Rank | What you get |

1 – 10 | 🌩 Storm + a second Genesis Legendary. A paid bracket, realistically |

11 – 50 | 🌩 Storm — the newest and hardest to earn |

51 – 250 | ⬜ Echo |

251 – 500 | 👻 Ghost |

501 – 2,000 | 🌸 Bloom (called Tide until the September docs update) — the widest Legendary band, and the realistic free stretch target |

2,001 – 5,000 | Rare Egg — comfortable on the routine below |

5,001 – 100,000 | Early access, waves 3 – 4. No airdrop |

100,001+ | No early access |

Set your target by how much reach you have. Top 5,000 is where an airdrop starts and is comfortably achievable on the routine below. Top 2,000 now earns a Genesis Legendary — the line moved out from rank 1,000 on 12 August, which makes a Legendary twice as reachable as it was. Referrals are uncapped, so this is not a paid-only bracket.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Do today — about an hour
chunks.text:
Do today — about an hour

Not registered yet? Register free with our code ↗ — it applies YAKKA-UDBVPX, which gets you a Gold Box in game. Referral link; costs you nothing.

These are worth 55 points and they never come round again. More importantly, one of them gates the single best reward on the board.

Get verified. Not optional and not the same as signing up. The mid-September free mint runs on a verified whitelist — an unverified account can't mint no matter how fast you click. Do this first, today, so there's time to fix problems.

Link a wallet — 10 points. You'll need a Ronin wallet for the mint anyway, so this kills two birds.

Connect X — 10 points. Also unlocks the weekly X post quest.

Join the Discord — 10 points.

Post in Discord five times — 5 points each, capped at 25. Do the five, then stop; further posts earn nothing.

Start your nurture streak today. Every day you delay is a day the streak isn't climbing.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Every day — two minutes
chunks.text:
Every day — two minutes

Tap your egg three times. That's the whole routine, and it's the backbone of a free run: about 526 points between now and the free mint.

Do it after 12:00 UTC. The 36-hour grace period only covers a whole missed day if you nurtured in the second half of the UTC day — the reasoning is here.

Streaks pay 6 points a day at the start and 10 a day from day 30. Breaking one drops you back to 6 and costs about 44 points climbing back.

Set a repeating alarm. This single habit outperforms every other free action except referrals and the mint.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Every week — five minutes
chunks.text:
Every week — five minutes

Post on X — 20 points the first time, rising with your posting streak. Over eight weeks that's 160–220 points for about forty minutes of total effort.

Check the weekly board. Weekly rank resets every week and pays a resource box, food box, raffle ticket and loot box. A free player earning 70–100 points in a week is competing against everyone else's weekly total, not their all-time one — which makes weeklies far more winnable than the final ranking.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — The one date that matters: the mid-September mint
chunks.text:
The one date that matters: the mid-September mint

Update, 2 September 2026 — the mint changed shape. The official free mint page now gives a date and a structure: 14 September on the Ronin Launchpad, in five waves gated by your leaderboard rank at a 10 September snapshot — top 1,000 guaranteed, then ranks 1–10,000 (with 5 $FLOWER deposited), a Ronin-gamers wave, ranks 1–20,000 (with 5 $FLOWER), and ranks 1–50,000 for whatever is left. Outside Wave 1 it is fastest-click, one NFT per wave per account, and 68 Legendaries are hidden in the 10,000. The verification-only whitelist described below is the old plan — verification is still required, but rank and speed now decide your wave. The 250 points for minting still stand. Reveal is 14 October. The step-by-step mint guide → · The full wave table →

Updated 14 August. The official docs moved the free mint from October 1st to mid-September. The point totals below were built around an October 1st date, so treat them as upper bounds — you have roughly two fewer weeks of daily nurture before the mint. The full revised schedule →

250 points for one click. The free mint is the best value on the entire board — more than three referrals, or half of everything else a free player earns in two months. You pay only the Ronin network fee, a few cents. If you do exactly one thing from this guide, do this. You must be verified beforehand.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Referrals are the whole free game — with an asterisk now
chunks.text:
Referrals are the whole free game — with an asterisk now

Updated 14 August: referrals past your fifth are no longer free. They now pay 75 points instead of 30, but from the sixth onward the friend must link a wallet and deposit 100 $FLOWER of their own. The numbers below assume you can find people willing to do that. A strictly free player — no money, and friends with no money — tops out at the first five referrals, so around 1,365 points by the mint window rather than 2,490. What changed and who it hits →

This is the part most free players underrate. Every other free action is capped by the calendar — you can't nurture twice a day or post twice a week. Referrals aren't capped at all. At 75 points each they scale as far as your reach does: about 66 valid referrals is worth the same as a 5,000 $FLOWER deposit. But they are no longer a free lever past your fifth — see the warning below.

Your first five referrals are instant and stay genuinely free — they pay the moment your friend signs up. From the sixth onward your friend must link a wallet and deposit 100 $FLOWER of their own before the points land. Linking Discord and X no longer counts, because bot accounts were clearing that bar in bulk. The rule change →

Here's what a realistic run to the mint actually looks like, with 50 referrals:

WHERE 4,741 POINTS COME FROM

REFERRALS ×50 — 79%

Valid referrals (50 × 75) — 3,750

Nurture streak — 526

Free mint — 250

Weekly X posts — 160

One-time quests — 55

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Referrals are the whole free game — with an asterisk now
chunks.text:
Grind every free action perfectly and skip referrals, and you finish on roughly 990.

Referrals are now 79% of this total — but only the first five of them are free. The other 45 each depend on a friend depositing 100 $FLOWER.

Real people only, and past your fifth they have to spend. After your first five, a referral only counts once that friend has linked a wallet and deposited 100 $FLOWER of their own. Referral points stay provisional until a final review. Unverified sign-ups, alt accounts, shared wallets, bots and dormant accounts all get stripped out — and removed referrals are deducted from your total, which can pull your rank down. Serious abuse disqualifies the account — and with a 100 $FLOWER deposit behind every referral past your fifth, faking them now costs real money as well as risk.

chunks.text:
Points per unit of effort

If you only have limited time, spend it top-down:

Action | Points | Effort |

Free mint, mid-Sept | 250 | One click, one window only |

Refer a real person | 75 each | Uncapped · first 5 free, then they deposit 100 $FLOWER |

One-time quests | 55 total | ~10 minutes, once |

Weekly X post | 20+ / week | ~1 minute a week |

Discord posts | 5 each, 25 cap | Stop after five |

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — What to ignore
chunks.text:
What to ignore

Discord posting past the 25-point cap. It pays nothing after five posts.

Chasing the top 100. That band is decided by 50,000-scale deposits — 70,000 points, or roughly 2,300 referrals. The bands below it are genuinely contestable; this one isn't.

Points beyond a band edge. Rank 4,999 and rank 1,500 get identical rewards. Once you're comfortably inside a band, extra points do nothing until the next one.

Raffle tickets as a plan. Nice when they land, but never something to organize your week around.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — Your realistic totals
chunks.text:
Your realistic totals

By | No referrals | 25 valid | 50 valid | 100 valid |

Mint window | ~990 | ~2,865 | ~4,740 | ~8,490 |

Nov 1 | ~1,380 | ~3,255 | ~5,130 | ~8,880 |

These are point totals, not ranks. Nobody outside the team knows what score lands in which band — that depends on how many people play and how hard they push. Treat the table as a measure of your own effort, not a prediction of your finish.

chunks.title: The Free-to-Play Guide to Early Access — The whole guide in six lines
chunks.text:
The whole guide in six lines

Get verified today — the free mint depends on it.

Clear the one-time quests today: 55 points, ten minutes.

Nurture daily, after 12:00 UTC, and never break the streak.

Post on X once a week.

Mint in mid-September. Best value on the board — be verified before it opens.

Refer real people. Uncapped, 60% of your final total, and the only route to a Legendary band without depositing.

chunks.title: What We Now Know About How Yakkamon Actually Plays
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›How Yakkamon Actually Plays

Community
How Yakkamon Actually Plays

Aug 14, 2026

▶ Prefer to watch? Gameplay explained in 4 minutes ↗
Almost everything written about Yakkamon so far — ours included — has been about pre-registration: points, ranks, the airdrop, the mint. Meanwhile a steady drip of official screenshots and dev messages has been filling in something more interesting, which is what you'll actually be doing once the doors open.

Pulled together, it's a good deal more mechanical than the marketing copy suggests. Our Gameplay section has been rebuilt around it, going from seven systems to fourteen, and there's a new full field guide that reads the whole thing top to bottom.

The whole thing on one sheet — tap to open it full size, or read the guide if you're on a phone.

chunks.title: What We Now Know About How Yakkamon Actually Plays — Four mechanics that change how you'd play
chunks.text:
Four mechanics that change how you'd play

1. Type locking. This is the big one. Every resource is gated to a monster type: a Grass type gathers Wood, and a Fire type simply can't — the game refuses, with an in-game message reading "Fire type cannot harvest wood!". The consequence is that your roster caps what you're able to produce at all. Collecting more species isn't a completionist's hobby, it's how you unlock more of the map's materials. Only Grass→Wood has been shown so far; Stone, berries and crops haven't been mapped.

2. Monsters run on stamina, and put themselves to bed. Gathering isn't a passive trickle. You assign a Yakkamon to a resource, the work cycle runs for a set time, it burns stamina, it drops a haul, and it repeats automatically. When stamina runs out the monster sleeps, recovers, and starts again by itself. So "idle" here means genuinely unattended — but it also means output is bounded by stamina rather than by how long you leave the game open.

3. Storage bins fill offline, then stop. Gathered resources don't go to your bag. They stack in a bin that keeps filling while you're away, capped at 20 early and 120 later, showing "MAX" when it's full. Every hour a bin sits at MAX is production you never banked. That quietly makes check-in frequency a real variable — the difference between a farm that runs all night and one that stops at 2am and waits for you.

chunks.title: What We Now Know About How Yakkamon Actually Plays — Four mechanics that change how you'd play
chunks.text:
4. Your monsters have needs. They get hungry, hurt, tired, or ask for a specific item — with status icons above them and a notification feed calling them out by name. There's an item bar of milk, flowers, mushrooms and health items for exactly this. Since a monster in a bad state stops producing, upkeep is part of the economy, not flavour.

Put those four together and the shape of the early game is clear enough to plan for: breadth of roster decides what you can gather, stamina decides how fast, bin capacity decides how much you keep, and upkeep decides whether any of it is running when you look away.

chunks.title: What We Now Know About How Yakkamon Actually Plays — Plus the detail from the dev streams
chunks.text:
Plus the detail from the dev streams

Around 50–60 species at launch, with real genetics and base stats underneath. Individual stat rolls vary within a species, so hunting the same creature again for a better roll is a legitimate strategy.

Traits are randomly rolled and define your build. Rare monsters can carry traits that change how they farm, opening approaches ordinary monsters can't run. The team put roll predictability at roughly 80–90%.

Breeding exists, with line degradation but no hard cap, and evolutions are planned.

Day and night run on a sped-up in-game clock, not real time. Worth knowing before anyone plans a schedule around it: no timezone gets a better night shift.

Weather is a separate system from the day/night cycle, with its own indicators in the HUD.

PvP is not in early access. Early access ships gathering, monsters, hunting and basic combat; PvP and advanced breeding come afterwards in chapter releases.

chunks.title: What We Now Know About How Yakkamon Actually Plays — What we've deliberately not done
chunks.text:
What we've deliberately not done

A lot of the numbers circulating come from UI mock-ups rather than tuned builds. The 999,999 currency figures and the level 99 cap are almost certainly filler. We've kept those out of the guide's conclusions and labelled every figure in the quick-reference table with where it came from, so you can weigh a dev statement differently from a screenshot.

We've also kept an honest list of what isn't confirmed. Stat ranges, rarity tiers, work-cycle durations, the full type chart, the levelling curve, the trait list and the battle rules are all unpublished. That list is the reason nobody can build a trustworthy farming calculator or roster planner yet — and it's worth being suspicious of anyone claiming otherwise.

None of this is a substitute for the pre-registration grind. Knowing the mechanics doesn't move your rank, and the leaderboard still finalises one week before early access launch. If you're choosing where to spend the next hour, the schedule matters more than the meta. The tips that actually move rank →

chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide

Event
Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide

Aug 14, 2026

Update, 2 September 2026. Two of the four names below have changed. The official Yakkapedia and airdrop table now run Storm / Echo / Ghost / Bloom: the 251–500 monster this article calls Bloom is now Ghost, and the 501–2,000 monster it calls Tide is now Bloom. The team says the monsters and their boosts are unchanged — the names were swapped to match their types. The utilities are also published now: Storm makes Yakkamon within range work 2× as fast (large AOE), Echo doubles the resources of those within range (small AOE), Ghost keeps those within range at maximum stamina (small AOE), and Bloom regenerates a share of its Max HP every combat turn. Total supplies are 75 / 275 / 400 / 2,000, with 68 of them hidden in the 14 September free mint. The rank bands below are unchanged. The full table →

The founding Legendary monsters have names. Yakkamon has published the four Genesis Legendaries — and with them, the detail that makes the 12 August ladder change finally legible.

To be precise about what the airdrop is: Monster NFTs go to the top 5,000 trainers on points. The top 2,000 of those receive a Genesis Legendary; ranks 2,001–5,000 receive a Rare Egg. It totals 5,010 Monster NFTs across 5,000 trainers, because the top ten receive two.

chunks.title: Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide — The Four Genesis Legendaries — Storm is the one that matters
chunks.text:
Storm is the one that matters

Storm is new, and it sits above everything else. The team describes it as the newest monster in the set and the hardest to earn — the only way to be airdropped one is to finish in the top 50. The top 10 receive Storm and a second Genesis Legendary alongside it.

That’s a meaningful shift. Until now the position was that the Legendaries are equal in power and differ in species and role. Storm is the exception, and it gives the top of the leaderboard a real gradient where ranks 1 and 99 used to receive an identical reward.

chunks.title: Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide — The Four Genesis Legendaries — Twice as many Legendaries
chunks.text:
Twice as many Legendaries

Legendary monsters used to stop at rank 1,000. They now run to rank 2,000. A thousand trainers who were in line for a Rare Egg now receive Tide, a Genesis Legendary. Total Legendary supply went from about 1,000 to about 2,010.

chunks.title: Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide — The Four Genesis Legendaries — Nobody moved down
chunks.text:
Nobody moved down

Echo is the monster that was previously Legendary Egg A, Bloom was Egg B, Tide was Egg C — each with its utility lifted. Storm was added above the ladder rather than pushing anyone down it. Checked band by band, 1,200 ranks improved, 3,800 held their slot, and none moved down.

We got this wrong first time. Our 12 August analysis read "Rare Egg A" at ranks 501–2,000 as a tier below Legendary, and concluded that supply had halved and 500 trainers had lost out. The names show that band receives Tide, a Legendary. The full correction →

Want the deep read? We've broken down every band, the supply maths, your actual odds, and one problem this update makes worse — the full analysis →

chunks.title: Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide — The Four Genesis Legendaries — You have to hold the rank, not just reach it
chunks.text:
You have to hold the rank, not just reach it

One detail in the official write-up deserves more attention than it’s getting. The airdrop settles when the leaderboard locks — and the team’s wording is that you have to earn your rank and hold it until that moment. Once it locks, the airdrop is closed for good.

So a position inside the top 2,000 today is not a position you own. It’s one you’re currently occupying, and others are still climbing.

Late to pre-registration? You are not locked out. The team says so directly: because the leaderboard is points-based, a trainer who signs up today and plays daily can pass someone who signed up on day one and stopped showing up. There is no sale and no buying your way in — every position is earned on points.

chunks.title: Meet Storm, Echo, Bloom and Tide — The Four Genesis Legendaries — What we still don’t know
chunks.text:
What we still don’t know

Update, 14 August. The lock now has a position in the sequence: the official Important Dates page puts it one week before early access launch, with rewards sent three days later and launch itself in November or December. The full schedule →

Monster utilities land in September. What these creatures actually do — battle, farm utility, or something else — is unpublished, and "utility lifted" is the team’s description rather than something anyone can verify yet.

The one number that changed for planning: the Legendary line moved from rank 1,000 to rank 2,000. If you were treating a Legendary as out of reach, it’s twice as reachable as it was.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players
chunks.text:
class="wrap article-head">
Home›News›Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something

Event
Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something — What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players

Sep 5, 2026

The Yakkamon team's guide series has reached hunting. It is eight numbered points long, it is written in the same breezy register as the economy and Regions posts, and it is the first official description of the active half of the game that is about catching rather than fighting. Read it quickly and it says wild monsters have moods. Read it slowly and it says something the idle half never did: every wild Yakkamon has a place, a time and a price, and none of the three is optional.

Here is what the eight points say, what each one does to the way this game has to be played, and what we would do about it before early access opens.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — The eight points, in plain terms
chunks.text:
The eight points, in plain terms

# | What the post says | New? |

1 | Hunting grounds are scattered across your Regions, and each one reveals different Yakkamon at different times of day. Dawn and midnight are different grounds — "learn the clock". | New (spawns are on a timetable) |

2 | You don't hunt alone. You send a Yakkamon out to passively roam a ground and it triggers encounters while you run your farm. | Confirms the stream, in writing |

3 | Some wild Yakkamon are affectionate — they come home only if the Yakkamon you sent wins them over. | New name for the ambient encounter |

4 | Some are greedy. They want resources and will not budge until you have paid — "bring the right goods". | New (a third encounter type, and a resource sink) |

5 | Some are just angry: cross their path and it is a battle. Send a Yakkamon that can't hold its own and you come back empty-handed. | Confirms the aggressive encounter |

6 | Legendaries and Rares appear sporadically in the grounds. No schedule — have "a strong, well-supplied team ready to go the moment one shows up". | New (Legendaries in ordinary grounds) |

7 | Grounds aren't infinite. The more you hunt one, the less populated it becomes — spread hunts across grounds and Regions. | Confirms depletion; adds the spread |

8 | It keeps changing. Future Seasons affect which Yakkamon are available and where, so today's map won't be next Chapter's. | Confirms rotation, and ties it to hunting |

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — The eight points, in plain terms
chunks.text: Points 2, 5 and 7 put in writing what the free-mint stream said out loud — hunting is a job, aggressive monsters fight, grounds run dry. Points 1, 3, 4, 6 and 8 are where the new information is, and they are worth taking one at a time.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 1: the ground has a timetable, and it isn't your clock
chunks.text:
Point 1: the ground has a timetable, and it isn't your clock

"What roams a ground at dawn won't be what you find there at midnight." That is a spawn table keyed to time of day, which means the same hunting tile is effectively several different grounds depending on when you use it. So far, so Pokémon. The twist is one the site has been carrying since the first dev stream: day and night in Yakkamon run on a sped-up in-game clock, not real time. The team said so on 6 August precisely so that no timezone gets a better night shift.

Put those two facts together and "learn the clock" means something more demanding than "log in at night". The in-game day turns over while you are watching, so a ground's population rotates within a session, and a roaming Yakkamon (point 2) will cross several time bands during one long hunt. Two things follow:

Timing a hunt is about the in-game hour, not yours. The clock in the HUD corner is the one to read. Nobody has published how long an in-game day lasts in real minutes, and until they do, every "hunt at 3am" tip you see is either about the wrong clock or a guess.

The timetable is knowledge you can accumulate. A player who writes down which species turned up on which ground at which in-game hour is building something the game does not hand you. The post says as much — "studying the grounds, learning the clock" is described as the skill, which strongly implies the game will not simply show you the table.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 2: the hunter is a worker you have taken off the line
chunks.text:
Point 2: the hunter is a worker you have taken off the line

Sending a Yakkamon out to passively roam "while you get on with running your farm" is the stream's hunting-as-a-job model, now official. It sounds like free value — the farm keeps going, the hunt happens on the side. It isn't quite. The Yakkamon on the hunt is a Yakkamon not on a job, and on the published rules every monster's value on the farm is set by type locking: a Grass type gathering Wood is production; the same Grass type roaming a ground is a bet.

That makes hunting an opportunity cost, and the post immediately makes it worse for anyone hoping to use their weakest monster as the scout. Point 3 says affectionate monsters only come home if your hunter wins them over; point 5 says an angry one sends a weak hunter home empty-handed; point 6 says a Legendary needs "a strong, well-supplied team". In other words, the quality of the hunter decides the outcome, and the monster you can most afford to take off production is the one least likely to bring anything back. The right way to think about a hunter is not "a spare" but a specialist — a role in its own right, sized against what it costs you in gathered output while it is away.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Points 3, 4 and 5: three temperaments, three currencies
chunks.text:
Points 3, 4 and 5: three temperaments, three currencies

The stream gave us two kinds of wild monster: aggressive ones that raise a red alert, and ambient ones you coax with bait and a short emoji conversation. The post keeps both, renames the second affectionate, and adds a third. Between them they describe three different things a hunt can cost you:

Temperament | What it wants | What decides it | What it costs you |

Affectionate | To be won over | The Yakkamon you sent — whatever "wins them over" turns out to depend on | The right hunter, and a bait if the stream's courtship mechanic survives |

Greedy | Resources — "the right goods" | Whether you brought what it asks for | Gathered or crafted goods, paid out of your stock |

Angry | A fight | Whether your hunter can hold its own | A strong enough hunter; possibly its condition afterwards |

Three points stand out.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Points 3, 4 and 5: three temperaments, three currencies
chunks.text:
Greedy monsters are a resource sink, and the free layer needed one. The economy post split the game into an easily gathered free layer and an effort-gated tradeable one, and the free-mint stream said the free layer's output is unlimited but untradable. That left an obvious question: what is all that untradable wood and berry for, once your bins are full and your tiles are bought? The Hunting post answers part of it. A greedy Yakkamon "won't budge until you've paid up", and the payment comes out of exactly the pile the economy post said you could not sell. Hunting is where surplus gathered goods turn into monsters — which, unlike the goods, can be worth something. If "the right goods" sometimes means a crafted item rather than raw wood, then the crafting system the team keeps deferring is the tollgate on the best catches, and the gap between a player with a stocked workshop and one without gets wider still.

"Wins them over" is doing a lot of unspecified work. The post does not say what an affectionate monster judges you on. Type? Level? A hidden stat? The species you sent? The stream's version had you sending a hunter across with bait and watching a little conversation play out, and Spencer called it "super cute" and still in flux. Until the rule is published, the honest reading is that affectionate catches reward having a variety of hunters to choose from, because you cannot know in advance which one the wild monster will like.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Points 3, 4 and 5: three temperaments, three currencies
chunks.text: Angry monsters are a strength check, not a coin flip. "Send a Yakkamon that can't hold its own and you'll come back empty-handed" describes a threshold. It also tells you what the downside is — empty hands, not a lost monster. The post says nothing about injury, and the care system already has a "hurt" state, so we would not assume a lost fight is free. But nothing published says a hunter can die, and that matters for how boldly you can send one out.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 6: Legendaries walk into ordinary grounds, and there is no bell
chunks.text:
Point 6: Legendaries walk into ordinary grounds, and there is no bell

This is the line to read twice. Until now the site's understanding — from the streams — was that rares can appear in any hunt while Legendaries "lean more on events, conditions and tournaments". The post says plainly that Legendaries and Rares will sporadically appear in the hunting grounds, with no schedule to memorise. That is a bigger claim than the stream made and we are updating the gameplay pages to match it.

Read it against the economy post's rule that Legendaries and rares "drop in limited supplies or windows" and become tradeable only once availability ends, and against the Important Dates page, which puts the first NFT hunt and the first Legendaries batch in Chapter 0, a month after early access. The picture that emerges is that the supply of post-Genesis Legendaries is released into the wild through the hunting grounds, unannounced, in limited quantity. That has two consequences.

Readiness beats reaction. "A strong, well-supplied team ready to go the moment one shows up" is the team telling you that the players who catch Legendaries will be the ones who had the fighter and the goods sitting idle when the sighting came, not the ones who scrambled. A Legendary that is angry needs a hunter that can hold its own; one that is greedy needs a stockpile you have not spent. "Well-supplied" suggests it may want both.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 6: Legendaries walk into ordinary grounds, and there is no bell
chunks.text:
It rewards being present. There is no schedule and no bell. Between the in-game clock (point 1) and sporadic Legendary spawns (point 6), a hunting ground rewards being looked at often. The free-mint stream was firm that being away pauses your farm rather than punishing it — and that is still true — but a paused farm is also a farm that missed the Legendary that walked through while you were gone.

One thing the post does not say, and nobody should read into it: how many. "Sporadically" is not a rate. The only Legendary numbers that exist are the Genesis supplies in the Yakkapedia — and those leave a remainder once the airdrop, the free mint and the raffle are taken out: 21 Storm, 66 Echo, 133 Ghost and 449 Bloom. Nothing says whether wild spawns draw on that remainder, on the Chapter 0 batches, or on a pool of their own.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 7: depletion is now a reason to own more than one ground
chunks.text:
Point 7: depletion is now a reason to own more than one ground

The stream told us grounds deplete and monsters don't. The post adds the strategic half: "spreading your hunts across grounds and Regions is part of the strategy". The word "Regions" connects this directly to last week's post, and the connection is expensive.

On the Regions post, a hunting area is a tile — land you claim with gathered resources, in competition with tiles you would otherwise spend on production or build space. If the fix for a depleted ground is another ground, then hunting has a land cost as well as a time and resource cost: every additional hunting tile is a production tile you did not claim. And if the fix is another Region, you are back in the bootstrapping problem from last week — a Region you have to earn your way into with the Region before it, and whose own hunting grounds are the only place its type lives.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 7: depletion is now a reason to own more than one ground
chunks.text: The post also quietly settles a question the Regions article left open. The stream spoke of "hunting regions you explore"; the Regions post put hunting areas on tiles inside your own Region. If grounds are yours — tiles on your land — then depletion is self-inflicted. There is no other trainer hunting your ground out from under you. Your ground empties at the rate you hunt it and refills at a rate nobody has published. That is a pacing mechanic aimed at you alone, and it means the early-game trap is obvious: one ground, hunted hard on day one, is a ground that gives you nothing on day three. We flag the alternative too: if some grounds turn out to be shared instances, everything above becomes a race instead, and the "spread across Regions" advice is about getting to grounds other players cannot reach yet.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Point 8: the map expires, and that is the supply window
chunks.text:
Point 8: the map expires, and that is the supply window

"The hunting map you master today won't be the one you're working next Chapter." Seasons will change which Yakkamon are available and where. The site has carried the seasonal system since the docs went up — a three-month cadence, with a weekly cadence under consideration — and this is the first time the team has tied rotation explicitly to hunting rather than to new monster drops.

Line it up with the economy post one more time. Legendaries and rares "become tradeable only once availability ends". The Hunting post is what "availability" looks like from inside the game: a species is on the map this Season and off it the next. The Season rotation is the mechanism that closes a supply window, and the moment it closes is the moment the monsters caught during it become the only ones there will be until they come back — if they come back. For anyone thinking about the tradeable layer, that reframes hunting from "filling your roster" to "buying inventory before the shop shuts".

It also means knowledge depreciates. The timetable you learn under point 1 is good for one Season. That is fine — it is the same for everyone — but it argues for treating hunting knowledge as something to share fast rather than hoard, because it is worth the most in the first week of a Season and nothing after.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — What this does to the advice already on this site
chunks.text:
What this does to the advice already on this site

Breadth beats depth gets a second leg. The Game That Starts the Next Morning argued that type locking makes roster breadth, not roster quality, the cap on production. The Hunting post says the hunter's quality decides the catch, and that affectionate monsters judge the specific Yakkamon you sent. Breadth now buys you two things: coverage of the type chart on the farm, and a wider choice of hunter to match whatever the ground offers. The one-Legendary roster is a worse plan than it was.

Your storage bin is your ceiling, unless you spend it. The same article said that past a point, more production only fills the bin faster. Greedy monsters are a sink that the bin can be emptied into. A full bin was waste; now it is a hunting purse. That changes the calculation on bin upgrades slightly — capacity is worth more if there is something to spend it on — and it changes what to do with a surplus entirely.

Absence pauses, but it still costs. The site corrected itself on 2 September when the stream said an unattended farm does not decay. Nothing here reverses that. But points 1 and 6 make the cost of absence an opportunity cost rather than a penalty: the in-game clock keeps turning, and the Legendary does not wait.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — What this does to the advice already on this site
chunks.text: Legendaries are hunted, not only gifted. Our gameplay pages said rares appear in any hunt and Legendaries lean on events. The post puts both in the grounds. We have updated the Crafting & Hunting system, the field guide and the FAQ to say so, sourced to this post.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — How to get an edge
chunks.text:
How to get an edge

None of the numbers exist yet — not the in-game day length, not the regeneration rate, not the price list a greedy monster works from, not what "wins them over" means. What does exist is the shape, and the shape is enough to plan around.

Keep a hunting log from your first hunt. Ground, in-game hour, what appeared, what it wanted. The post says the skill is "studying the grounds, learning the clock", which is a strong hint the game will not show you the table. A player with a table in week one is ahead of one who hunts on instinct, and it costs nothing but attention.

Build a hunting squad, not a spare. At minimum: one Yakkamon that can win a fight and one that is likely to be liked, plus whatever the type of the ground favours. Size the squad against what those monsters would have gathered if they had stayed on the farm — that is the real price of every hunt.

Hold a hunting purse. Set aside a stock of varied goods that you do not spend on tiles or crafting — the "right goods" for a greedy monster, and the supplies a Legendary is said to need. A full bin you never dip into is exactly what point 6 is asking for.

Claim a second ground before the first one runs dry. Depletion is real and the regeneration rate is unknown. Two grounds hunted lightly beat one ground hunted out. Budget the tile for it before you spend everything on plots.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — How to get an edge
chunks.text:
Catch broad early, especially anything that looks seasonal. Point 8 says the map rotates. A species that leaves the map is a species you cannot catch again until it returns, and on the economy post's rules it is the moment it becomes tradeable. Surplus of a rotating species is inventory; surplus of an evergreen one is just a crowded farm.

Treat contract hunts as the coin faucet they are. The stream said contract hunts pay in coins, and coins are what gate the tradeable layer. A well-supplied hunting squad is also the machine that turns free-layer time into tradeable output. Nothing in the post changes that; it just makes the squad worth more.

Check the grounds more often than you check the farm. The farm pauses politely. The grounds don't. If you have one login a day to spend, spend it looking at the ground, not the bin.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Recommendations by where you are
chunks.text:
Recommendations by where you are

If you are… | What the Hunting post means for you | Do this |

Wave 1 with a Genesis Legendary | Your Legendary is one type and one monster. It may be a superb angry-monster hunter or useless against an affectionate one that wants something else. The aura utilities (Storm's 2× work speed, Echo's double resources) are farm utilities as published — nothing says they touch hunting. | Use the Legendary as the fighter of the squad, not the whole squad. Fill the rest with breadth from ordinary hunts before the first Season turns. |

Wave 2–3, a week or two behind | Grounds are (probably) yours, so nobody has hunted them out before you arrive — your map is as fresh as theirs was. Your handicap is the Season clock, not the queue. | Borrow the timetable. The players ahead of you will have a week of sightings; the log is the thing to ask for, and the thing this site will publish when we have it. |

Free-to-play | Hunting is the free layer's best use. Gathered goods you cannot sell buy greedy monsters; monsters, unlike goods, can be worth something; contract hunts pay the coins that open the tradeable layer. | Point your surplus at the grounds rather than letting the bin cap it. Hunting is the one activity where a free player's time converts into something with a market. |

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — Recommendations by where you are
chunks.text: Thinking about the market | Season rotation closes supply windows. Legendaries and rares appear in the wild sporadically and in limited supply. The catches made in a Season are that Season's float. | Catch for the window, not for the farm. Know which species are on the map now and are likely to leave, and hold them through the rotation. |

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — What's genuinely good here
chunks.text:
What's genuinely good here

Hunting has more than one answer. Three temperaments mean a strength check, a charm check and a resource check can all be the right tool for a different monster. That is a real design, not a capture button.

The free layer finally has a sink that matters. Greedy monsters give untradable goods something to buy. That was the missing piece in the two-track economy.

Knowledge is a resource. A timetable you have to learn, and a map that rotates, reward the player who pays attention over the player who pays. That is the right thing to reward in a game with a free layer.

Legendaries can be earned in play. Not only airdropped, not only minted, not only auctioned. Sporadic wild Legendaries are the first published path to one that starts with a hunt.

Depletion pushes you outward. Spreading hunts across Regions gives the Regions system a reason to exist beyond bigger farms.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — What to be wary of
chunks.text:
What to be wary of

Every rate is unpublished. Day length, regeneration, spawn odds, the price a greedy monster asks, and what "wins them over" means. The post describes a system with no numbers in it, and the numbers are the game.

Attention is now rewarded on the grounds as well as the farm. No schedule for Legendaries plus an in-game clock that rotates the ground means the player who looks most often sees most. The team has said the farm is not punitive about absence; the grounds may quietly be.

Hunting competes with everything. The hunter is off the line, the goods are out of the bin, and the ground is a tile that could have been a plot. A poorly judged hunt loses on three fronts at once.

"Greedy" may mean crafted. If "the right goods" turns out to be a specific crafted item rather than raw resources, the deferred crafting system becomes the gate on the best catches, and the team has been candid that crafting is still being built.

Per-player or shared is still not stated. Our reading that grounds are your own tiles rests on the Regions post. If any ground is shared, depletion becomes a race and the advice above changes.

chunks.title: Every Wild Yakkamon Wants Something: What the Official Hunting Post Means for Players — The six questions we'd put to the team
chunks.text:
The six questions we'd put to the team

Is a wild Yakkamon's temperament visible before you commit a hunter, or only once the encounter starts?

What does an affectionate Yakkamon judge — the hunter's type, level, species, a stat, or a bait?

Can a hunter be hurt by losing to an angry monster, and does that use the care system's "hurt" state?

Is a hunting ground your own tile, or can other trainers hunt the same ground?

How long is an in-game day in real minutes, and does a roaming hunter cross time bands during one hunt?

Do wild Legendaries come from the same limited supply as the Chapter 0 batches, or from a separate pool?

The fourth and the sixth are the ones that decide whether hunting is a pacing mechanic or a competition, and whether a wild Legendary is a lottery ticket or a market event.

Source and standing. This is our reading of an official Yakkamon guide on hunting, published on the team's own channels. The eight points are summarised in our words; the temperament table, the per-player-ground reading and every recommendation are ours, are marked as such, and are not endorsed by anyone. If the team publishes rates, we will put them on this page.
